title: What to know about Falcons – Buccaneers in Week 8
summary: It’s back to the division for the Falcons, who play the Tampa Bay Buccaneers for the first time in 2026. They’ve lost to the Panthers and beaten the Saints already, but a win here gets Atlanta to 4-4 and puts the hapless Bucs down at 2-6, a hole that will be tough for them to […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - DECEMBER 11: Bijan Robinson #7 of the Atlanta Falcons runs with the ball during the first half against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Raymond James Stadium on December 11, 2025 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Julio Aguilar/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s back to the division for the Falcons, who play the Tampa Bay Buccaneers for the first time in 2026. They’ve lost to the Panthers and beaten the Saints already, but a win here gets Atlanta to 4-4 and puts the hapless Bucs down at 2-6, a hole that will be tough for them to climb out of even in the dismal NFC South. That would be a good time. The question is whether the Falcons will. The Bucs have been finding their footing a bit, with two wins and one overtime loss in the last three weeks against the Cowboys, Steelers, and Panthers. The Tampa Bay defense is rounding into form as an aggressive, problem-causing unit, dragging a poor offense behind them. If Tampa can force multiple turnovers and get the ground game going, they have a genuine shot in this one. If not, the Falcons could give us a very fun afternoon. Here’s what you need to know about the game ahead. Team rankings Team Record Points Scored Yardage Passing Yards Rushing Yards Points Against Yardage Against Passing Yards Against Rushing Yardage Against Turnovers Created Turnovers Surrendered Falcons 3-4 10 17 23 6 20 19 29 4 14 27 Buccaneers 2-5 17 26 32 3 14 3 14 2 3 23 On paper, the Buccaneers are not really that much worse than Atlanta. Their passing game is abysmal, but the defense has been good and improving quickly, they run the ball well, and they’ve forced plenty of turnovers. I wouldn’t say Tampa Bay is good, but if they can drag their passing game up to passable, they’ll probably hang around in the division. Atlanta, meanwhile, is better than its numbers but also inconsistent enough that those numbers can seem like a true reflection of where they’re at. The passing game is league average at worst, the ground game is effective, and the defense has been solid much of the season. It’s just about finding a way to string together quality performances of the caliber they managed against Green Bay, New Orleans, and San Francisco. How the Bucs have changed in 2026 A fateful decision this offseason was the hiring of Zac Robinson to run the offense after he flamed out in Atlanta. Robinson knows how to put together a compelling run game and has gotten a lot out of Bucky Irving and Kenneth Gainwell, but the passing attack has utterly cratered with Baker Mayfield, injured Baker Mayfield, and rookie Jalon Daniels. You can’t put all of their failures on Robinson, but our criticisms of his passing attacks are carrying over to Tampa Bay. The Bucs went shopping for Alex Anzalone at linebacker, A’Shawn Robinson for their defensive line, Al-Quadin Muhammad off the edge, and…well, not much else. It was a fairly quiet offseason with an emphasis on defense, which was a little striking after they lost Mike Evans. They also invested their first two picks in the defense, adding linebacker Josiah Trotter and edge Rueben Bain Jr., with promising receiver Ted Hurst their only major addition on offense. This was a team that believed it had outsized defensive needs but a stable offense; that’s not how things have really worked out. Critically, Tampa Bay also caved and gave Baker Mayfield a contract extension just in time for him to turn into a pumpkin. Mayfield’s numbers were still quite solid but took a nosedive in 2025, and now he’s been either injured or a shadow of himself. You hate to see it*. *I do not, in fact, hate to see it. What to know about Week 8 This is a classic letdown matchup that the Falcons must be cautious of. You have a divisional rival that has struggled to this point, but divisional matchups are always a little crazy. The Falcons are riding high after knocking off the undefeated 49ers, but so is Tampa Bay, which dominated Carolina despite a complete lack of a functional passing attack. That should make Atlanta wary and likely will. We’ll start with the obvious caveat: The Buccaneers have not been able to pass in 2026. Mayfield has started four games and has labored in nearly all of them, throwing for just three touchdowns and two interceptions, absorbing 13 sacks, and playing poorly under pressure, with a measly 4.6 yards per attempt average when the heat is close by. Last week in his return from injury, he threw the ball just 11 times for 64 yards, and his mobility seems to be limited as he’s recovering. There’s talent here—Emeka Egbuka, Chris Godwin, and Cade Otten among them—but Otten’s been quiet, Egbuka has not quite emerged as a difference-making talent, and Godwin is now 30 and has slowed somewhat. Mike Evans is gone, and predictably, the loss of a future Hall of Famer and ageless wonder has indeed slowed this group. Even if Mayfield and company bounce back somewhat, this is a more pedestrian group than many of the offenses Atlanta has faced. The bigger danger is on the ground, where Bucky Irving and (to a much lesser extent) Kenneth Gainwell have been superb. Irving is a dangerous, slashing runner who is thriving in Robinson’s scheme, and the Falcons have struggled in two of the past three weeks to contain capable runners in Christian McCaffrey and Derrick Henry. They’ll want to make the Bucs one dimensional by getting an early lead and shutting down Irving in the first two quarters, but that’s easier said than done. Presuming there are no colossal screwups from a defense that largely impressed against a much better team, the Falcons should be able to hold the Bucs to 20 or fewer points. The question concerns whether their offense will be up to the task of overcoming a Bucs defense that very quietly has only allowed more than 17 points once in the past month, has held opposing passing games under 250 yards in all but one game, and has only allowed one team to rush for more than 100 yards against them. Most concerning is the habit of creating turnovers, as the Bucs have eight in their past three games and an ability to create pressure, something Michael Penix Jr. has struggled with more than just about any other quarterback in the NFL. Compounding the problem is the fact that Bijan has consistently struggled to get going against the Bucs run defense, with his career high of 93 yards against them coming late last year and no other games above 63 yards. The Falcons survived a pedestrian day from Bijan (by his lofty standards, at least) against the 49ers, but if the Bucs can get that done again and impact Penix, it could be a long afternoon for this offense. The formula is simple enough: Force Mayfield to beat you by bottling up Irving, keep Penix clean and in rhythm, and don’t become one-dimensional. This is a very winnable game against a diminished team, but the Falcons have stumbled many times in the recent past coming off a big win against an inferior opponent. It’s time to buck the trend.
author: Dave Choate

title: Methodical Falcons deliver a new winning recipe
summary: One of the most common descriptions of the Falcons’ offense is explosive. It’s a unit with playmakers, headlined by arguably the NFL’s best running back and one of the NFL’s most physically imposing wide receivers. Bijan Robinson and Drake London have proven they can take over games. With Kyle Pitts always capable of breaking out […]
full_text: One of the most common descriptions of the Falcons’ offense is explosive . It’s a unit with playmakers, headlined by arguably the NFL’s best running back and one of the NFL’s most physically imposing wide receivers. Bijan Robinson and Drake London have proven they can take over games. With Kyle Pitts always capable of breaking out a monster performance, Jahan Dotson’s knack for stretching the field, and Zachariah Branch’s potential, expectations are understandably high for Kevin Stefanski and Tommy Rees. Top offenses can’t be reliant on explosive plays every week. Long drives will be required to put points on the board. Not getting bored of taking yards underneath can be necessary to thrive, especially with a young quarterback coming off multiple frustrating performances. Mixing in heavier personnel sets and getting the ball out faster to shore up pass-protection woes is another part of how a methodical offense can operate. The Falcons produced four consecutive drives of ten plays or more in an impressive upset win over San Francisco. Three of those drives ended in passing touchdowns to three different players. Michael Penix Jr. was assured in his progressions. He made sharp decisions across the short and intermediate areas. With better pass protection and designed high-percentage looks, the enigmatic quarterback bounced back nicely. Per Pro Football Focus, Penix Jr. completed 24 of 31 passes for 194 yards and three touchdowns when not faced with pressure. As the 49ers stifled Bijan Robinson on the ground, the onus was on the passing game to deliver against the coach who first believed in Penix Jr., Raheem Morris. They did exactly that in an unglamorous, yet highly efficient manner. Calm and patient It’s hard to say whether the Falcons were caught off guard by Morris opting not to blitz. Given how successful Baltimore and Chicago were at bringing extra rushers to rattle Penix Jr., it felt inevitable that San Francisco would ramp up the pressure. That never came to fruition, as Morris used primarily his signature Cover 3 looks to take away the deep area of the field. It largely consisted of taking away the vertical opportunities and forcing Penix Jr. to take what the defense allowed him underneath. The former top ten pick happily did that. By using a wider variety of heavy formations, Stefanski and Rees created high-percentage looks on early downs to keep drives moving. Role players made valuable contributions on a few of those passes, as Charlie Woerner and Khalil Herbert caught passes underneath to put the offense in striking distance. That’s where Penix found Nick Muse on a classic goal-to-go leak play for his first passing touchdown. The personnel usage was notable on the score. Backup offensive linemen Kyle Hinton and Corey Levin lined up overloaded on the right. Muse lined up alongside Jake Matthews on the left. Using a variety of skill-position players as the lead fullback has become a staple of the offense. Woerner was the player on this occasion, which was sensible given his blocking capabilities. With no Pitts or Austin Hooper on the field, all signs pointed to Robinson running the ball behind the jumbo package in for the touchdown. Instead, Penix Jr. sold the play-fake well and lofted the ball to a wide-open Muse into the end zone. Although the next drive didn’t end in a touchdown after 14 plays and 56 yards, the Falcons were finding a rhythm through the air. They needed it after the previous two games, where the dropback passing game looked disjointed for long stretches. London and Branch caught passes for solid gains on 1st down, putting the offense in more favorable positions. The offense faced far too many third-and-longs against Baltimore and Chicago. Quick completions on early downs helped the offense manufacture long drives. With the running game largely ineffective, those early down gains through the air were needed to pull off a massive win. That’s what pushed them to turn the coaching staff’s vision into successful game-day execution. Slicing and dicing toward deep shots When a scoring drive features London and Pitts making multiple catches, it usually involves explosive highlight-reel plays. On a ten-play, 59-yard drive that resulted in a Pitts touchdown, the two star pass catchers combined for five receptions for 38 yards. That stat strongly indicates how the Falcons were going to win off efficiency rather than being prolific. Pitts was used largely on short outs and hitches, while London won on slants and choice routes. Both players produced solid gains on screens, which mattered given how much the team has struggled to execute them in recent weeks. What made the difference on the second touchdown drive came on a third-and-seven. London ran a well-timed choice route where Penix Jr. hit him in stride to convert. That set the tone for the Falcons to take the lead. The drive ended with play action, with Penix Jr. rolling to his left as Pitts ran a crosser to the same side. The play misdirection gave the dynamic tight end the leverage he needed to catch his fourth touchdown pass in three games. The coaching staff mixing in 12, 13, and 22 personnel gave the 49ers fits. Their defense got baited into fakes and often allowed easy completions. After Jessie Bates delivered another second-half turnover, the Falcons were in prime position to take a two-possession lead. This is where the aggression turned up. Penix Jr. attempted multiple passes past 20 yards following three quarters of being limited to short and intermediate passes. Jahan Dotson ran a clever out-and-up on Jack Jones, forcing the cornerback to panic downfield. The excessive contact led to a defensive pass interference call on 3rd and 8. Facing fewer two-high looks, Penix Jr. pushed the ball downfield. A quarterback with his arm and confidence will always try to stretch defenses and exploit mismatches. That’s where he found his favorite receiver downfield inside for his third touchdown pass. Running alongside Dotson on a two-vertical route concept, London found space over the top to get in the end zone, with Renardo Green unable to make a play at the catch point. While it looks like a routine touchdown, Penix Jr. does a fantastic job looking right at Pitts down the seam to get the deep safety moving toward that direction. That quick nod gives him the space needed to hit London over the top for the beloved wide receiver’s first touchdown of the season. Those nuances are needed for a young quarterback to be productive in the pocket, especially when his athletic limitations prevent him from making out-of-structure plays. Gradual progression As frustrating as it is to be unable to attack downfield, that frustration quickly fades when your team comes out victorious. Winning in a gritty way shows maturation, as the offense’s biggest gain came on the 21-yard touchdown pass to London. Coaches must be adaptable with game planning. Quarterbacks must be able to alter their approach for certain matchups. That’s been one of many changes for Penix Jr. in a new offensive system, where his air yards per target has dropped from 8.4 in 2024-2025 to 7.0 in 2026. That low total can be attributed to certain matchups, but the schematic changes were bound to reduce his air-yards-per-target average. By operating more under center with more multiple tight end sets, there will be fewer throws past 15 yards. The days of running 11 personnel in shotgun or pistol on 75% of plays are long gone. This regime uses more variation, disguises, intentional motions, and structured quick game. That has allowed Penix Jr. to grow as a quarterback. It’s made the offense more dangerous overall, proving they can find the winning formula without relying on the running game to take over or three to four explosive passing plays producing scoring drives. Being methodical can go a long way in pulling off more upsets with daunting matchups against Cincinnati and Kansas City on the horizon.

summary: The Baltimore Ravens upgraded seven players on their Thursday injury report, including returns to practice from Kyle Hamilton, Vega Ioane, and Roquan Smith after absences on Wednesday. Safety Jaylinn Hawkins was the only player on the active roster to miss practice entirely. Ioane is expected to miss time due to an MCL sprain, but the […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OH - OCTOBER 18: Baltimore Ravens guard Olaivavega Ioane (71) on the field during the second quarter of the National Football League game between the Baltimore Ravens and Cleveland Browns on October 18, 2026, at Huntington Bank Field in Cleveland, OH. (Photo by Frank Jansky/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens upgraded seven players on their Thursday injury report, including returns to practice from Kyle Hamilton, Vega Ioane, and Roquan Smith after absences on Wednesday. Safety Jaylinn Hawkins was the only player on the active roster to miss practice entirely. Ioane is expected to miss time due to an MCL sprain, but the first-round pick is pushing to play through the injury and take the field against the Buffalo Bills on Sunday, per CBS Sports’ Matt Zenitz . Even while injured, there is a steep drop-off in play to backups Andrew Vorhees and Emery Jones, and line play has been the offense’s kryponite this year. However, this may be a case when the Ravens have to protect a young player from himself, as they have in the past with Hamilton. Both are physical, full-effort players who will give their all whenever they are on the field. Hamilton in particular has spoken about being willing to sacrifice for those he cares about. But short-term injuries can quickly turn into long-term ones, especially when the injured players in question are banging heads in the trenches. Hamilton was able to play the full game in Week 7, so his knee appears to be in better shape. Progressing to full participation on Friday would likely mean he is playing in Buffalo, but that may not be the case for Ioane, especially with a short week ahead of next Thursday’s matchup with the Jacksonville Jaguars. Less is known about Smith’s injury, which looked concerning initially but only sidelined him for one practice. Zenitz also reported on Thursday morning that Lamar Jackson is “on track” to return from his three-game absence. The 29-year-old quarterback was a full participant for a second day in a row; a repeat on Friday would set him up to play against the Bills, but the quick turnaround before Week 8 could be a factor as it was last year. Here is the Ravens’ full Thursday injury report ( * denotes change in status): Full participation TE Mark Andrews (hand) DL Calais Campbell (rest) * OLB Trey Hendrickson (finger) TE Matthew Hibner (hand) QB Lamar Jackson (full) NT John Jenkins (knee) * RB Adam Randall (neck, designated to return from IR) LT Ronnie Stanley (rest/toe/ankle) * CB T.J. Tampa (knee, designated to return from IR) * DT Broderick Washington (ankle) * Limited participation S Kyle Hamilton (knee) * RG Vega Ioane (knee) * LG John Simpson (groin) LB Roquan Smith (knee) * Did not participate S Jaylinn Hawkins (knee) The rest of the squad is in relatively good shape heading into Sunday. Hawkins will likely miss a second game in a row, but Simpson has been playing with limited practice participation for weeks. The Ravens could slowplay the returns of Tampa and Randall from injured reserve, but both could fortify key areas of the team. The former still has another week to practice before he must be activated, while the latter was only designated to return this week. Comparatively, the Bills had a worse Thursday, downgrading three players. Linebacker Joe Andreessen (knee, limited) and running back Ray Davis (illness, DNP) were both added to the Week 8 injury report, while cornerback Dee Alford (knee) went from limited to DNP. Right tackle Spencer Brown (back) was sidelined for a second day in a row, putting him at real risk of missing Sunday’s game.

title: Buffalo Bills reportedly “looking for another piece or two” per NFL insider
summary: No trades for the Buffalo Bills… yet. But that could change soon. And, sure, Bills fan probably want more than the “check-in” at this stage, but according to the Albert Breer, in his Trade Deadline Notes piece for Sports Illustrated, “the Bills are looking for another piece or two on defense.” And that’s really all […]
full_text: No trades for the Buffalo Bills… yet. But that could change soon. And, sure, Bills fan probably want more than the “check-in” at this stage, but according to the Albert Breer, in his Trade Deadline Notes piece for Sports Illustrated, “the Bills are looking for another piece or two on defense.” And that’s really all Breer mentioned on the Bills. No expanding on that sentence or follow-up later in the piece. It was part of his “Other Buyers” subheading, and here’s that whole section: “As for the buyers, the Chiefs and Steelers have asked around on receivers. The Giants and Jaguars are sniffing around on defensive tackles—Jacksonville’s looking for pieces for its defensive front in general. The Vikings have asked around on interior offensive and defensive linemen, and running backs. The Bills are looking for another piece or two on defense. And the Browns, suddenly thrust into the “buyer” category, are checking out options for another designated pass-rusher and a blocking tight end.” While I’m essentially always down for a receiver add, that seems highly unlikely at this point for Buffalo. After all, the Bills are first — or near the top — in many offensive metrics entering Week 8. The aerial attack, even with DJ Moore only on the field for 33.9% of the offensive snaps through six games, has largely been fine. As we all know, the defense has struggled and now C.J. Gardner-Johnson has stacked a one-game suspension on top of inconsistent tackling. Defensive back or linebacker feel like positions Buffalo could be targeting. Also, in the past two games, Buffalo’s pass rush, that was sensational in the first month of the season, did not make much of an impact. Defensive line and outside linebacker are possibilities too. The NFL trade deadline is November 10, and we now have our first legitimate report about the Bills being interested in buying.

title: Buffalo Bills record book Week 8: Josh Allen eyes history vs. Ravens
summary: The Buffalo Bills are back from their bye week, which means it’s time to dust off the Record Book, sharpen the pencils, and make sure the erasers haven’t gone missing during the week off. After all, there are a few names and numbers that could need some adjusting before Week 8 is over.  Josh Allen […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills are back from their bye week, which means it’s time to dust off the Record Book, sharpen the pencils, and make sure the erasers haven’t gone missing during the week off. After all, there are a few names and numbers that could need some adjusting before Week 8 is over. Josh Allen has a chance to move past Jim Kelly in one of the franchise’s biggest statistical categories, while Tyler Bass is one successful kick away from claiming a Bills record all to himself. James Cook, meanwhile, is gaining ground on his quarterback in a different category, and that could make for some interesting bookkeeping when the Baltimore Ravens come to town Sunday. _____________________________________________________________________________ Chapter 1: Sure Things The pencils are sharpened, but there’s nothing we’re quite ready to write in this chapter just yet. With a tough Baltimore defense coming to town, even the milestones that look close on paper aren’t guaranteed. _____________________________________________________________________________ Chapter 2: A Good Bet There are three names on our list this week, and all three have a chance to make some changes to the Bills’ record books without needing anything particularly extraordinary to happen. Of course, having the numbers within reach and actually getting the opportunity are two different things. Josh Allen — One More Than Kelly Allen’s rather unconventional backhanded shovel pass to Keon Coleman against the Las Vegas Raiders did more than put six points on the board. It also gave him his 258th career touchdown pass, including the postseason, tying him with Hall of Famer Jim Kelly for the most in Bills history. Now, just one more touchdown pass will give Allen sole possession of the franchise record. Kelly still holds the regular-season mark with 237 touchdown passes to Allen’s 229, but when playoff performances are included, the two quarterbacks are dead even. Here’s hoping that we get to rewrite this entry on the Bills’ first drive of the game. Josh Allen — Closing in on 5,000 Allen is approaching another major career milestone, this time with his legs. With 4,961 regular-season rushing yards, the Bills quarterback needs just 39 more to reach 5,000 for his career. Reaching that mark would put Allen in some pretty exclusive company, joining a short list of quarterbacks that includes Baltimore’s own Lamar Jackson, who will be on the opposite sideline Sunday. And with James Cook closing in on Allen on Buffalo’s all-time rushing list, the Bills quarterback has a little extra incentive to keep those legs moving. Tyler Bass — Kicking His Way Into History Bass has made 18 consecutive regular-season field goals dating back to 2024, matching Rian Lindell’s franchise-best streak from 2007. His next successful attempt would give him the record outright. Bass has been perfect on all 13 field-goal attempts this season, including four against Las Vegas before the bye. The only question now is whether Buffalo’s offense gives him an opportunity to put his name alone at the top of the list. _____________________________________________________________________________ Chapter 3: Not Impossible The erasers might have to work a little harder in this chapter. Neither milestone is out of reach, but both will take some work, especially against a Baltimore team that has given Buffalo plenty of trouble in recent meetings. James Cook — Closing in on his Quarterback For a while, it looked like Josh Allen might be able to hold off James Cook on the Bills’ all-time rushing list. But Cook made up a lot of ground against Las Vegas, and suddenly the race for fourth place is getting interesting. Cook rushed for 95 yards against the Raiders, while Allen managed just one. That leaves Allen in fourth place in franchise history with 4,961 career rushing yards and Cook right behind him in fifth with 4,886. The gap is down to just 75 yards. For Cook to take over fourth place against Baltimore, he’ll need to outgain Allen by at least 76 yards. T That’s certainly possible, but with Allen chasing a few milestones of his own, the quarterback isn’t likely to make it easy for him. Greg Rousseau — Getting his hands on Lamar We’ve had Rousseau’s name penciled in for a couple of weeks now, but that half-sack he needs to move past Darryl Talley on Buffalo’s all-time sack list has remained elusive. Rousseau enters Week 8 with 38 career sacks, including six this season. That’s already just two shy of his career-best eight, but he hasn’t added to his total in either of Buffalo’s last two games. This week, the challenge gets a little tougher. Lamar Jackson isn’t exactly known for standing still and waiting for defenders to catch him. Rousseau has the opportunity to make another move up the franchise list, but bringing down Baltimore’s elusive quarterback might require a little more than an ordinary Sunday. _____________________________________________________________________________ Chapter 4: Superhuman We’ve reached the part of the Record Book where the pencils are probably safe, but we’re keeping the erasers nearby anyway. After all, when Josh Allen is involved, even the most ridiculous possibilities deserve a little consideration. Josh Allen — Running With the Legends Allen already owns the NFL record for rushing touchdowns by a quarterback, but he’s still working his way up the all-time list that includes players at every position. With 87 career rushing touchdowns, Allen sits in 16th place in NFL history. Eric Dickerson and Curtis Martin are tied for 14th with 90 apiece, meaning three rushing touchdowns against Baltimore would put Allen alongside both Hall of Fame running backs. Four would move him ahead of them. That’s a pretty tall order, especially against the Ravens. But Allen has scored three rushing touchdowns in a single game before, and we’ve learned that ruling anything out when No. 17 is on the field isn’t always the smartest move. _____________________________________________________________________________ Baltimore won’t make any of these milestones easy to reach, but the Bills have never needed perfect conditions to make a little history. The pencils are sharpened, the erasers are ready, and the permanent ink is standing by. We’ll see which one gets the most use Sunday.

full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 29: Devin Lloyd #55 of the Carolina Panthers gives a speech in the team huddle prior to an NFL football game against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field on October 29, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Week 8 of NFL action gets underway tonight, with yet another NFC matchup in primetime. If you’ve lost count how many night games have featured NFC team exclusively, you’re not alone. It’s been an interesting schedule, to say the least, and they’re going to continue shoving the NFC down our collective national throats. It’s true the Carolina Panthers haven’t had a great share of the national spotlight in recent years, but this season corrects that oversight for a 3-3 Panthers team that currently leads the NFC South (really). If the networks didn’t force every last NFC East matchup on fans, there might be more opportunity for the AFC to shine on the biggest stage. You see, tonight’s game is the meat sandwiched between a pair of awful NFC East “rivalries” in last Monday’s Philadelphia Eagles-Dallas Cowboys game, and this coming Sunday night’s Eagles-Washington Commanders game. That’s two marquee games in the span of a week featuring a quarterback I’m almost certain 99% of NFL fans can’t name. You might have wondered why no article/open thread for that Philly-Dallas game last Monday. Because: Truly. Terrible. Football. But I digress… Here we are, yet again tuning in because even bad football is impossible to ignore. Is that selling the Packers and Panthers short here? Not intentionally, but the reality is that this is a last place 4-3 NFC North team hosting a 3-3 team few are sure about, and doing it in the spotlight. Both teams really need a win tonight, but for vastly different reasons. For the Pack, it’s to hopefully begin clawing out of the base, while the Panthers need to keep ahead of their closest competition, the Atlanta Falcons, in a frequently messy division. Maybe my sardonicism nudges tonight’s game in the right direction, pushing this one into “game of the season” territory by evening’s end. There’s always the scouting angle, with Green Bay on the Buffalo Bills’ schedule later this season. With that, here’s your open thread for Week 8 of Thursday Night Football . As always, be kind to one another — and in all things… Go Bills!

summary: Thursday brought an array of news on the injury front for the Buffalo Bills. full_text: Thursday brought an array of news on the injury front for the Buffalo Bills. It was there second full day of practice following a bye week, but not everyone is getting healthier. What Changed: On the positive side of things, Ed Oliver was a full participant in Thursday’s practice. This is good news for the defensive lineman who has been nursing a knee injury for a month now. However, Dee Alford wasn’t able to participate on Thursday after being limited on Wednesday as the ankle injury he has been dealing with is apparently still giving him trouble. Ray Davis didn’t practice either, but he’s just dealing with an illness and, unless it’s something serious, I would expect to see him back on the field before game time Sunday. In addition, Joe Andreesen was back on the daily report. The Buffalo linebacker had been on the report on Week 6, although he was well enough to play in Las Vegas. On Wednesday, his name was not among those needing attention from the Bills’ medical staff, but it would appear that one day of practice sent him back to the trainers. Here’s a full look at today’s injury report: Thursday injury report pic.twitter.com/dh0aOWdn3P — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) October 29, 2026 Not Practicing: CB Dee Alford T Spencer Brown RB Ray Davis Limited Practice: LB Joe Andreesen OLB Bradley Chubb TE Dalton Kincaid WR DJ Moore OLB TJ Parker WR Tyrell Shavers (PUP) Full Practice: DL Ed Oliver G Ar’Maj Reed-Adams DL T.J. Sanders Worth Watching: Spencer Brown not practicing for a second straight day, although on Wednesday he told members of the media that he was just resting his back. DJ Moore getting two straight days of practice – albeit limited – is a good sign that the wide receiver will have a game jersey come Sunday. Whatever is going on with Dalton Kincaid. The tight end has a chest injury – and all we can say is: at least it isn’t his knee. Tyrell Shavers practice window is open. I wouldn’t expect him to be added to the active roster this week, but if he gets some full practice in next week, we can start speculating about when. _____________________________________________________________________________ Here’s a quick look at what the Ravens are reporting as they prepare to make the trip to Orchard Park: Thursday's Injury Report pic.twitter.com/9QZapMK9oC — Baltimore Ravens (@Ravens) October 29, 2026 Worth Watching: Lamar Jackson continues to have full practice. I, as I’m sure all of you, have little doubt that we will see him in uniform at Highmark Stadium Sunday. Roquan Smith hyperextended his knee in the fourth quarter of the Ravens Week 7 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals. He didn’t practice Wednesday, but the linebacker seems to be headed in the right direction to suit up for Week 8. Rookie guard Vega Ioane surprisingly returned to the practice field after spraining his MCL on Sunday. Kyle Hamilton and Roquan Smith also returned to the field. Both were limited on Thursday.

title: NFL trade deadline: Buffalo Bills trade candidate – Zack Baun
summary: Let’s take a break from safety trade options for the Buffalo Bills ahead of this year’s NFL trade deadline and focus on the linebacker position. Today we’ll zero-in on Eagles linebacker Zack Baun, a seven-year, late-blossoming veteran with over 3,300 career snaps on his NFL resume (counting playoffs) who resides on a Philadelphia team that […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 18: Zack Baun #53 of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on prior to the game against the Carolina Panthers at Lincoln Financial Field on October 18, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Let’s take a break from safety trade options for the Buffalo Bills ahead of this year’s NFL trade deadline and focus on the linebacker position. Today we’ll zero-in on Eagles linebacker Zack Baun, a seven-year, late-blossoming veteran with over 3,300 career snaps on his NFL resume (counting playoffs) who resides on a Philadelphia team that sits at 2-5 entering Week 8 and has already placed Jalen Hurts on season-ending IR. This article is the eighth in the trade-candidate series I’ll continue to sprinkle onto the site until the actual trade deadline until November 10, which is 12 days from now and lands after Week 9. Past installments in this series: Derwin James , Brian Thomas Jr. Jessie Bates , Tariq Woolen , Amani Hooker , Antoine Winfield Jr. , Cam Bynum Age: 29 Baun was a star at the University of Wisconsin from 2015 – 2019, and vitally here, emerged under the direct tutelage of then Badgers defensive coordinator and current Bills defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard. He was a third-round pick by the Saints in 2020 and began his career mostly where he thrived in college — on the edge, as a two-point stance rusher. While he never flourished in New Orleans, his final season there was respectable productive, as he finished with 10.9% pressure rate, 30 tackles, four for a loss, two pass breakups, and one interception. It did feel like the Saints never really knew how or where to deploy the uniquely built 6’3”, 225-pound outside rusher. He signed a one-year, $3.5M deal with the Eagles in 2024, and Philadelphia transitioned him to a full-time off-ball linebacker role — that also provided plenty of pass-rushing opportunities as a blitzer. All Baun did was earn first-team All-Pro honors with 151 tackles, 11 tackles for loss, 3.5 sacks, five forced fumbles, and four pass breakups during the regular season. Baun also led the team in tackles (33) and interceptions (2) during the playoffs as the Eagles won the Super Bowl. That led to Philadelphia signing Baun to a three-year, $51M deal. 2026 snap splits Box: 82.5% Slot defender: 11.7% Defensive line: 4.6% *Baun has played two snaps each at free safety and wide corner — among his 408 snaps to date — this season. It’s rare to see a mid-career team and position switch go as magnificently as what has transpired in Philadelphia with Baun. The past two seasons with the Eagles, he actually set career highs in pressures (16 each year), despite never reaching 100 pass-rushing opportunities. He’s fast, fluid, surprisingly adept in coverage, a relatively sure tackler, and has maintained his pass-rushing skill despite being off the ball at linebacker. How he’d fit with Bills As a huge believer in Kaleb Elarms-Orr, who has started to play more in Buffalo’s three-man inside linebacker rotation, I can’t say there’s a clear-cut spot for Baun to seamlessly move into right now. However, if the Bills feel either Dorian Williams — who’s rookie deal expires after this season — or Terrel Bernard — who’s playing on the second year of his four-year extension — aren’t playing to their standard, Baun could certainly be viewed as a plug-and-play option who’d also provide some pass-rushing juice. Financial obligation for Bills to trade for him 2026 salary: $1.215M If the Bills trade for Baun after Week 9, they’d be on the hook for $607,500 in prorated 2026 base salary. Cheap. However, there’s a $14.405M option bonus in 2027. That, coupled with his $1.315M in base next season, a $1M roster bonus, and a $250k workout bonus would bring his 2027 cap number to an even $17M. Of course, the Bills could negotiate and come to terms on a new agreement with Baun if this trade is made. Projected cost to acquire Using Syndicate32.com’s trade machine , the projected cost to trade for Baun, is an late Round 2 pick in 2027 plus a Round 7 pick in 2028 . While it initially seems a touch high for a nearly 30-year-old linebacker… Baun’s super-cheap base salary in 2026 does boost his value on the trade market for the Eagles. Should the Bills trade for Zack Baun? I love the Baun-Leonhard connection. And that very well could be the catalyst for this move. I do not love the idea of moving a second-round selection for someone at linebacker who turns 30 in December. As a player, Baun can be an all-encompassing force multiplier for the front seven. And if the Bills linebackers are having problems grasping the nuances of Leonhard’s scheme, in theory, Baun would be able to mentor others while acting as extension of Leonhard on the field at one of the inside linebacker spots. Baun would be fun — and the low 2026 financial commitment makes this possibility more likely than others — I would not love Buffalo coughing up a second-round selection for an off-ball linebacker who’ll turn 31 next season. If the Bills can acquire Baun for a Day 3 pick, then I’d view it as a shrewd move for the Buffalo at this juncture.

title: Just One Before I Die: The Stories, the Fans and the Making of a Bills Mafia Docuseries
summary: If you’ve been a Buffalo Bills fan long enough, you’ve probably said it. Maybe you’ve whispered it after another heartbreaking playoff loss. Maybe you’ve shouted it during a fourth-quarter comeback. Or perhaps you’ve said it every offseason when convincing yourself that next year will finally be THE year. Just one. Just ONE before I die. […]
full_text: If you’ve been a Buffalo Bills fan long enough, you’ve probably said it. Maybe you’ve whispered it after another heartbreaking playoff loss. Maybe you’ve shouted it during a fourth-quarter comeback. Or perhaps you’ve said it every offseason when convincing yourself that next year will finally be THE year. Just one. Just ONE before I die. For generations of Buffalo Bills fans, those words have represented the ultimate wish: to see their beloved team finally hoist the Lombardi Trophy. But what happens when filmmakers decide to explore the people behind that wish? The result is Just One Before I Die , a five-part documentary series that premiered October 21st on Tubi. Created by Buffalo natives Kevin Polowy, Addison Henderson, and Clayton Polowy, the series explores the traditions, personalities, friendships, and heartbreak that have transformed Bills Mafia into one of the most recognizable fan communities in professional sports. And while the documentary features plenty of the outrageous behavior that has made Bills Mafia famous, there’s much more to this story than folding tables, ketchup and mustard, and questionable decisions in freezing temperatures. It’s about the people behind it all. And, perhaps most importantly, why they keep coming back. How It All Began: A Love Letter to Buffalo The inspiration behind Just One Before I Die came from a question that most Bills fans have probably asked themselves at some point: Why do we keep doing this? Why do we invest so much time, money, energy, and emotion into a football team that has repeatedly broken our hearts? For filmmakers Henderson and Polowy, the answer went far beyond football. They wanted to explore what makes Bills Mafia different, why the connection between the team and its fans runs so deep, and how an entire community has embraced the shared pursuit of a championship that continues to elude them. In an interview with WKBW, Polowy described the documentary as a love letter to Buffalo, explaining that supporting the Bills is ultimately another way of supporting the city itself. The filmmakers initially envisioned the project as a 90-minute documentary. But as filming progressed, something unexpected happened. They discovered there were simply too many stories worth telling. What started as a feature-length film eventually expanded into five episodes, allowing the production team to explore the people, traditions, and relationships that make up Bills Mafia in much greater detail. And considering the personalities involved, it’s probably safe to say squeezing everything into 90 minutes would have been nearly impossible. Two Years Behind the Cameras The production of Just One Before I Die was no small undertaking. Henderson and Polowy spent over two years developing the project, following Bills fans through games, tailgates, personal milestones, and the emotional roller coaster of the 2024 and 2025 season and playoffs. The cameras traveled alongside fans as they celebrated victories, endured heartbreaking losses, and continued traditions that have become synonymous with Buffalo football. But the filmmakers weren’t simply interested in capturing the loudest or most outrageous moments. They wanted to understand the people behind them. That meant spending time with fans away from the stadium, learning about their families, their lives, and the personal experiences that shaped their devotion to the Bills. For some, football has been a lifelong family tradition. For others, Bills Mafia has provided friendships, support systems, and a sense of belonging that extends well beyond game day. And for many, the pursuit of a Super Bowl championship has become intertwined with memories of loved ones who shared that dream. The result is a documentary that balances humor and sometimes chaos with moments that are unexpectedly personal. Having experienced part of the filming process myself, I can tell you that the amount of work involved was remarkable. The production team spent countless hours interviewing fans, following them through stadiums and tailgate lots, and capturing moments that couldn’t possibly have been scripted. And then came the difficult task of deciding what would actually make it into the finished series. I can only imagine how much incredible footage ended up on the cutting-room floor. The Team That Brought Bills Mafia to the Screen At the heart of the production are Kevin Polowy, and Addison Henderson, who served as creators, directors, and executive producers alongside co-creator and executive producer Clayton Polowy. The series was produced through AKC Film Productions, UNINTERRUPTED, and Five All in the Fifth Entertainment. UNINTERRUPTED, the sports and entertainment media company co-founded by LeBron James and Maverick Carter, helped bring the project to a national audience. The executive production team also includes former Bills wide receiver Andre Reed, actor and Buffalo native Chad Michael Murray, Jamal Henderson, Mac Cappuccino, Marty Polowy, Amy Polowy, Kayme Crowell Gianatasio, and Jose Padin among others. But a project of this size requires far more than the names appearing at the top of the credits. Behind the scenes, producers and crew members spent years building relationships with the people they were documenting. Among those contributing to the production were Leah Lynette Cohen-Mays, Trent Boling, KJ Zielezinski, and Andy Morin, along with other cinematographers, editors, and creative professionals responsible for bringing the series together. What makes their involvement particularly meaningful is that the production wasn’t simply a group of filmmakers arriving in Buffalo, recording a few interviews, and leaving. They became familiar faces at games and tailgates. They developed friendships with the people they followed. And somewhere along the way, the relationships behind the cameras began to resemble the very community they were documenting. Meet the Faces Behind Bills Mafia Anyone who has attended a Buffalo Bills tailgate knows that Bills Mafia has no shortage of personalities. Some are famous for their outrageous traditions. Others have built organizations dedicated to helping their communities. And some have simply made attending Bills games such a central part of their lives that they’ve become familiar faces throughout the fan base. Just One Before I Die brings many of these personalities together, giving viewers an opportunity to learn more about the people behind their game-day identities. Follow the stories of Steve Brown, Kenny “Pinto Ron” Johnson, John “Elvis” Lang, Norm and Poo “The Chefs,” Joanie “Mama J” Podwoski, Del Reid, Kristen Kimmick, Leslie Willie, Frank “HannaBill-Lecter” Barber, Sterling “SirrBaby” Woods, Norm “Torpedo Dan” Brumfield, Becky Rice-Kane, Kris Rose Brown, Kimmie Kaliszewski, Keita Nakagawa, Donald Grant, Ehlimana Imamovic, Chuck “Billsquatch”Shelly, and Michael “The Handler” Skelly, Renee DeWald, Damsel n’ Disdress, Therese Forton Barnes, Aunt Rita Michaels, and yes, (me) Sara “Shades” Larson. From the Football Field to the Big Screen The documentary also features interviews with several familiar names from the football and entertainment worlds. Former Bills legends Jim Kelly, Andre Reed, Bruce Smith, Steve Tasker, Darryl Talley, Scott Norwood, Stevie Johnson, and Ryan Fitzpatrick contribute their perspectives, alongside current Bills offensive lineman Dion Dawkins. Actor Chad Michael Murray, rapper Benny the Butcher, and national sports personalities including Adam Schefter, Rich Eisen, and Nick Wright, appear in the series, as well as our Buffalo “Broadcaster of the Year”, Sal Capaccio doing the game day voiceovers. Their involvement provides additional context about Buffalo’s football history and the unusual relationship between the franchise and its fans. But while the documentary includes plenty of recognizable names, its real stars are the people who fill the stands every Sunday. The fans who travel thousands of miles. The…
author: Sara Larson

title: Buffalo Bills rooting interests Week 8: The AFC’s top seed is in play
summary: The Buffalo Bills won Week 7.  Before you come at me, I know. I KNOW.  The Bills were on their bye week. They didn’t play a single snap. But they may have walked away as the biggest AFC winners of the weekend anyway.  Just about everything that could go right for Buffalo did. The Bills […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills won Week 7. Before you come at me, I know. I KNOW. The Bills were on their bye week. They didn’t play a single snap. But they may have walked away as the biggest AFC winners of the weekend anyway. Just about everything that could go right for Buffalo did. The Bills now have a game-and-a-half lead over the New England Patriots in the AFC East, with a chance to make it two if they play their cards — or calls — right this weekend. And they’re just a Patrick Mahomes interception away from taking over the AFC’s No. 1 seed. Both Buffalo and Kansas City are sitting at 5-1, but the Chiefs still hold the tiebreaker. Buffalo’s lone loss came against an AFC opponent, while Kansas City’s came against an NFC team, giving the Chiefs the better conference record. For now, anyway. The Bills will get their chance to settle that themselves when the two teams meet on Thanksgiving. But why wait until Thanksgiving to start getting some help? Week 7 was awfully good to Buffalo. Let’s see if Week 8 can be even better. _____________________________________________________________________________ AFC Standings – through Week 7 1. Kansas City Chiefs (5-1) 2. Buffalo Bills (5-1) 3. Cleveland Browns (5-2) 4. Jacksonville Jaguars (4-2) 5. Denver Broncos (5-2) 6. Pittsburgh Steelers (5-2) 7. Cincinnati Bengals (4-2) 8. New England Patriots (4-3) 9. Baltimore Ravens (4-3) 10. Las Vegas Raiders (3-4) 11. New York Jets (2-5) 12. Indianapolis Colts (2-5) 13. Houston Texans (2-5) 14. Miami Dolphins (1-5) 15. Tennessee Titans (1-6) 16. Los Angeles Chargers (0-6) _____________________________________________________________________________ AFC EAST Baltimore Ravens at Buffalo Bills Root for: Bills The Ravens are coming off an ugly loss to Cincinnati, but that doesn’t make Lamar Jackson and Derrick Henry any less dangerous. In fact, they’re probably angry. Buffalo has a chance to strengthen its hold on the AFC East, improve its conference record, and potentially move into the AFC’s top spot with a little help from Denver. Of course, none of that matters if the Bills don’t handle business against Baltimore first. Go Bills! New England Patriots at Miami Dolphins Root for: Dolphins It feels a little strange cheering for Miami, but here we are. New England’s loss to Chicago last week gave Buffalo some much-needed breathing room in the AFC East, and another Patriots loss would make that cushion even more comfortable. The Dolphins aren’t exactly having a season worth celebrating, but they did manage to beat the Jets last week. Asking them to knock off another division rival doesn’t seem entirely unreasonable. Besides, with Miami sitting at the bottom of the division, a Dolphins win does far more damage to New England than it does to Buffalo. Las Vegas Raiders at New York Jets Root for: Raiders Neither of these teams is currently threatening the AFC playoff picture, so this one comes down to a couple of smaller advantages for Buffalo. The Bills already beat Las Vegas, meaning another Raiders victory would give Buffalo a little boost in strength of victory, which could matter if the playoff tiebreakers get complicated down the road. More importantly, the Jets are still the Jets, and they’re still in the AFC East. There’s absolutely no reason to let them get a big head. _____________________________________________________________________________ Rest of the AFC Tennessee Titans at Cincinnati Bengals Root for: Titans Cincinnati is 4-2 and still very much in the playoff race. Tennessee, on the other hand, has just one win. A Titans victory would knock the Bengals down a peg without creating another threat for Buffalo. w Indianapolis Colts at Jacksonville Jaguars Root for: Colts Jacksonville is holding the AFC’s No. 4 seed, and we’d rather not see the Jaguars get too comfortable there. Indianapolis is sitting at 2-5, so giving the Colts another win isn’t going to hurt Buffalo much. Besides, another AFC loss for Jacksonville could come in handy when the playoff tiebreakers start getting interesting. Cleveland Browns at Pittsburgh Steelers Root for: Steelers Cleveland is sitting in the AFC’s No. 3 seed, but Pittsburgh has the same 5-2 record. A Steelers win would pull the Browns back toward the pack and keep the AFC North race tight. Buffalo doesn’t play either team this year, so there’s no strength-of-victory angle to worry about. Just two division rivals beating each other up, and we’re rooting for the one currently looking up at the other. Los Angeles Chargers at Los Angeles Rams Root for: Rams Buffalo already has a win over the Rams, so another Los Angeles victory would give the Bills a boost in strength of victory. The Chargers are 0-6 and aren’t much of a threat in the AFC race, and, sure, we could argue about getting them away from premium draft spots, but there’s no reason to pass up a little tiebreaker help when it’s available. Kansas City Chiefs at Denver Broncos Root for: Broncos This is the big one. Kansas City is the only team standing between Buffalo and the AFC’s No. 1 seed, and Denver has a chance to do something about it. Sure, the Broncos are 5-2 and another win would make them a little more dangerous in the playoff race, but that’s a problem for another day. A Chiefs loss, combined with a Bills win, would put Buffalo in the driver’s seat for the conference’s top spot. And if Denver wants to make Patrick Mahomes miserable for an afternoon, who are we to complain? _____________________________________________________________________________ NFC Rooting Interests Green Bay Packers over Carolina Panthers — Strength of schedule, with a chance for strength of victory in December. Detroit Lions over Minnesota Vikings — Strength of victory. Buffalo already beat Detroit. Chicago Bears over Seattle Seahawks — Strength of schedule, with a chance for strength of victory later this season. Games that don’t move the needle for Buffalo: Atlanta Falcons at Tampa Bay Buccaneers Arizona Cardinals at Dallas Cowboys Philadelphia Eagles at Washington Commanders _____________________________________________________________________________ Teams on Bye Houston Texans, New Orleans Saints, New York Giants, San Francisco 49ers _____________________________________________________________________________ Week 7 gave Buffalo just about everything it could have wanted. Week 8 offers the chance to make something of it. Of course, we’re asking the Broncos to beat Patrick Mahomes, the Dolphins to beat the Patriots, and the Titans to win a football game. Nobody said rooting interests had to be realistic. But after the way Week 7 went, who’s to say Week 8 can’t deliver a few more surprises? Go Bills!
author: Rachel Auberger

title: Ejiro Evero fired by Carolina Panthers; Todd Wash named interim DC
summary: The Panthers took an ugly 27-19 loss to the Packers on Thursday Night Football, and Carolina responded to that loss by parting ways with defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero and defensive passing game coordinator Jonathan Cooley. Todd Wash was named interim defensive coordinator and will call the defensive plays, according to a release from the Panthers […]
full_text: Photo by Erica Denhoff/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Panthers took an ugly 27-19 loss to the Packers on Thursday Night Football, and Carolina responded to that loss by parting ways with defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero and defensive passing game coordinator Jonathan Cooley. Todd Wash was named interim defensive coordinator and will call the defensive plays, according to a release from the Panthers shared by Joe Person of The Athletic. Panthers fired defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero and defensive pass game coordinator Ejiro Evero. DL line coach Todd Wash named interim DC. pic.twitter.com/7zFf3cZeYj — Joe Person (@josephperson) October 30, 2026 Ejiro was hired by the Panthers as the team’s defensive coordinator in 2023 after one season in the DC role with the Los Angeles Rams. He was hired during Frank Reich’s tenure as the Panthers’ head coach, but Dave Canales retained him when he was hired by Carolina. Wash spent five seasons as the Jaguars’ defensive coordinator. From the Panthers’ release : Wash originally joined Carolina’s staff in 2023 and has 31 years of coaching experience, including 20 in the NFL. He spent five seasons (2016-20) serving as the defensive coordinator for the Jacksonville Jaguars, including in 2017 when the team had the second-ranked defense in the league and advanced to the AFC Championship Game. It wasn’t just Thursday night’s loss that led to the decision. The loss to the Packers on a short week came on the heels of an embarrassing 43-13 loss to the Buccaneers in Week 7. But Baker Mayfield only threw for about 63 yards, and the Buccaneers ran all over Carolina. On Thursday night, the Panthers let Jordan Love throw for 288 yards and three touchdowns while Bryce Young took six sacks and finished with a QBR of 36.2. In addition to the termination of Evero and Cooley, the Panthers announced that OLB/run game specialist AC Carter will also take on defensive line coaching responsibilities. Secondary coach Renardo Hill will retain his position. The Panthers are sitting at 3-4 and remain in first place in a very weird NFC South, but if the Falcons win this week, that will change. If you’ve paid any attention to the Atlanta Falcons, you know that’s always a big “if.” We will update this story as more information becomes available.

title: The Optimist: That could have been worse
summary: The Carolina Panthers put up an honestly decent showing against a superior opponent. Jordan Love and the Green Bay Packers were the best combination of quarterback and defense Carolina has faced this season. They faced them with their worst and worsening combination of secondary and offensive line injuries. It was a match made in some […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 29: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers warms up prior to an NFL football game against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field on October 29, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Carolina Panthers put up an honestly decent showing against a superior opponent. Jordan Love and the Green Bay Packers were the best combination of quarterback and defense Carolina has faced this season. They faced them with their worst and worsening combination of secondary and offensive line injuries. It was a match made in some Wisconsinite cheese-fever dream. Factor in the deflation of team ego off last week’s embarrassment against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and you could easily have expected worse than a one possession loss. Instead the team was outmatched on almost every level and still hung in to make a game of it. If they have to lose a corner and a guard every week of the season then at least they can keep things entertaining along the way. If Jaelan Phillips, Jaycee Horn, Mike Jackson, Will Lee III, and Brady Christiansen can all come back from injury by the end of the season then maybe things can turn around. Even one of them making one more impact play last night could have made the difference in a one possession game. Nobodies presence was more missed than Lewis’, who left the Bucs game with a knee injury. Unlike most Panthers players this season, that did not immediately land him on injured reserve. He is the lone bright spot on the Panthers current line, with rookie Monroe Freeling coming close to being a second one. There is more to be said about both the offensive line and the secondary, but now isn’t the time. I’m not nit-picking the day after an eight point loss when the only thing I know about the Panthers Week 9 starting corners and left guard is that they weren’t on the roster during training camp. We’ll be back next week with more information than that. For now, take heart in the fact that this was an infinitely better team than we saw against the Bucs. That loss showed us a low discipline floor more than anything closely resembling Carolina’s current ceiling. Last night was more a middle ground, a shadow of what could be. But a loss is what you get when your quarterback has no time to throw, your opponent has all day, and half your team is probably wondering if they’ll be the next ones carted off. Still, not all losses are created equal and this one was vastly more promising than the last. Also, the season isn’t over yet. In fact, if it ended today, we might get to watch the funniest matchup in the history of the playoffs. All four NFC North teams would make the playoffs. The 5-3 Packers are in fourth place in the division and would be the seventh seed. They would play the 3-4 Panthers in Charlotte in a wildcard game. If you can’t love the Panthers right now then you have to at least love the NFC South.

title: Panthers vs Packers TNF recap: Well, who’s next at guard and corner?
summary: First Quarter A forced and recovered fumble on the opening kickoff earned the Panthers the ball to start the game and their first turnover in three games. Interior pressure buckled the opening drive before it got started and the Panthers had to settle for a field goal. The defenses traded three and outs from there […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 29: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers warms up prior to an NFL football game against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field on October 29, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images First Quarter A forced and recovered fumble on the opening kickoff earned the Panthers the ball to start the game and their first turnover in three games. Interior pressure buckled the opening drive before it got started and the Panthers had to settle for a field goal. The defenses traded three and outs from there until a big pass interference penalty opened things up for the Packers. A big pass against an unsuccessful big blitz followed that penalty and led to the Packers first TD. A missed extra point then kept the spirit of Panthers football alive. The Panthers stretched the perimeter of the field to move away from the interior pressure and into the red zone after, getting to a 4th and 1 with 1:00 left in the first quarter. Chuba Hubbard ran for a hard one yard, showing success where the panthers have struggled in short yardsge. The next play he carried them to the 1 yard line and the end of the 1st quarter. Second Quarter Hubbard punched it in on second and goal to start the wuarter and regain a Panthers lead A second Green Bay fumble on ensuing drive gave the Panthers a big opportunity to expand their lead. Unfortunately, their offensive line did their best impression of tissue paper and the Panthers punted after three plays. Packers game plan seems to be attempting therapy for their running game. So far so therapeutic for the Panthers run defense. Unfortunately, less could be said for the pass defense. A deep bomb surrendered to Christian Watson led to both him and Will Lee III leaving the game with injuries. Chau Smith-Wade and Marco Wilson were the corners left standing. Somehow, the defense held the Packers until third and goal from the one, but Josh Jacobs found plenty of room for a score at the end of the drive to retake a Packers lead. The Panthers started their second possession of the second quarter with 6:28 left on the clock. A Green Bay penalty on third and eight turned into a tipped pass for an interception on third and three. Green Bay ended up with the football at the 48 yard line with 5:18 left in the half. Quick, short passes moved the Packers safely down the field. The occasional running play allowed the Panthers defense to flash competence, but the Packers leaned on the pass as needed to score a touchdown that felt inevitable. Inside of two minutes left in the half, it felt like the Panthers were out of answers in their secondary. Edge pressure and bad offensive tackle play killed the two-minute drill and the Panthers went in to the half with what had been a one possession game feeling increasingly out of reach. Half Time The Panthers were firing on zero cylinders in the first half. Injuries have exposed paper thin depth along both fronts. Young had no time to throw, highlighted by Tetairoa McMillan and Jalen Coker combining in the first half for one reception on five targets. Meanwhile, the defense couldn’t cover, couldn’t pressure, and thus couldn’t get the Packers off the field when they needed to. Writing this at halftime, I expect the second half to be long and unsatisfying to watch as a Panthers fan. Third Quarter McMillan exceeded his first half receiving numbers in the first three plays of the half with two receptions for 22 yards. Unfortunately, that was the only success on the drive. Two consecutive failed plays led to a turnover on downs. The Packers then started to find success on the ground to complement their uncontested passing game. Another Green Bay touchdown pushed the score to 27-10 with only 22:30 left in the game. The Panthers opened the next drive with a nine yard gain by Hubbard. They lost Corey Bullock on the play, who had started the game in relief of an injured Damien Lewis. Strong running by Hubbard and tight end Mitchell Evans kept the drive alive long enough to get the Panthers into field goal range. The fourth sack of the night for the Packers defense forced a 50-yard field goal that brought the Panthers back within two touchdowns at 27-13. This was the Panthers first score in 25:10 of game time. Fourth Quarter Watson returned to the game after a brief hospital trip, but had his heroic moment cut short by a goal line interception courtesy of Panthers rookie safety Zakee Wheatley. A return to the 20 yard line saved the Panthers from what was looking to be a knockout punch by the Packers. Alas, pressure on Young and another sack killed another drive. The Panthers offense has no answers for the Green Bay defense. Three turnovers by the defense and special teams has resulted in three points. Kirk Herbstreit and Al Michaels spent much of the fourth quarter discussing how few teams have been able to field a consistently healthy offensive line and how important that is for on field success. At the same time, Rasheed Walker, Jake Curhan, Luke Fortner, and Rob Hunt put on display how much a liability they can each be in pass protection. In spite of that, Young and Hubbard managed to gut out another scoring drive. Fourth and three from the Green Bay 26 turned into a Jalen Coker touchdown catch that brought the Panthers back within eight points after a failed two-point conversion. The Packers next drive began with a penalty that erased a 21-yard screen to Tucker Kraft. A well defended deep shot by Wilson after that brought up second and 15. Third and ten then led to a bad snap and an intentional grounding penalty. That gave the Panthers 4:35 and three timeouts to tie the game. That, uh, that didn’t happen. A few minimal gains led to fourth and five at the 50. Heavy pressure and decent coverage led to a poor throw by Young and a grounder meant for McMillan that turned over the ball on downs. The Packers returned the ball to the Panthers with 22 seconds left, only to close out the game with another sack. It was hard fought, but rarely in doubt. This wasn’t the Panthers team that lost to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, but it is hard to imagine them getting much better with their current injury situation.

title: Chicago Bears at Seattle Seahawks: Keys to a Chicago victory
summary: In the race for the NFC crown, the Chicago Bears and the Seattle Seahawks each took big swings this week to shore themselves up for the second half of the season. The Bears obviously made the huge trade for Jeffery Simmons from the Tennessee Titans, while the Seahawks landed Quenton Nelson from the Indianapolis Colts. […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - OCTOBER 25: Jaxon Smith-Njigba #11 of the Seattle Seahawks catches a touchdown pass against Mansoor Delane #5 of the Kansas City Chiefs during the second quarter at Lumen Field on October 25, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images In the race for the NFC crown, the Chicago Bears and the Seattle Seahawks each took big swings this week to shore themselves up for the second half of the season. The Bears obviously made the huge trade for Jeffery Simmons from the Tennessee Titans, while the Seahawks landed Quenton Nelson from the Indianapolis Colts. Now the Bears and Seahawks face off on Monday Night Football with a lot at stake. These two teams play in the two best divisions in the conference. The Seahawks are the defending Super Bowl champions. Their record may be 4-3, but they’re hitting their stride, coming off a 20-3 beatdown of the previously undefeated Kansas City Chiefs. This game should be a great Monday night game, truly a playoff-type atmosphere. The Bears are eager to show they’re ready to hang with the NFL’s best. The Seahawks want to show they haven’t fallen off from their Super Bowl run. So we got our crew to weigh in on what it’s going to take for the Bears to go to one of the toughest stadiums in the NFL and come back with the W. Sam: The biggest defensive test since the Vikings game looms for Caleb and Ben as they go on the road to one of the toughest and loudest stadiums in the league to play in. The Bears will have to take what the defense gives them and grind out long drives to keep JSN off the field. On defense — pressure Sam Darnold and double, heck, triple JSN if you have to. Thieneman over the top, please. Josh: Caleb needs to level up and display all of his powers, ranging from sack avoidance to completion percentage to explosive plays. Monangai is likely out, and the run game is not as powerful. Defense is just going to have to mitigate damage. Ben needs to be smart and tricky at the same time. Jeff Berckes: The Seahawks have the best defense by DVOA. The Bears counter with one of the best offenses in the league with Caleb Williams under center. Best on best in a hostile environment – Ben Johnson needs to use that extra rest to his advantage with a game plan that gets the running game back on track to maximize play action. On the other side of the ball… make someone other than JSN beat you. He’s the best receiver in the league and the corners have been rough all year – special attention to him every single play. Mongo Peanut: The Bears have to contain JSN. He’s the lone offensive weapon that can beat you on a Seattle team still trying to figure out their running game. You won’t keep JSN from catching the ball, but you have to keep him from turning 10-yard catches into 40-yard house calls. ECD: Offense: Keep as balanced as possible and stay ahead of the chains. It’ll be a classic “immovable object vs unstoppable force” matchup that’ll require strict discipline and situational awareness. Defense: Do… something. At least bracket JSN as much as possible and find a way to rattle Sam Darnold’s cage. This unit has to play much better on the road than they have in previous weeks. P.S. Let’s wrap up that trade for a defensive difference-maker soon. (Editor’s note: This piece was mostly written before Thursday’s big trade!) Special Teams: Let Zavion Thomas cook. He’s recording longer kick returns each week as he gets more opportunities. And keep the FG attempts to a minimum – Seattle is a notorious place to attempt long-range kicks. What are your keys to the game?

title: NFL Predictions: Can the Bears’ defense slow down the Seahawks’ offense?
summary: A Monday Night Football matchup between the Chicago Bears and the Seattle Seahawks is a circle-the-calendar game that NFL fans got excited about on schedule release day. Those games don’t always feel quite as big once the season gets rolling, but this one gets the full court press of hype (even more so with each […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - DECEMBER 26: Wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba #11 of the Seattle Seahawks is tackled by safety Jonathan Owens #36 of the Chicago Bears during the third quarter of an NFL football game, at Soldier Field on December 26, 2024 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images A Monday Night Football matchup between the Chicago Bears and the Seattle Seahawks is a circle-the-calendar game that NFL fans got excited about on schedule release day. Those games don’t always feel quite as big once the season gets rolling, but this one gets the full court press of hype (even more so with each team making a big-time trade). The (5-2) Bears are coming off a prime-time win over the New England Patriots, and the (4-3) Seahawks are coming off a prime-time win over the Kansas City Chiefs. These are two legit Super Bowl contenders. Ben Johnson’s Bears have one of the NFL’s most explosive offenses, and Mike Macdonald’s Seahawks again have one of the league’s most suffocating defenses, but this game might come down to the other side of the ball. Can Chicago’s defense slow down a Seahawks offense with a refocused rushing attack and one of the game’s best wide receivers, Jaxon Smith-Njigba? The Bears’ huge trade for Jeffery Simmons, who has more tackles for loss since 2021 than any other defensive tackle in the NFL, will immediately help the run defense, and his ability to collapse the pocket will immediately help Chicago’s pass rush. I could see him on a limited snap count since he won’t know the calls, twists, and stunts, but he’ll play in some obvious passing or running situations. But JSN will still be a problem. Smith-Njigba, the 2025 NFL Offensive Player of the Year, is having an even better 2026, averaging 8.3 receptions and 123.9 receiving yards per game. He’s the type of game-altering talent who can win a game on his own. So far, Chicago’s defense has played better than many expected, but I don’t know how they’ll limit JSN. Our partners at FanDuel Sportsbook have his over/under on receptions at 7.5 and receiving yards at 99.5, and while those are high — relatively speaking — they seem easily attainable for him vs. Chicago’s secondary. The Bears don’t have a corner on the roster who can hang with him. But to be fair, neither do most teams. I like the over on both of those. My guess is the Bears will be focused on stopping the run, knowing JSN will get his, while trying to heat up Seattle quarterback Sam Darnold into making mistakes. And now with a game-wrecking defensive tackle in Simmons, the Bears won’t need to blitz as much, so they’ll be able to keep a safety over the top of JSN a few more times. Another over I like is Caleb Williams’ rushing yards, which is at 21.5. This will be his third game back after the hamstring injury, and the extra rest following their Thursday nighter should have his legs feeling good enough to take off when the opportunity presents itself. If you were wondering about the over/under for Caleb’s passing yards, it’s at 227.5. Considering the most passing yards Seattle’s defense has allowed this year is 189, by Justin Herbert and Brock Purdy, that’s a decent-sized leap by the oddsmakers and what they think of Williams. I like the over here as well, but not by much, and mostly because I think the Bears may try the short passing game in place of the run, especially if Kyle Monangai misses another game. As for the game itself, the Bears are a 3-point underdog, and I was teetering on who to pick in what I expect to be a close game, but the Simmons deal has me feeling too good to pick against the Bears.
