title: Lions vs. Vikings preview: 3 key matchups
summary: The Detroit Lions look to start 2-0 in the NFC North as the undefeated Minnesota Vikings travel to Ford Field. Are you expecting a breakdown of Brian Flores’ top ranked defense against the newly recognized MVP candidate Jared Goff? Sorry. Sure, this matchup boasts the Vikings’ league best defense against the Lions potent offense. But […]
full_text: Detroit Lions defensive back Brian Branch (32) warms up ahead of the game between Detroit Lions and Green Bay Packers at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions look to start 2-0 in the NFC North as the undefeated Minnesota Vikings travel to Ford Field. Are you expecting a breakdown of Brian Flores’ top ranked defense against the newly recognized MVP candidate Jared Goff? Sorry. Sure, this matchup boasts the Vikings’ league best defense against the Lions potent offense. But that isn’t where this game will be won or lost, in my opinion. No, the key matchups lie in the other two phases of the game to give either team the edge. For this week’s key matchups, I’ve drawn inspiration from defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard, who said the defense hit on each of his keys to victory the past two weeks. “I don’t think I’ve ever seen back-to-back games where we went out, we do these keys to victory and they’ve gone out back-to-back games and I mean hit every single one of them” Against the Packers, those three keys to victory were: 1) Don’t let wide receivers Christian Watson and Matthew Golden get behind them, 2) dominate in the run game and make them one dimensional, and 3) force takeaways. Here are our keys to victory against the Vikings: Kyler Murray vs. the front seven When asked about the Vikings’ offense, Sheppard listed off the top offensive skill players as being threats they have to account for, but singled out quarterback in particular. “And then probably the most dangerous of them all is my guy back there, number one in Kyler Murray. If you let him out of that pocket, he can hurt you.“ Per SumerSports , Murray is fourth in the NFL with a scramble rate of 9.9% for quarterbacks with at least 10 dropbacks. While creating pressure is important, more important this week for the Lions’ front seven on defense is to contain and keep Murray in the pocket. On the year, Murray ranks 27th overall in EPA/play at -0.09 amongst quarterbacks with at least 100 dropbacks. However, while outside of the pocket, Murray has an EPA/play of -0.04, which ranks eighth best. After watching the Vikings vs. Indianapolis Colts game from Week 7, the biggest takeaway I had of the Minnesota offense was that Murray struggled to sit in the pocket, read the defense, and deliver an accurate ball. Most of the offensive success was predicated on designer plays or off-script improvisation. Defending this is a complete unit assignment. If one player is unsound in their rush integrity, Murray can find a seam and create problems. Key to victory: the front seven must maintain discipline to force Kyler to play a style of game he is least comfortable in. Justin Jefferson vs. the secondary The Lions cannot let Jefferson beat them, and I don’t expect Sheppard to call on one guy to make that happen. While cornerback D.J. Reed has played better recently, I expect the focus on Jefferson to be a collective effort. Whether it’s unique double teams and bracket coverages , or a deep shell safety making sure 18 doesn’t get over top. This is a complete-unit matchup. Looking into Jefferson’s usage tendencies, he’s lining up in a wide alignment at the highest rate of his career at 84.7% . Further, Jefferson is being put in presnap motion at the lowest rate in his career at 8.4% overall and just 2.2% at the snap. This helps the Lions defense to more predictably run help coverage toward Jefferson without complication. The Vikings are tied with the Chicago Bears as the only teams in the NFL to have not been the beneficiary of a defensive pass interference this season . Discipline on critical downs is important to not give this Vikings offense any help in changing this. Key to victory: do not give up explosives to Jefferson by leaving him one-on-one on critical down-and-distances. DeAndre Carter vs. touchback field position Lastly, the special teams phase of the game is the hidden key to victory against the Vikings. With how stout the Minnesota defense has been, one critical way to overcome the challenge is to win the field position battle. Following a season-ending injury to typical return specialist Tom Kennedy, the Lions signed wide receiver DeAndre Carter to be the team’s new top returner. The veteran showed burst and looked close to breaking off some big returns in his first action as a Lion against the Packers in Week 7. Against the Vikings, yards will be at a premium and every bit of positive field position takes pressure off of Goff and the rest of the offense to sustain a long drive to get into at least field goal range to net points. While the Vikings rank No. 1 in special teams DVOA per FTN Fantasy , they rank 29th in net punt yards per attempt at 39.26 and 14th in average kickoff return yards allowed of 25.23, per SumerSports . Key to victory: create short fields through special teams to limit the impact of the Vikings’ defense. Three key matchups. Three keys to victory and one game closer to reclaiming the top spot in the NFC North.

title: Before the Roar: Previewing Detroit Lions vs. Minnesota Vikings
summary: After a thrilling win over the Green Bay Packers in Week 7, the Detroit Lions are back at home for another divisional matchup against the Minnesota Vikings. Sitting at 6-0, the Vikings are the last undefeated team left in the NFL, and they’ll be making the trip to Detroit for the first of two games […]
full_text: After a thrilling win over the Green Bay Packers in Week 7, the Detroit Lions are back at home for another divisional matchup against the Minnesota Vikings. Sitting at 6-0, the Vikings are the last undefeated team left in the NFL, and they’ll be making the trip to Detroit for the first of two games against Detroit. To break everything down ahead of the game, Meko Scott and I (Morgan) are back with another episode of “Before the Roar.” Naturally, much of our focus was on Minnesota’s defense. Led by one of the best defensive play-callers in the NFL in defensive coordinator Brian Flores, the Vikings have the best defense in football by many metrics. We discuss how their veteran group allows Flores to be really creative and aggressive from week to week, and what fans can expect when the Lions’ offense is on the field. Flipping to the offense and we start by giving flowers to the Vikings skill players. The play on the field has been up and down for the majority of the 2026 season thus far, but it’s tough to pin the performance on players like wide receiver Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison, tight end T.J. Hockenson, and running back Aaron Jones. Can quarterback Kyler Murray continue to improve under Vikings coach and play-caller Kevin O’Connell? Lastly, we wrap things up by going over key matchups and giving our predictions for Sunday’s game. You can watch the entire episode right here . If you haven’t done so already, please be sure to like and subscribe to the Pride of Detroit YouTube Channel.

title: Lions, Vikings Week 8 injury report: All 7 starters return to practice on Thursday
summary: The Detroit Lions (4-2) and Minnesota Vikings (6-0) were back on the practice field on Thursday as they prepare for their Week 8 NFC North showdown. The Lions returned all seven starters to practice on Thursday, as planned, including Jahmyr Gibbs (shoulder) and Amon-Ra St. Brown (ankle). Let’s take a look at Thursday’s injury report […]
full_text: Detroit Lions wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown (14) scoring a touchdown against New Orleans Saints with running back Jahmyr Gibbs (0) during the overtime at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions (4-2) and Minnesota Vikings (6-0) were back on the practice field on Thursday as they prepare for their Week 8 NFC North showdown. The Lions returned all seven starters to practice on Thursday, as planned, including Jahmyr Gibbs (shoulder) and Amon-Ra St. Brown (ankle). Let’s take a look at Thursday’s injury report and get you up to date with what we know. Note: Any changes from the most recent injury report will be bolded . N o practice None All 53 players on the Lions’ active roster practiced Thursday. Limited practice CB Ennis Rakestraw (ankle) S Kerby Joseph (Knee, PUP) — Days remaining in injury evaluation clock: 19 Rakestraw was forced from Week 7’s game against the Packers, and while that typically means no practice early in the week, he hasn’t missed a practice yet. While limited, he is on track to be available for his rotational outside cornerback role again this weekend. Joseph is slowly being worked back into football shape, but has stacked two practices as he moves through the injury evaluation process. He still has 19 days remaining in that window, and the Lions will use all of them if they deem he needs them in order to be ready. Considering he hasn’t been on the practice field in basically a year, it’d be a stretch for him to be ready for the Vikings; the Dolphins game could also be in question, meaning his first game back could end up being against the Patriots in Germany. Full practice RB Jahmyr Gibbs (shoulder) — upgraded from no practice on Wednesday RB Jacob Saylors (neck) — upgraded from limited practice Wednesday WR Amon-Ra St. Brown (ankle) — upgraded from no practice on Wednesday OT Penei Sewell (rest) — upgraded from no practice on Wednesday DT Alim McNeill (rest) — upgraded from no practice on Wednesday DT Tyleik Williams (illness) — upgraded from no practice on Wednesday EDGE Aidan Hutchinson (rest) — upgraded from no practice on Wednesday EDGE DJ Wonnum (rest) — upgraded from no practice on Wednesday Gibbs was unexpectedly added to Wednesday’s injury report due to a shoulder injury, but it did not restrict him from getting back to practice on Thursday. After practice, Gibbs told reporters he was surprised to see he was listed as questionable on an alert on his phone and downplayed the injury. “It said ‘questionable’ I don’t know what was questionable. I was confused. It popped up on my phone, and I’m like ‘What the hell?’” Gibbs said. “Yeah, just got dinged up a little bit, a little shoulder thing, but I’m good, though. I’m straight.” Lions coach Dan Campbell will likely address the injury at his Friday press conference, but there are no indications this will impact his ability to contribute against the Vikings. Saylors was also unexpectedly present on the Lions injury report, but his getting in two practices so far this week is a good sign he’s on track to be available on Sunday. With DeAndre Carter only starting his second game at kick returner, the Lions would feel more comfortable if Saylors could also start alongside him. St. Brown tweaked his ankle in Week 7, and while he missed practice on Wednesday, he was back in the fold on Thursday, following the plan Campbell detailed earlier in the week. St. Brown is expected to be good to start on Sunday. “It’s good,” St. Brown told reporters Thursday. “It just got stepped on throughout the game. So it just got swelled up a little, but I’m all good.” Sewell, McNeill, Hutchinson, and Wonnum got the veteran rest day on Wednesday, and as Campbell suggested earlier in the week, they returned to the practice field on Thursday. The Lions hope the extra day of rest will give their superstars a little more juice against the Vikings this Sunday. Williams technically missed practice Wednesday due to an illness, which is common in Michigan this time of year, but he was able to get back to work Thursday. He is expected to be good to go this weekend. title: Lions vs. Vikings 5 Qs preview: Are the 6-0 Vikings real or “frauds”?
summary: The Detroit Lions face their second NFC North opponent in as many weeks, facing off against the “perfect” Minnesota Vikings. We had the pleasure of connecting with Christopher Gates, the Lead Writer for Daily Norseman, to give us some insight into this Vikings team ahead of this week’s matchup. We learned about the prevailing local […]
full_text: Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (16) talks to center Graham Glasgow (60) before a play against Minnesota Vikings during the second half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, November 2, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions face their second NFC North opponent in as many weeks, facing off against the “perfect” Minnesota Vikings. We had the pleasure of connecting with Christopher Gates, the Lead Writer for Daily Norseman , to give us some insight into this Vikings team ahead of this week’s matchup. We learned about the prevailing local sentiment surrounding Minnesota’s 6-0 start, Kyler Murray’s struggles in Kevin O’Connell’s offense, and Brian Flores’ hyper-aggressive, ‘Borg-like’ blitz scheme—plus the unsung heroes of this Vikings team. 1. The Minnesota Vikings stand alone as the last undefeated team in the NFL, a perfect 6-0 on the season, but some people are labeling this team as “frauds.” For a team that was projected to finish last in the NFC North, and their preseason win total was set at 8.5 wins, what’s the prevailing vibe among the fanbase heading into Week 8? Given the circumstances in recent years, unfortunately, the “fraud” label is going to be attached to anything the Vikings do until they do something that shows that they’re not. In 2022, they went 13-4, but in the four losses they got absolutely hammered and wound up with a negative point differential, and then they lost in the Wild Card round at home. In 2024, they were 14-2 going into the final week of the regular season, but they utterly imploded in the regular season finale and the Wild Card round and wound up going home early again. Now, they’re 6-0, but the offense has been less than stellar (to put it in exceedingly polite terms) and the Vikings haven’t exactly played a Murderer’s Row of opponents to this point. So, until something changes, the “fraud” label is going to continue to be thrown around. Yes, it’s nice to stack wins and you don’t control the schedule and all that, but with the schedule that the Vikings are looking at over the next four weeks (at Detroit, vs Buffalo, at Green Bay, at San Francisco in Mexico City), we’re going to find out a lot about this team. As far as the fan base, it’s pretty much normal. The Vikings are 6-0 and somebody needs to be fired. But, seriously, even with the 6-0 record, there are a lot of things that people have doubts about, and all of them are on the offensive side of the ball. Oh, and the fact that the 23-year-old quarterback that the team bailed on about a month ago suddenly looks really good with his new team. . .yeah, that’s a bit of a contentious situation around here, too. I think a lot of folks are genuinely happy to be 6-0, but they also understand that the way things have gone is genuinely unsustainable and that if something doesn’t change the pendulum has the potential to swing the other direction pretty dramatically. 2. Brian Flores is… the best coach in the NFL? Regardless of role or position? From the outside looking in, it sure looks that way. How has Flores continued to keep opposing offenses in the dark, and what about this defense, be it scheme or personnel or both, has led to such a dominant start to the 2026 season? I think a big part of what makes Flores’ defense what it’s become is the fact that so many of these guys have played together for so long that they just all know what they’re doing all the time. It’s like the Borg. That’s why the Vikings can put 6 or 7 or 8 guys up on the line of scrimmage and make it look like they’re bringing everybody all the time, because when the ball is snapped, everyone on their side just knows where they’re going to be and what they’re supposed to be doing and nobody is going to get themselves out of position trying to cover for someone else’s assignment. I can’t remember who I saw it from on X, but the Vikings have basically reversed the element of surprise when it comes to blitzing at this point. Generally, teams use the blitz as a surprise to try to force teams into doing things they’re uncomfortable with. With the Vikings, teams are more surprised when they don’t bring the blitz because Flores is bringing it at such a ridiculously high rate. Obviously, you have to have the personnel to pull it off, but Flores has had a pretty significant say in the players that the team has brought in defensively in the time that he’s been here, so this entire defense is essentially “his guys.” But I do believe that the level of continuity between the players that have been here for a while contributes greatly to it and allows Flores to do a lot of the things that he’s able to do. 3. Minnesota has scored just 125 points through six games this season–the fewest in the NFC–and of those 125 points, 54 points have come via the leg of Will Reichard on just his made field goals. The Vikings offense ranks 31st in success rate, 30th in DVOA, and 29th in EPA/play. They’ve dealt with injuries at both the quarterback and running back position, but how and why has Kevin O’Connell’s offense so woefully underperformed this season? Is there reason to believe they can improve to being a respectable offense? Simple. It’s the quarterback play. More specifically, it’s Kyler Murray. The popular narrative all offseason was that Murray was the sort of quarterback that the Vikings needed in order to help push the ball down the field, specifically to Justin Jefferson, and help to open up the Vikings’ offense in ways that they couldn’t last season with the quarterback carousel of J.J. McCarthy, Carson Wentz, and Max Brosmer. There were those of us who said that Murray just really wasn’t a fit for the sort of offense that Kevin O’Connell wanted to run, and we were told that Murray was actually really good. Here’s the thing: No, he’s not. Over the past four games with Murray as the starter, the Vikings’ offense has generated four touchdown drives. Some teams have games with four touchdown drives. And, again, it’s not as if they’ve been playing the ’85 Bears every week or anything like that. Last week against a Colts team that was missing its top three corners by the end of the game, Murray had 150 yards, Justin Jefferson had 44 yards receiving (all before halftime), and the Vikings managed one touchdown. The defense has been playing lights out, certainly, but there’s going to come a point where one touchdown a game isn’t going to cut it. The Vikings had a quarterback competition. . .allegedly. . .during training camp, and Murray was declared the winner. This is his team. If the Vikings are going to be a serious contender going forward, he’s going to have to turn things around pretty dramatically. The talent is there at the other positions on offense. If the offense can even start performing at an average level, people will start feeling a whole lot better about this team, I think. 4. Who have been some under-the-radar contributors for the Vikings, and why have they been such important contributors to Minnesota’s early-season success? There have been a lot of players on the defensive side of the ball who have been getting recognition for this team, but one who continues to fly under the radar is defensive lineman Levi Drake Rodriguez. Lions fans may remember him from last year’s game in Detroit, when he blocked a field goal attempt in the fourth quarter that could have cut the Vikings’ lead to four, but he’s played a bigger role in the defense this year. He generally plays right in the middle of the defense and has been very impressive against the run in his third season. Jalen Redmond is starting to get more recognition when it comes to the Vikings’ defensive line, but it’s Rodriguez who eats up a lot of double teams and still manages to make an impact. He does a lot of the dirty work to allow the rest of the Vikings’ defenders to move around more freely and make the plays that get more attention. Max Bredeson, a guy who Michigan sports fans are likely familiar with, has stepped into C.J. Ham’s…

title: 6 Lions coordinator takeaways: Detroit’s defense starting to hit its goals
summary: The Detroit Lions’ three coordinators held their weekly press conferences on Thursday to recap the Green Bay Packers win and preview the upcoming game against the Minnesota Vikings. Here’s what you need to know. Offensive coordinator Drew Petzing Time to get the run game going Detroit’s running game has been relatively effective, but there have […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 27: Defensive Coordinator Kelvin Sheppard of the Detroit Lions looks on against the New York Jets at Ford Field on September 27, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions’ three coordinators held their weekly press conferences on Thursday to recap the Green Bay Packers win and preview the upcoming game against the Minnesota Vikings. Here’s what you need to know. Offensive coordinator Drew Petzing Time to get the run game going Detroit’s running game has been relatively effective, but there have been a lot of negative plays, too. Petzing identified three reasons those negative plays have been happening: Poor identification up front “Are we going to the right people? Is everybody on the same page? Did we get that communicated out?” Losing your matchup “Losing your one-on-ones, are we using proper technique? Did we create a bad matchup?” Poor scheme “Is that a good play? Should we have called in that situation? No, we can’t get to that guy. The angle’s not great.” Against the Packers, Petzing said all three were at play, but picked out “poor identification” as the main culprit. This week against the Vikings, Petzing noted the importance of getting the running game going and avoiding negative plays. “It’s huge. And I think if you can make us one dimensional as an offense, you know exactly what you’re attacking. And we need to keep a defense like this and any defense for that matter off balance because if they know they have to do this to win the game, well, here’s what we do to take that away. But if they’re constantly trying to figure out, is it a run? Is it a pass? Can we stop this and this? Can we stop that and that? I think it limits their flexibility too and makes them a little bit more predictable.” Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard Defense has hit its goals the last two games Each week, Sheppard sets three specific goals/benchmarks for their defense. He says in each of the past two games, they have successfully ticked off each goal, which sounds more rare than you’d think. “I don’t think I’ve ever seen back-to-back games where we went out, we do these keys to victory, and they’ve gone out back-to-back games, and I mean hit every single one of them. And that’s when you know you’re trending the right way. That’s when you know it’s hitting home with the players.” Sheppard wouldn’t give out the three goals for Vikings week, but he detailed the three for last week’s game against the Packers: Don’t let Christian Watson and Matthew Golden get behind them and limit them in the passing game Combined 11 catches for 96 yards, 0 TDs Dominate the run game 19 carries, 60 yards, 3.2 YPC Force takeaways 1 interception The explosive plays are still happening, but decreasing Sheppard was very happy with the way the Lions played against the Packers, but he still points to six explosive plays given up, several of which were self-inflicted. “It was six explosive plays in that game, and half of those were nothing that the Green Bay Packers did. It’s what we did. And I said, ‘Imagine you clean that up. Imagine we hit on the six, seven plays of those details. Imagine what that’ll look like.’” Sheppard later clarified that three of the self-inflicted mistakes all came on Green Bay’s fourth-down conversions. He believes they were simple mistakes and they’re getting corrected. “Those were three of the busts, if I’m being honest with you. And the players know it, so it’s not like I’m saying anything that you guys don’t see. Pretty much everybody around the league runs that coverage, and they know who was supposed to be where they were supposed to be. The player took accountability towards it, and we’re moving onward and upward.” When asked if some of the repeated coverage busts were the result of youth and inexperience, Sheppard refused to play the blame game. “Those are excuses, and those are for losers. And if you start to go down that road, your role will diminish here. So, we don’t even travel down there. If you get an opportunity, I don’t care if you’ve never gotten a rep, if you’ve never gotten it in practice, and we call you off the sideline because you’re the last man that we have. You’re expected to go in there and play at the same level as the guy that’s taking every rep.” Credit to Deshea Townsend Last week, the Lions came out with a cornerback rotation to help combat the Packers’ deep-ball offense. When talking about the origins of that idea, Sheppard gave a ton of love to Lions defensive backs coach Deshea Townsend. “He gave me kind of some different scenarios of how he could do it and keep guys in the flow of the game and things like that. With him playing 12 years in the league, being out there, knowing how a DB flows in the game. And I’m going to be honest, I trusted him. I trusted him the same way I trust all my staff. That’s what leadership is, I believe.” Special teams coordinator Dave Fipp How the Lions knew they may get a blocked FG DJ Wonnum’s key blocked field goal that earned him Special Teams Player of the Week honors did not just happen with pure luck. It happened because the Lions recognized something mid-game and exploited it. Fipp credited special teams linebacker Trevor Nowaske with identifying the weakness. “You love when the players talk to you throughout the course of the game and give you information, and really, when that information is good. And earlier in the game, Nowaske came to me and said, ‘Man, we really like that call that we made on that field goal rush.‘ So, it ended up coming down late in the game, and it was like, okay, for me, you have got a choice of one of a couple calls. And it’s like, well, they obviously liked that one, so let’s go back to it. We went back to it, and that’s the one that made the difference.” Vikings returner Myles Price is a weapon This year, Vikings returner Myles Price ranks first in the NFL in punt return average (19.2) thanks to an 86-yard touchdown return. He’s also third in kick return average (30.7). Fipp explained what makes him so dangerous. “He’s got a great feel for setting up blocks. He’s got a great feel for where space is. He can see the whole field. So, if they’re setting up a return to take it down the left side, let’s say, he’ll take it down the right side if it opens up and he’ll see it.”

title: Detroit Lions mailbag: How does one beat the Vikings defense?
summary: The Detroit Lions, despite scoring just 20 points last week, did a pretty good job against the Green Bay Packers defense last week. Jared Goff was cooking in the first half of that game, and it led to him getting some serious recognition. But this week’s contest against the Minnesota Vikings is an entirely different […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 02: Defensive coordinator Brian Flores of the Minnesota Vikings looks on during the second half of a game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on November 02, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Mike Mulholland/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions, despite scoring just 20 points last week, did a pretty good job against the Green Bay Packers defense last week. Jared Goff was cooking in the first half of that game, and it led to him getting some serious recognition. But this week’s contest against the Minnesota Vikings is an entirely different beast. Whether it’s their ridiculous blitz rate, the outstanding play from their linebackers, or just how well they disguise everything, Minnesota is operating on an elite level on defense. They’re allowing just 12.3 points per game (first), with only a single team managing more than 20 against them so far. And in that game, the Vikings produced four sacks and two turnovers. On this week’s Midweek Mailbag podcast (recorded Tuesday), Erik Schlitt and I discussed the matchup against the Vikings defense this week. Will Jared Goff continue his success against the blitz? Where are the vulnerabilities against Brian Flores defenses? How will Detroit’s offensive line hold up amidst the chaos? On top of that discussion, we also hit the following topics: What’s going on with Detroit’s short-yardage running game and why not more QB sneaks? Explaining EPA and success rate statistics Did Dan Campbell cause a looser-officiated game vs. GB when it comes to pass interference? Thoughts on the recent play of Derrick Barnes and Jack Campbell What non-CB positions could the Lions trade for at the deadline? Dan Campbell’s strength in football awareness/situational readiness Could the Lions still be in the market for a defensive assistant should a good coach get fired (ie: Todd Bowles, Aaron Glenn)? title: Packers’ running game can’t close out Panthers in win
summary: The Packers had two chances to end the game against the Carolina Panthers and couldn’t close out either opportunity. The first came after the Panthers scored a touchdown (but missed the two-point conversion) to narrow the Packers’ lead to eight points. They kicked the ball back to the Packers with just over 5:30 to go […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 29: Josh Jacobs #8 of the Green Bay Packers runs the ball against Tre'von Moehrig #7 of the Carolina Panthers during the second quarter at Lambeau Field on October 29, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Packers had two chances to end the game against the Carolina Panthers and couldn’t close out either opportunity. The first came after the Panthers scored a touchdown (but missed the two-point conversion) to narrow the Packers’ lead to eight points. They kicked the ball back to the Packers with just over 5:30 to go in the game, and the offense promptly went nowhere. A screen pass to Tucker Kraft on first down was called back. Jordan Love threw incomplete to Matthew Golden on the re-do of first down, and although there was a lot of contact, no flag flew for defensive pass interference. On second down, Josh Jacobs caught a short checkdown pass but went out of bounds, stopping the clock. Then, after a bad snap on third down, Jordan Love was called for an intentional grounding penalty (a completely legit one, too, in a welcome change). Less than a minute had elapsed from the game clock and the Packers hadn’t attempted a run. The Panthers couldn’t generate a game-tying drive, turning the ball over on downs with 2:41 to go. Josh Jacobs scraped out eight yards on two carries, then Christian Watson, broken rib and all, caught a third down pass to convert, forcing the Panthers to burn their final timeout. With 2:28, the Packers just needed one first down to end any chance of the Panthers pulling off something miraculous. Instead, the Packers went the wrong way. Jacobs lost three yards, then gained one total yard back on his next two attempts, forcing the Packers to punt the ball away with about 30 seconds remaining. Carolina had a long way to go and no timeouts to help them, but they were technically in business until a Dani Dennis-Sutton sack put them in an even deeper hole. Their final lateral-heavy play went nowhere, and the game mercifully ended. The questions, however, were just starting. Why couldn’t the Packers close out the game, especially on their second chance? Matt LaFleur didn’t have an answer. “It was disappointing. I would say it’s disappointing,” he said. “Obviously got the one first down, and then we tried to lean on the run game and we went backwards. So that’s an area of emphasis that we have to improve upon because it puts a lot of pressure on your pass game to continue to just find ways to move the ball down the field.” LaFleur is right to focus on the run game. If there’s ever a time when you have to be able to move the ball on the ground, it’s in those crucial close-out drives. Keeping the clock moving while grinding out yards is perhaps the purest form of football; as every coach since the dawn of time has pointed out, as long as you can eke out three yards on every play (cloud of dust optional), your offense is technically unstoppable. You will never run out of downs and you can drain the clock at will. The Packers cannot do that, and Matt LaFleur is obviously frustrated. “We have got to find something that we can hang our hat on in the run game and unfortunately we have not done that yet,” he said. At least his assessment is accurate. As long as the Packers struggle to run the ball, the passing game will have to shoulder more and more of the load. That’s not necessarily a bad thing; Jordan Love has shown he’s more than capable of carrying the load (he’s on pace for career highs in just about every passing stat that matters), but the more you lean on him, the more things can break down. Take Love’s ill-advised interception early in the fourth quarter. Are the Packers taking end zone shots on 3rd and 8 if they thought there was a chance they could set themselves up for a short fourth down run instead? We’ll never know, but it makes you wonder, and the more passing plays you feel like you have to call, the more opportunities arise for one poor decision to result in a turnover. LaFleur doesn’t seem optimistic that things are going to turn around, either. Asked if he was seeing anything that makes him optimistic better rushing days ahead, he was blunt. “I mean, if I’m being honest, not a lot right now. And that’s our job as coaches. We got to figure it out because it’s not good enough.” It certainly isn’t, but at this point any improvement would be a surprise.
author: Jon Meerdink

title: Matt LaFleur explains Packers’ offensive line decisions
summary: Another week, another new offensive line configuration in Green Bay. This time, the Packers had three different starters than in their last game, featuring new or different faces at all three interior line spots. Aaron Banks made his long-awaited (or, perhaps, long-feared, depending on your opinion of Banks) return to his left guard spot, finding […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 29: Head coach Matt LaFleur of the Green Bay Packers runs onto the field prior to an NFL football game against the Carolina Panthers at Lambeau Field on October 29, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Another week, another new offensive line configuration in Green Bay. This time, the Packers had three different starters than in their last game, featuring new or different faces at all three interior line spots. Aaron Banks made his long-awaited (or, perhaps, long-feared, depending on your opinion of Banks) return to his left guard spot, finding his way into the lineup for the first time since he played 22 snaps in Week 2. Laken Tomlinson flipped from left guard to right guard, making his first start on the right side since the Obama administration. And John Williams made his first ever NFL start at the position he played where he played game snaps for the first time ever last week. But, you know, other than that it was basically a normal week up front. Why this configuration, though? John Williams at center makes logical sense; he played there last week and is the only remaining player the Packers seem to like at the spot with Jacob Monk on injured reserve, although Jager Burton may end up there eventually. But at the guard spots, Matt LaFleur offered little explanation for the moves he made. “Well I just think when you look at it, you know, the way Laken’s been playing, you can’t take him out of the lineup. And I thought Aaron Banks coming back…so we went with that route,” he said postgame. “That’s not to take anything away from [Kevin] Zeitler. Certainly we feel good about him as well. But we thought that was the move.” There’s plenty to unpack there, assuming LaFleur is being completely forthright (and that’s a big assumption, given he has no incentive to shoot straight with us). First, LaFleur asserts Tomlinson has been playing well. “Playing well” might be a bridge too far for me, but he’s at least better than Donovan Jennings, Jager Burton, and Jacob Monk, so I’ll concede the point. He’s at least been okay in pass protection (and LaFleur praised the Packers’ pass protection later in his postgame remarks). Second, LaFleur seems to take it as a matter of course that Banks deserves to be in the lineup. But Banks was active last week and didn’t play. Travis Glover started at right guard and Tomlinson was at his familiar left guard spot. The lineup math there would seem to indicate LaFleur thinks Banks is worse than Glover and better than Zeitler (who was inactive against the Lions). And what of Zeitler? The Packers signed him to a one-year, $4.05 million deal on September 30, but he hasn’t been on the field for a single snap on offense so far, though he’s played 15 snaps on special teams. His contract includes heavy playing time incentives and he stands to reap some not-inconsiderable financial rewards if he hits certain playing time thresholds, but it’s hard to believe the Packers would really be pinching pennies that hard. So what gives? Is he not in game shape? Is he really not better than Tomlinson or Banks (or Glover, for that matter)? It’s a mystery, and LaFleur didn’t give us any significant explanations after the Packers’ Thursday night win. In fact,he muddied the waters even further, pointing out when asked that Tomlinson was not getting regular reps at right guard before the Packers installed him there this week. “It’s definitely a challenge and he answered the bell,” LaFleur offered of Tomlinson’s sudden appearance on the right. That may be so, but it appears to be a challenge of the Packers’ own making. But that describes a lot of their offensive line issues this year, for what it’s worth. Until the Packers can get out of their own way, it seems doubtful the offensive line will improve much more.
author: Jon Meerdink

title: Green Bay Packers News: Run game remains abysmal despite win
summary: The Green Bay Packers had a perfect opportunity to get their running game back on track on Thursday. They were facing the Carolina Panthers, who had just allowed 258 rushing yards to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers four days earlier, and they got them on a short week. Josh Jacobs was back — and although mileage […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 29: Josh Jacobs #8 of the Green Bay Packers scores a touchdown during the second quarter against the Carolina Panthers at Lambeau Field on October 29, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers had a perfect opportunity to get their running game back on track on Thursday. They were facing the Carolina Panthers, who had just allowed 258 rushing yards to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers four days earlier, and they got them on a short week. Josh Jacobs was back — and although mileage will surely vary on whether or not an individual Packers fan thinks that’s a good thing in general, he is clearly the most talented running back on the team’s roster. So what did the Packers actually do on the ground? They picked up 66 net yards on 26 carries. One of those runs was an end-around to Savion Williams for 18 yards, so the running backs combined for 48 yards on 25 carries, less than two yards per carry on average. It does not feel like hyperbole to say that this is the worst rushing attack in Packers history, and it may well be the worst in NFL history. The fact that the Packers threw the ball on 3rd and 2 late in the game to try to run out the clock should come as no surprise, because this offense has no choice but to run through Jordan Love. And Love played well once again on Thursday night, generally getting the ball out quickly and accurately. Love had just one mistake — a terrible decision on an interception towards the end zone early in the fourth quarter — but otherwise he put up a great performance. 30 of 41 for 288 yards and three touchdowns will get the job done most days, and it certainly did against the Panthers on Sunday. The Packers still made their share of mistakes. Two fumbles, including one on the opening kickoff, could have been a death sentence against a better team. There were still drops, though Matthew Golden made up for one in the end zone with a touchdown on the very next play. But the penalty issues were better, and maybe there’s something to build on here. It just isn’t the running game. Game recap: 5 takeaways from Packers’ victory over Panthers | Packers.com While the offense still has major issues to iron out, the defense stifled Carolina for much of the game, getting some big 4th down stops and posting six sacks, one each from six different players. Christian Watson’s return from hospital leaves Packers teammates stunned | Packers Wire Watson left the game in the first half and got checked out at a local hospital, but he returned in an ambulance after halftime and made a clutch catch on 3rd-and-2 to all but seal the game. Packers Report Card: Big Win Over Panthers Comes With Two F’s | SI.com The run game, as expected, gets a failure, but so does the special teams, thanks to another missed PAT by Trey Smack and the fumble by Coleman Owen on the opening kick. Packers’ Josh Jacobs: TD celebration was ode to gospel song, not mocking arrest | ESPN I’m sorry, when you have more than 20 carries and fewer than 40 yards, it’s tough to celebrate too much at all. But the lack of awareness by Jacobs for how his “handcuffs” celebration would be perceived is just another example of poor judgment on his part. Here’s a good recap on just how badly the Packers missed their chance to get the run game going again: Patrick Stewart, legendary actor of ‘Star Trek’ and ‘X-Men’ fame, dies at 86 | AP.com No funny link tonight, just a sad one: one of the iconic actors of the last several decades, and a genuinely excellent human being, passed away this week. title: Packers Snap Counts, Week 8: It’s the Josh Jacobs show in Green Bay
summary: The Green Bay Packers made a couple of adjustments to their roster this week, starting with who they decided to activate for their 48-man game-day active list. Let’s go position-by-position through the Packers’ snap counts from their Week 8 win over the Carolina Panthers, noting where some things have changed with the team. Quarterback Running […]
full_text: (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers made a couple of adjustments to their roster this week, starting with who they decided to activate for their 48-man game-day active list. Let’s go position-by-position through the Packers’ snap counts from their Week 8 win over the Carolina Panthers, noting where some things have changed with the team. Quarterback Jordan Love: 67 snaps Tyrod Taylor: 0 Running Back Josh Jacobs: 47 MarShawn Lloyd: 11 Pierre Strong Jr.: 9 Scratch: Kaleb Johnson Last week, Josh Jacobs took 35 snaps to MarShawn Lloyd’s 24 and Pierre Strong Jr.‘s 8. This week, Jacobs took 70 percent of the offense’s snaps compared to just 52 percent a week ago, when Lloyd was closer to Jacobs than Strong. Moving forward, it appears that it will be the Jacobs show in the backfield, though none of the backs had a great night on the ground against Carolina. In total, the three backs combined for 1.9 yards per carry. Receiver Matthew Golden: 58 Savion Williams: 36 Christian Watson: 33 J. Michael Sturdivant: 28 Bo Melton: 24 Coleman Owen: 0 Christian Watson left this game in an ambulance when he broke a rib and was spitting up blood, leading to him getting tests at a local hospital before returning to Lambeau Field. That’s the explanation for why Watson, who had a 100-yard game, was out-snapped by Savion Williams, who previously filled the role of the team’s slot receiver. Tight End Tucker Kraft: 59 Mark Redman: 27 Josh Whyle: 3 Scratch: Jonnu Smith In an interesting move, the Packers made Jonnu Smith a healthy scratch for the first time in 2026, allowing the team to call up practice squad edge defender Arron Mosby. Unfortunately for Green Bay, a team used to having four tight ends active on game day, it was terrible timing to be short at the position, as Josh Whyle left the game with a concussion early on, leaving the Packers with just Tucker Kraft and Mark Redman at the position for the vast majority of the game. Whyle was the only player who dropped out of play and did not return against the Panthers. Offensive Line Jordan Morgan: 67 Aaron Banks: 67 John Williams: 67 Laken Tomlinson: 67 Anthony Belton: 67 Kevin Zeitler: 0 Mekhi Becton: 0 Jager Burton: 0 Scratches: Donovan Jennings, Sean Rhyan and Travis Glover Many expected the Packers to roll with Kevin Zeitler at right guard when it was announced that Travis Glover (along with center Sean Rhyan) was going to be scratched in this game due to injury. Instead, Green Bay pushed Laken Tomlinson over from the left side, allowing for Aaron Banks to come off the bench and make a start at left guard. In his post-game press conference, head coach Matt LaFleur stated that due to the way that Tomlinson was playing, he didn’t believe it was right for the guard to be benched. So that’s your explanation for why Zeitler didn’t get looks today. Already, Mekhi Becton, who was brought up from the practice squad this week, was a healthy nod over Donovan Jennings, who was a full-time guard for the Packers early on in the season. 13 different offensive linemen have now been active for Green Bay in 2026. title: Packers-Panthers Final Score: Pressure gets to Carolina’s Bryce Young
summary: The Green Bay Packers are up to a 5-3 record after their Thursday Night Football win over the Carolina Panthers. The Packers won. The Milwaukee Brewers trotted around their new trophy. Kevin Harlan gave a speech at halftime on behalf of his father, who was added to the team’s ring of honor. It feels like […]
full_text: (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers are up to a 5-3 record after their Thursday Night Football win over the Carolina Panthers. The Packers won. The Milwaukee Brewers trotted around their new trophy . Kevin Harlan gave a speech at halftime on behalf of his father, who was added to the team’s ring of honor. It feels like it should be more of a joyful night for Green Bay, but their lack of a run game, which has been a season-long issue for the team, is what kept the Panthers alive with a chance to tie on the final play of the 27-19 ballgame. Despite getting Aaron Banks back at left guard, which pushed Laken Tomlinson to right guard, Green Bay’s backs weren’t able to get anything going against the NFL’s worst rush defense. On the night, the Packers’ three backs combined for 25 carries and 48 yards, just a 1.9 yards per carry average. Eventually, this team is going to need to turn the corner in the rushing game, or it’s going to cost them down the line. The game flow of tonight’s action went back and forth. Receiver Coleman Owen, who was limited to just punt return duty before tonight, fumbled the opening snap of the game, giving the Panthers a 3-0 lead. The Packers eventually rallied to go up 27-13 before Carolina drove on a long 12-play, 70-yard series that gave them an opportunity at the end. Another swing of momentum was when kicker Trey Smack, who has had his struggles as of late, missed an extra point on Green Bay’s first go-ahead drive of the game. The leading receiver for the Packers was Christian Watson, who had nine receptions for 113 yards, despite taking a trip to the hospital mid-game for a chest injury. This game had a little of everything. Defensively, the story of the game was that Green Bay was able to get pressure on Panthers quarterback Bryce Young, something they weren’t able to do to Detroit’s Jared Goff on Sunday. Young ended up taking six sacks and posting just 176 total yards on 47 dropbacks (3.7 yards per play), much lower than Jordan Love’s 288 on 41 (7.0). The Packers will have a “mini-bye” leading up to next Sunday’s matchup against the New England Patriots.

title: Packers Roster: Which kickers could replace Trey Smack?
summary: I didn’t think I was going to have to post this midway through a game, but after Green Bay Packers kicker Trey Smack missed his first extra point after missing two chip shots last week, it seems pretty clear that it’s a question of when — not if — Smack will be replaced. Going into […]
full_text: (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images I didn’t think I was going to have to post this midway through a game, but after Green Bay Packers kicker Trey Smack missed his first extra point after missing two chip shots last week, it seems pretty clear that it’s a question of when — not if — Smack will be replaced. Going into this game, I had done some research on who is available, so I want to share that with you folks. I looked at all kickers who even attempted a field goal from 2024 to 2026, the last three seasons. Outside of punters, there are a total of 55 players who have attempted kicks. Of those 55 players, 46 of them are under contract for other teams or appear to be out of the league entirely, either due to injury or retirement. As far as players on the street go, here’s the list that the Packers can look at during their “mini-bye.” Generally, kickers are worked out before they’re signed, not poached off a practice squad, so I’m not going to include the practice squadders in this list. Riley Patterson Since 2024: 38 of 45 (84 percent field goal rate) Recent: Released by Dolphins, 10/20 Younghoe Koo Since 2024: 31 of 43 (72 percent) Recent: Worked out by 49ers, 9/19 Note: Played five games for Packers SPT coordinator Cam Achord in 2025 Matt Prater Since 2024: 24 of 26 (92 percent) Recent: Worked out by Rams 10/20 John Parker Romo Since 2024: 22 of 26 (85 percent) Recent: Worked out by Titans 8/8 Harrison Mevis Since 2024: 17 of 22 (77 percent) Recent: Released by Rams on 10/14 Greg Joseph Since 2024: 16 of 20 (80 percent) Recent: Worked out by 49ers, 9/19 Note: Former Packer Note: Played six games for Packers SPT coordinator Cam Achrod in 2024 Cade York Since 2024: 9 of 13 (69 percent) Recent: Waived by Jets, 8/25 Michael Badgley Since 2024: 11 of 12 (92 percent) Recent: Worked out by Dolphins, 10/20 Lucas Havrisik Since 2024: 4 of 4 (100 percent) Recent: Worked out by Dolphins, 9/22 Note: Former Packer Unless Green Bay goes the practice squad poaching route, this is likely the list the team will work from, whenever they eventually move off Smack. title: Why the Houston Texans are the worst franchise in the NFL
summary: It’s almost more painful to read that headline than it was to write it. The worst franchise in the NFL. Especially given all the hope from this past off/pre-season. Leading up to this season, it seemed like that might not be true. It felt different. It felt like this was finally the year the Texans […]
full_text: It’s almost more painful to read that headline than it was to write it. The worst franchise in the NFL . Especially given all the hope from this past off/pre-season. Leading up to this season, it seemed like that might not be true. It felt different. It felt like this was finally the year the Texans would break through. National media had them in Super Bowl conversations. A line for white out merch wrapped around the stadium. It really seemed like the Texans had finally arrived. Then, reality struck. Head coach Demeco Ryans and defensive coordinator Matt Burke made a fundamental scheme change to the defense. Offensive coordinator Nick Caley regressed the offense. No one from Cal & Hannah McNair down to the ball boys thought the team needed a great offensive line coach who could take a ragtag bunch of linemen and teach them to be winners. And here we are, sitting at 2-5, staring down the barrel of another year cementing the “worst NFL franchise” tag. Why are the Houston Texans the worst? Is it year after year of Bill O’Brien/Jack Easterby nonsense? Is it an owner who would rather play video games than run a successful NFL team? Is it simply that the NFL is rigged and some team needs to be the worst, and H-Town houses that team? A series of unfortunate events that follow the franchise around like a delusional Cowboy fan? All of those are possible contributors, but this isn’t about opinion or theory or #Hawtakez or anything of the sort. It’s simply about success rate. For a very long time, the Oakland/LA Raiders and the Baltimore Orioles were the best franchises in pro sports. Not because of any immeasurable sentiment, but due to success rate. At their height, the Raiders had the highest win percentage in pro sports history, including 3 Super Bowl championships and 4 AFL/AFC championships. That’s the stat set, winning games and winning championships. Stadium-Maps.com Over 2 decades without a Conference Championship There are nine teams to have never won an NFL championship (since its inception in 1920), but only two of those franchises have never even made it to a Super Bowl final (1970-present). They are the Houston Texans (the NFL’s newest franchise established in 2002) and the Jacksonville Jaguars established just 6 years earlier in 1996. The Jacksonville Jaguars , however, have appeared in a conference championship game whereas the Houston Texans have not, so statistically, the Lone Star State outfit is the least successful NFL franchise in terms of getting closest to the Vince Lombardi Trophy. That’s a bitter pill to swallow. The Texans are worse than the Glitter Kitties. A paraphrase of that sentence has probably launched it’s fair share of stadium and bar fights over the last 2.5 decades. But, numbers don’t lie. When it comes to championship game appearances, the Texans are .000 all time. When it comes to actual win/loss rate, the Texans are ahead of the Jags, with H-Town sitting at .446 when this season started, while the Kitties are .432. The Tampa Bay Buccaneers hold the lowest spot at .411, but have 2 Lombardis in their trophy case. If all this isn’t depressing enough for you, the Texans diehard, then give this interview a listen to hear former Texans Steven Nelson break down what he saw from the stands last weekend: Former Texan Steven Nelson EXPOSES What's Wrong With Houston's Defense?! 👀 DeMeco Ryans INSIDE LOOK https://t.co/Z8353HAiM2 — Will Kunkel (@WillKunkelV) October 28, 2026 My takeaway from the interview with Nelson: Demeco needs a fire lit under him to get this defense back into a scheme that utilizes all the star power. Caserio needs to hire an OC who is his own man, not a yes man, not an extension of himself or Ryans, but a true offensive mind who can utilize this offense properly. Said OC and Caserio need to hire an offensive line coach who can whip the o-line into shape. Best of all, there’s still a (very, very small) statistical chance this team can pull its act together and get to the Super Bowl this year. It won’t be easy, and it has zero margin for error, but it can still be done. The time to move this franchise off the “never made it to a championship game” list is now. The upcoming Houston Texans schedule is winnable, but not unless they use the bye week to make some legit changes. And if not, it’s time to stop pushing alternate uni merch and start giving away paper bags for fans to wear on game day. O’Brien is gone. Lovie is gone. Culley is gone. Time to leave the losing behind with them. #GoTexans

title: Where do the Houston Texans go from here?
summary: Reality isn’t that the Texans are 2-5, that Stroud is deserving of a mega contract, or that the offensive line hasn’t materially improved in a decade of reconstruction. Houston has already lost as many games this year as all of last season. This season is oddly reminiscent of the 2013 and especially the 2020 campaigns […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - OCTOBER 25: C.J. Stroud #7 of the Houston Texans drops back to pass against the New York Giants during the first half of an NFL football game at Reliant Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Reality isn’t that the Texans are 2-5, that Stroud is deserving of a mega contract, or that the offensive line hasn’t materially improved in a decade of reconstruction. Houston has already lost as many games this year as all of last season. This season is oddly reminiscent of the 2013 and especially the 2020 campaigns where the Texans came off of historic years and completely floundered under the spotlight. The reality is that this roster isn’t good. The Giants proved that. Houston is 2-5 and with an 8% chance to make the playoffs according to New York Time’s simulator. The remaining schedule offers little room for opportunity to make it back into playoff contention. Houston Texans remaining schedule At Los Angeles Chargers (0-6) At Cleveland Browns (5-2) Vs Indianapolis Colts (2-5) Vs Baltimore Ravens (4-3) At Pittsburgh Steelers (5-2) At Washington Commanders (1-4-1) Vs Jacksonville Jaguars (4-2) At Philadelphia Eagles (2-5) At Green Bay Packers (4-3) Vs Tennessee Titans (1-6) Houston only plays five team with losing records, which includes the Eagles who are a sleeping giant. The loss against the Giants was a critical blow to their chances. At 3-4, they would have been squarely in the Wild Card race with three winnable games in a row after the bye week. Now, they are still being asked to dig out of a trench that’s far too deep. So, with little to no chance to win the division, let alone make the playoffs, Houston is in a horrible spot. What’s worse is the Texans are ALREADY $33.8M over their 2027 salary cap. They are going to have to make aggressive cuts to this already weak roster. Plus, they won’t have a second round pick due to the Marvin Harrison Jr. trade. This article and my thoughts specifically aren’t around tanking. Tanking is only for teams with draft assets that need complete, multi-position overhauls. That isn’t the Texans. Besides, there are at least four teams (Tennessee, Miami, Los Angeles, Arizona, and Washington who are capable of out-tanking Houston. Coming in at least sixth in the draft is not a worthy proposition to tank for. 🤯 𝐓𝐇𝐈𝐒 𝐌𝐀𝐊𝐄𝐒 𝐍𝐎 𝐒𝐄𝐍𝐒𝐄: The Houston Texans are tied for the NFL lead with 21 sacks. Yet their secondary has allowed: • 34 completions of 20+ yards — MOST in NFL • 5 completions of 40+ yards • Just 2 interceptions all season pic.twitter.com/eOR4tLQmYp — Polymarket Football (@PolymarketBlitz) October 28, 2026 The defense must evolve because the equation to beat the Texans has gotten simple. Chip the Texans defensive ends as much as possible, then beat them down the sidelines on deep balls. Keep away from the middle where they will hit you and flood the defense with options to make them play one-on-one. The Texans secondary in a tricky spot where when they play soft coverage they are beaten underneath, but when they press and get physical they are beaten down the field. They can’t generate pass rush in the interior and even worse can’t stop the run to save their lives. It’s a crumbling system built off of talent alone, but when the entire league has the same playbook, talent won’t win the day. Houston moved to a five-man front often against the Giants. It moved rookie Kaydem McDonald back to his normal nose tackle position and took the pressure off of Tommy Togiai, who has wildly under-performed against the run. While this paid off early, it limits Houston’s versatility in the secondary. More bodies up front means less players to cover and JJ McCarthy put that together quite quickly on Sunday. The issues Houston is facing are directly related to mistakes made this offseason. The two second round picks rarely see the field or even suit up on game day. The two marquee offensive lineman from free agency Wyatt Teller and Braden Smith play as much football as you or I do. Reed Blankenship is verging on Ed Reed territory of historic free agent busts. David Montgomery is injured and confirmed cannot run through a wall. The house that Nick Caserio build is all crashing down in real time. The Marvin Harrison move, while instantly productive, was a hasty decision made of good intentions but poor long-term planning. Tank Dell is back and looks strong. The other WRs are now playing well. Did Houston need a WR more than a top-end defensive tackle? Houston’s future assets could have been much better utilized than a semi-capable receiver with only one more full season on his contract. The problems are real and will not be solved in one bye week. With a difficult schedule and AFC with nine teams over .500, there’s little to no-chance Houston can turn this horrific start into another miracle run. With nowhere up to go and nowhere down to move, the only place to go is young. Get valuable reps for Marlin Klein. See how Kamari Ramsey does at safety and Jaylin Smith at corner. Run Wade Woodaz instead of Jake Hansen. Most importantly, I don’t think firing Nick Caserio nor DeMeco Ryans is the right decision. The braintrust did get us in this position, but we are only here because of them. Caserio is one of the most dynamic GMs in the league and outside of the offensive line and safeties is a quality evaluator of talent.
author: Kenneth Levy

title: The Colts have gotten off the merry-go-round and onto the roller coaster.
summary: There is a great 1989 film called Parenthood. Steve Martin wants normalcy in his life, but there is a lot going on that makes this difficult for him. His grandmother offers a story about how some of her friends liked the merry-go-round, but she didn’t because it just went round and round. She preferred the […]
full_text: The Hoosier Hurricane roller coaster at Indiana Beach. 070516 News Indbeach | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co There is a great 1989 film called Parenthood. Steve Martin wants normalcy in his life, but there is a lot going on that makes this difficult for him. His grandmother offers a story about how some of her friends liked the merry-go-round, but she didn’t because it just went round and round. She preferred the ups and downs of the roller coaster. Martin didn’t really get the story as a metaphor until a little later when he was able to embrace it. Colts fans need to be ready to embrace the ride. With the Ballard era over, we can no longer expect the consistency of playing around .500 football. It had it’s minor ups and downs, but is better categorized as a boring mediocre ride. The biggest spike could have been seeing the low of firing Riech and hiring Saturday, but the subsequent haul from that bad season did not see the high of the Colts return to the playoffs. The big swing on AR was a miss, so QB purgatory remained. The miss put them back firmly on the meh ride. Make no mistake, the new ride is going to be come with more of those ups and downs. It doesn’t feel like we are at the apex, but we are at the point of the ride, where you plunge fast and hard to build momentum for the rest of the ride. Coasters are cool, you just have to survive the plunge, before you get some loops and climbs. We are definitely going to plunge some more and may not see that exciting twist until the new GM and coaches are picked. We may get another rush when we dip into free agency and again when we draft. Here are some other things that will contribute to the volatility of the ride: Not everyone is going to be happy with the GM hire. Those not happy with the GM hire, are likely not going to like the new staff either. Not everyone is going to be happy with free agency. We will either be too active while destroying the salary cap, or not active enough and slipping back into Ballard’s frugal ways. We may or may not like the draft, as that is one that we seldom agree on and it can take a little time to determine whether a pick is good or not. For me, the hard part is going to be trying to enjoy the plunge, or at least get excited about the rest of the ride. As we watch long tenured players leave the building, you know that some of their teammates will now get an opportunity, and it will make room for next year’s acquisitions. I probably will get a little rush when Steichen and Lou get their walking papers, but a twist that sees them retained would put me further into plunge mode. I guess that is what a roller coaster is all about. Some things to keep our interest moving forward this year: The continuation of the purge and just how much Dodd will be allowed to do, while still in that role. It is too bad that Burks is the only young WR we could get a better look at. With Downs gone (likely), we will have to use draft capital or cap space to reload the WR room. Maybe we see Mallory more frequently in the flex role? He’s had flashes, but certainly nothing sustained. There is no reason for Pierce to suit up the rest of the year. If JT can’t get traction behind the makeshift OL, just sit him and plan for a healthy 2027. I wouldn’t play him until the deadline passes and would prefer seeing him dealt. He did essentially sit out and ask for a trade, while also committing the AD sin of celebrating short of the goal line. McGowen probably profiles better with his downhill, hit the first thing that looks like a hole approach. We are going to run a lot the rest of the year. I have no reason to believe that AR will be with the team next year, as it would cost 50+ million to franchise tag him and he has already asked to leave. However, I’d give him the opportunity to bump up his price tag by putting him out there until his next injury occurs. Jones is a shell of himself and seeing him behind a line without Nelson, is a recipe for an injury that could run into next year. Worst case, you have a 3rd string QB who you need to see if is a viable QB2 moving forward. He’s probably not, but his run with the 1’s last year was serviceable. It might be interesting to see what Farmer can do at one of the Guard spots. If Dalton Tucker gets the start, it is evidence that Farmer was not a great pick. It couldn’t hurt to give someone else a look at RT as well. Not much reason to play Warren until he is 100%. We know what we have in our veteran TEs, so keep an eye on that position next Spring. Maybe someone asks about Cox or Ogletree and their expiring contract? Give Adebawore as many snaps as he can handle, so he has a reason to re-sign here. Quit playing the rookie ends at the same time and put one of them opposite Latu more often. I assume that they have talked to Grove and asked his wishes for this year. Moving him and re-signing him next year could be an option if he fits the new regime’s plans. He wouldn’t bring a lot, but he could be somebody’s Booger McFarland. I’d see if I could get a 7th or possibly a 6th by adding our 7th, to find another home for ADG. It is not likely that anyone not named Lou will see him as an asset. Obviously, play the rookie LBs as much as possible. I’m not sure that you get the kind of offer you hope for with Sauce and he should be kept for the next group to decide how he fits their plans. Then there are brass considerations: At what point do you announce that Dodds will or will not be considered for the GM role next year? Is it worth it to see what your position coaches could do in a coordinator or even HC role? If you fired Shane, would you give Reggie the role and let Jim Bob call plays? Reggie has to be like most position coaches, as they see their job as a stepping stone toward being the boss. Giving him that opportunity could be a real plus for him down the road. I would think the team’s situational awareness would double with such a move. He’d certainly have a leg up on Saturday. Just how much will we hear from Carlie over the next few weeks? What will be the message to the fans? “Bear with us, it is not as urgent as we stated earlier this year”? We are relevant right now, only because we are making moves. As soon as that process is over, the best we can hope for is, “They haven’t packed it in.” Unless you do hope they pack it in to have a better 2nd, 3rd,etc.. round pick. I’m mainly hoping that I have a reason not to constantly use the FF button when watching my stream. It may not be long before I go ahead and watch the 1:00 games, even if I run the risk of knowing the outcome of our game, before I watch. A lot of folks have been asking for the roller coaster for a while now. Pull that harness down and hold on!

title: Should the Colts trade Jonathan Taylor?
summary: Whether one should or shouldn’t do something isn’t as much about the action itself but more about the downstream effects. What is the risk vs reward? Is this a good thing with a positive net outcome, or is it potentially riddled with consequences? Trading Jonathan Taylor is now on the table after the fire sale […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 25: Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts runs with the ball past Isaiah Rodgers #2 of the Minnesota Vikings to score a touchdown in the first quarter at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images Whether one should or shouldn’t do something isn’t as much about the action itself but more about the downstream effects. What is the risk vs reward? Is this a good thing with a positive net outcome, or is it potentially riddled with consequences? Trading Jonathan Taylor is now on the table after the fire sale started for the Indianapolis Colts. That doesn’t mean he will be traded. Then again, it all comes back to the risk and reward. What is Taylor worth on the NFL trade market? That is the million dollar question. The Colts are seemingly asking for at least a first-round pick to headline the trade. Although this year isn’t his best, Taylor is one of the best backs and players in the league. He finds the end zone and makes big plays. That is worth a lot. He is a running back, however, and the league has shown how that position’s value fluctuates. This is the back half of his prime too, but he should still have enough juice for a team to make a trade. The Colts have to determine if the juice is worth the squeeze, however, based on the return compensation. Entering a rebuild, draft capital is huge. Taylor can certainly fetch some of that. What he is worth on the NFL trade market and what he is worth to the Indianapolis Colts are two different things, though. He is a captain, although that hasn’t held as much weight the last few days. He is a leader and franchise player. Taylor is one of the few remaining big names on the team. His value with a new/rookie quarterback could be invaluable. Giving a rookie a strong running game is the perfect way to ease them into things. Letting Taylor go, especially for less than desired, and seeing him tear it up with another team would be a hard pill to swallow. Every decision comes with the unknown. In sports, those decisions are under a microscope as everyone is trying to determine who got the better deal. Terms like “fleeced,” “hosed,” and “heist” are thrown around in the immediate. The long-term can change those views, but that will be the talk if the Colts move on from Jonathan Taylor. Take the draft picks to rebuild, or hold on to the last pillar this team has? What’s the move?
author: Jon Spradley

However, he did acknowledge his current uncertain future, which still […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - OCTOBER 18: Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts warms up prior to the game against the Tennessee Titans at Lucas Oil Stadium on October 18, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Thursday, Indianapolis Colts star running back Jonathan Taylor, who’s arguably the franchise’s last longstanding veteran cornerstone still remaining after the recent trades of both Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner, indicated that he has not requested a trade from the only organization he’s ever known. However, he did acknowledge his current uncertain future, which still appears to be very fluid in Indianapolis: #Colts RB Jonathan Taylor confirmed that he has *NOT* requested a trade, but he acknowledged that he doesn’t have full control of his future. — James Boyd (@RomeovilleKid) October 29, 2026 As a major subject of ongoing trade rumors, Taylor seems proud and comfortable to continue to wear the Horseshoe, and earlier reports indicated that Indianapolis team owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon potentially considers Taylor a major part of the Colts recently jumpstarted rebuilding efforts . That being said, Taylor is 27-years-old with 1,691 career carries in the NFL and 926 more collegiately at Wisconsin, at a running back position where players typically don’t age gracefully past the age of 30-years-old. Either the Colts or an acquiring team are realistically looking at 2-3 prime years left regarding Taylor, and for Indianapolis, that’s likely about the minimum amount of time that it would take to complete a successful rebuild these days—assuming conditions go well with a new quarterback, head coach, and general manager all likely. However, keeping a future Colts Ring of Honor player and potential Hall of Famer in the building around young players could be a beneficial thing as far as teaching them an elite work ethic, preparation, approach, etc. It seems to me that the Colts could be persuaded to trade Taylor soon, but it would have to take a significant haul in draft capital from a suitor, presumably the ask right now appears to be at least a first round pick, maybe more. Whether that asking price will go down, like say a second round pick, as we get closer to this year’s trade deadline on Tuesday, November 10th, remains to be seen. However, for now, Taylor is still remaining in Indianapolis.
