title: Stampede Blue Reacts results (Week 8): Colts fan confidence plummets amid roster overhaul
summary: The latest SB Nation Reacts survey shows a significant decline in confidence among Indianapolis Colts fans, with just 31 percent believing the franchise is headed in the right direction. That’s a substantial 16-percentage-point drop from last week’s 47 percent, suggesting that whatever optimism emerged following the firing of general manager Chris Ballard has quickly begun […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 25: Carlie Irsay-Gordon, owner of the Indianapolis Colts looks on before the game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The latest SB Nation Reacts survey shows a significant decline in confidence among Indianapolis Colts fans, with just 31 percent believing the franchise is headed in the right direction . That’s a substantial 16-percentage-point drop from last week’s 47 percent, suggesting that whatever optimism emerged following the firing of general manager Chris Ballard has quickly begun to fade. Last week’s results suggested that fans were beginning to regain some hope following Ballard’s dismissal, despite the team’s embarrassing loss to the previously winless Tennessee Titans. However, another disappointing performance against the Minnesota Vikings did little to improve the mood surrounding the franchise. Indianapolis fell 16-10 on Sunday, dropping to 2-5 and extending its losing streak to three games. While the defense kept the Colts competitive throughout the afternoon, another ineffective offensive performance raised further questions about Shane Steichen’s ability to turn things around with Daniel Jones under center. The situation became even more complicated Tuesday when Indianapolis traded two of its most accomplished veterans, sending eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks and three-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle DeForest Buckner to the San Francisco 49ers. In return, the Colts acquired a 2027 third-round pick, a 2027 fourth-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round selection. The moves represented a significant shift in the organization’s approach, suggesting that Indianapolis is now prioritizing the future rather than attempting to salvage an increasingly disappointing season. While accumulating draft capital could prove beneficial in the long run, losing two of the franchise’s best players undoubtedly creates additional uncertainty. Nelson had been a cornerstone of the offensive line since 2018, while Buckner remained one of the defense’s most reliable contributors (maybe the most reliable). Their departures leave significant holes on both sides of the football, and with wide receiver Josh Downs reportedly requesting a trade as well, there is growing speculation that additional veterans could be moved before the November 10 trade deadline. The decline to 31 percent reflects a fan base with plenty of reasons to question where the organization is headed, although the results do not tell us which developments influenced individual voters. Some may welcome the decision to begin rebuilding through the draft, while others are understandably frustrated with the prospect of another lengthy transition after years of disappointing results. With Indianapolis also lacking its first-round selection in the 2027 NFL Draft following the Sauce Gardner trade, whoever takes over as general manager will face considerable challenges in rebuilding the roster. For now, the Colts still have ten games remaining and an opportunity to show some progress under Steichen. However, with the franchise increasingly focused on the future and uncertainty surrounding several of its remaining stars, restoring confidence among fans will likely require more than a few organizational changes. Indianapolis needs to demonstrate that it has a clear plan for returning to contention, something that has been missing for far too long. FanDuel Sportsbook
author: Andrew Aziz

title: 5 Questions with Stampede Blue: The Colts’ Rebuild is Underway
summary: As the Jacksonville Jaguars prepare to face the Indianapolis Colts in Week 8, we exchanged questions with Chris Shepherd of Stampede Blue to learn more about the opposing side. Question 1: The Colts are officially in “rebuilding” mode. Did the firing of general manager Chris Ballard catch you by surprise? And how long a leash […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - NOVEMBER 30: Indianapolis Colts running back Jonathan Taylor (28) runs up the sideline behind Indianapolis Colts guard Quenton Nelson (56) during and NFL game between the Houston Texans and the Indianapolis Colts on November 30, 2025 at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis, IN. (Photo by Jeffrey Brown/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images As the Jacksonville Jaguars prepare to face the Indianapolis Colts in Week 8, we exchanged questions with Chris Shepherd of Stampede Blue to learn more about the opposing side. Question 1: The Colts are officially in “rebuilding” mode. Did the firing of general manager Chris Ballard catch you by surprise? And how long a leash will head coach Shane Steichen be given? After losing to a very bad and previously winless Titans team, in a year when the owner made clear the urgency to win had never been higher, it was no surprise someone was fired. I was a bit surprised it was Ballard. I thought there was a chance it would be offensive coordinator Jim Bob Cooter, for several reasons if for nothing else just to appease the bloodthirsty fans inside of Lucas Oil Stadium. Instead, Owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon did the right thing and fired the guy most responsible for the failures of this team. It was a bit of a good surprise. How long of a leash is a fantastic question. Back in April, Irsay-Gordon sat down to do an interview with the Colts’ internal media department and gave an interesting answer to hiring general managers and head coaches: Mark this down for future reference. As long as Carlie Irsay-Gordon is calling the shots for the #Colts , they'll never hire a GM and head coach in the same year. If Ballard isn't back in 2027, Steichen will be. pic.twitter.com/bbsPEvwtL0 — Chris Shepherd (@NFLscheme) April 11, 2026 I admit my initial reaction to that answer was simplistic and there is a very real chance the Colts move on from Steichen and hire both a GM and head coach in the same offseason. Irsay-Gordon said hiring the GM and HC simultaneously was something they would never do, but they can always hire one and then the other, though not rushing either decision would be difficult. They also have a massive head start in finding their next GM. The issue comes down to the end-of-season hiring window and how short it is. Even with a head start they’ll still need to conduct interviews and find the right fit. Then they would have to move on to finding the right head coach. If I had to guess, I would say the next GM will find himself with an immediate decision to make regarding his head coach. Does he fire Shane Steichen and hire a new staff quickly, or does he run it back for one more year with Steichen in a likely lame duck situation? I don’t think the owner will be the one deciding. Question 2: Were you surprised by the timing of the Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner trades? One could argue that the Colts could have driven up the asking price with two full weeks remaining until the NFL trade deadline. They also don’t have their own 2027 first-round pick (sorry to remind you). A bit surprised on the timing, I thought it would happen after this weekend’s drubbing in Jacksonville but I don’t think it would have changed the return. Buckner and Nelson were ultimate team guys. All accounts were that they both showed up every day, outworked everyone around them, led by example, were loved by their teammates and they never once complained about the absolute disaster that had been happening around them since they arrived in Indianapolis. They worked hard, did all of the right things and were loyal to the organization for years on end and when the time came, all reports indicate that both Nelson and Buckner had a say in choosing their next spot. Given the circumstances, I’m okay with that. At the end of the day football is a whole lot of fun and it’s more fun if your team is good, but it’s not as important as treating people with respect, especially people like Nelson and Buckner, rather than squeezing every last drop of value out of them. Of all of the decisions that have been made by leadership in Indy in the past decade, I don’t think the decisions to sell a round low on those two are the ones that will be remembered as what set the franchise back. With a couple of clicks you can visit Dawgs By Nature and learn everything you need to know about this week’s opponent! Fewer ads Seamlessly jump between communities and conversations Faster commenting and posting experience! Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Question 3: From a team-building perspective, it would be wise to also trade Jonathan Taylor… but he’s on pace to have his jersey hanging in the rafters at Lucas Oil Stadium one day. Do you want to see the Colts trade him for maximum value or keep him for sentimental reasons? I think their motivations are different than that. Thus far, all of the serious trade talks have been for players in contract years. My belief is they’re setting up the next GM to have as much agency over the roster as possible. GM changes usually come with massive roster turnover for better or worse, and if on day one the GM has a stack of re-signings to decide on, there may be one or two players they’re interested in bringing back. There’s a very real chance neither of those players will want to spend his second contract with a rebuilding franchise in the Midwest. So moving them now, instead of losing them then and getting zero return for them, makes a whole lot of sense. As it stands, Taylor is under contract. I think the goal is to give the next GM the opportunity to do with Taylor what they like, but if someone makes a ridiculous offer, sort of like the Bears giving two firsts and a fourth for Jeffery Simmons (fortunately it’s the Titans so they’ll bust those picks, but still, that’s wild), then I don’t think they’ll hesitate to move him. Personally, I hope they do move him. Sending JT somewhere he can compete in meaningful games, combined with the fact that his value will never be higher than right now, is enough for me to want them to. I’m just not sure they’ll get that kind of offer. Question 4: Who are some under-the-radar players that Jaguars fans should know of before Sunday’s kickoff? Let’s go with the two guys who will be replacing Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner. At left guard, the Colts will start rookie Jalen Farmer out of Kentucky. As a run blocker Farmer was an animal at Kentucky but he’s only played three offensive snaps this season so there are a lot of unknowns. OL coach Tony Soprano Jr. was famously quoted as saying, “Draft this guy and I’ll make it work,” and reportedly loved Farmer as a prospect. Soprano has garnered a lot of trust within the Colts building as they have drafted and developed offensive line talent as well as anyone in the league since his hiring. I expect Farmer to have his ups and downs, but on offense I’ll be dialed in on the Colts’ left guard all day. Defensively, Adetomiwa Adebawore will fill in for Buckner at defensive tackle. Adebawore is currently tied for the team lead in sacks with 4.0 despite having only played 36% of the team’s defensive snaps. Obviously his sack numbers won’t scale with his playing time but Ade Ade is an athletic freak of a 3-tech and I’m excited to see what he’ll do with an expanded role- that said, he is in a contract year and Mike Garafolo just told everyone on NFL Network’s The Insiders that Indy is shopping him as well, so who knows if he’ll be active on Sunday. Question 5: Do you expect the Colts to cover as 8.5-point underdogs, and do you have a favorite player prop for the game? Cover? Absolutely not. As far as a prop bet, I’d wager the Jaguars defense scores a touchdown on Sunday. I’d also take the over on yards for most Jacksonville offensive…

title: Kingdom Keys: 3 Keys to a Chiefs victory over the Broncos in Week 8
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs were thoroughly outplayed in all three phases of last Sunday’s loss to the Seattle Seahawks. The Chiefs must now respond on the road against the Denver Broncos in an important AFC West matchup. Kansas City defeated Denver 31-10 in Week 1, but the Broncos have won five of their last six […]
full_text: (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs were thoroughly outplayed in all three phases of last Sunday’s loss to the Seattle Seahawks . The Chiefs must now respond on the road against the Denver Broncos in an important AFC West matchup. Kansas City defeated Denver 31-10 in Week 1, but the Broncos have won five of their last six games and enter the rematch at 5-2. Here are three keys to a Chiefs victory in Week 8: Offensive key: Get Kenneth Walker III going again Denver has one of the league’s better overall defenses, but stopping the run remains its biggest weakness. The Broncos have surrendered 933 rushing yards through seven games, an average of 133.3 per game. Opponents are averaging 4.6 yards per carry against them. Denver has been far more effective defending the pass, holding opposing quarterbacks to a 56.4% completion rate and a 74.2 passer rating while recording 21 sacks and seven interceptions. That should make Kansas City’s offensive approach straightforward: lean on Kenneth Walker III. Walker dominated the first meeting with Denver, rushing for 173 yards and producing a 60-yard touchdown. The Chiefs finished that game with 220 rushing yards, controlled the football for nearly 34 minutes and converted nine of their 17 third downs. Seattle became the first opponent this season to truly slow Walker, holding him to 36 yards on 14 carries. It was also the first time this season that he failed to rush for 100 yards or score a touchdown. Despite that performance, Walker still enters Week 8 with 701 rushing yards, 116 receiving yards and eight total touchdowns. Andy Reid cannot allow one poor performance to move the offense away from what has worked throughout the season. Running Walker will keep Denver’s pass rush from attacking on every down and prevent Patrick Mahomes from repeatedly facing obvious passing situations. The offensive benchmark should be at least 125 scrimmage yards for Walker. The passing game must also provide more support than it did in Seattle. Xavier Worthy caught three of his six targets for only 11 yards, while Jalen Royals was held without a reception on two targets. Denver’s aggressive coverage will challenge Kansas City’s receivers to create separation and win contested catches. Rashee Rice’s potential return would help after he practiced on a limited basis Wednesday and Thursday. Regardless of Rice’s availability, Mahomes’ receivers must be better when Denver commits additional defenders to stopping Walker. Defensive key: Keep Bo Nix in the pocket Denver’s traditional running game has been unproductive. The Broncos are averaging only 3.8 yards per carry, while leading rusher J.K. Dobbins has produced 293 yards at 3.4 yards per attempt. The threat comes when Bo Nix escapes the pocket. Nix has 110 rushing yards and two touchdowns this season. That total includes a 62-yard touchdown run against Arizona last week, when he finished with 73 yards on seven carries. Kansas City’s defensive ends must remain disciplined. George Karlaftis and the other edge defenders cannot consistently rush beyond Nix and create open escape lanes. Collapsing the pocket means little if Nix can step outside it and turn a broken play into a first down. The Chiefs should make him beat them by consistently throwing from inside the pocket. Nix has completed 59.2% of his passes while averaging only 5.8 yards per attempt, with seven touchdowns, three interceptions and an 80.7 passer rating. We finally found a role for Jeffrey Bassa in the Chiefs' defense He played 2 snaps in Seattle, both as a QB Spy. Remember this for the Buffalo matchup pic.twitter.com/CZYX1U8TzS — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) October 27, 2026 Kansas City could also expand Jeffrey Bassa’s role as a quarterback spy. Bassa received snaps in that assignment against Seattle and helped the defense produce two third-down stops in the red zone. His athleticism makes him a logical option when the Chiefs believe Nix may scramble. The plan should be to stop Denver’s running backs on early downs, keep the edges secure and make Nix operate as a pocket passer on third-and-long. X-factor: Make your kicks The Chiefs cannot afford another game in which missed kicks leave points on the field. Harrison Butker missed two field goals against Seattle and has now missed five field goals this season — tied for the most in the NFL — along with an extra point. His 15 missed kicks since the beginning of last season are also the most in the league over that span. Kansas City responded by signing Justin Tucker to the practice squad. Special teams coordinator Dave Toub continues to say that Butker is the preferred kicker and explained that the primary objective is to help him work through his struggles . Tucker provides both competition and a veteran sounding board. He has experienced his own kicking struggles and can communicate with Butker in ways the coaching staff cannot. During Tucker’s workout, he reportedly converted all 30 of his attempts, including seven from beyond 50 yards and a 60-yarder. Butker then made all 10 attempts during Wednesday’s windy practice, with Tucker watching. Whether Butker remains the kicker or Tucker is eventually elevated, the standard is simple: Kansas City must make its kicks. A close divisional game on the road may be decided by three points. The Chiefs cannot leave those points on the board. The bottom line Seattle punched the Chiefs in the mouth, but one poor performance doesn’t erase everything the team accomplished during the 5-0 start. Kansas City must reestablish its identity by getting Walker beyond 100 scrimmage yards and forcing Denver to respect the run. Defensively, the Chiefs must maintain edge discipline and make Bo Nix beat them from inside the pocket. On special teams, whoever handles the kicking duties must convert every reasonable opportunity. If Kansas City can accomplish those three things, it will have an excellent opportunity to respond to its worst performance of the season, complete the season sweep of Denver and regain control of the AFC West race.

title: Which receiver trades could the Chiefs consider before the deadline?
summary: It’s deadline season, which means we’re back to wide receiver talk. There will come a time when that’s no longer the case for the Kansas City Chiefs. Today is not that day. Tyquan Thornton is (more or less) out for the year. Rashee Rice is expected back this week from his hamstring injury. Cyrus Allen […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s deadline season, which means we’re back to wide receiver talk. There will come a time when that’s no longer the case for the Kansas City Chiefs . Today is not that day. Tyquan Thornton is (more or less) out for the year. Rashee Rice is expected back this week from his hamstring injury. Cyrus Allen is playing sparingly. Xavier Worthy has once again been up and down in his performance. The Chiefs’ top wide receiver finished last week with 18 receiving yards. It’s a problem. It needs a solution. The next two weeks should help clarify the direction. I understand why fans are requesting (demanding?) a significant trade. It would be nice to see the team kill this fly with a sledgehammer, metaphorically speaking. I would love nothing more than to watch Patrick Mahomes throw the football to Garrett Wilson, Nico Collins or Devonta Smith. I suppose I could be wrong, but I think the odds of any of those trades coming together are roughly equal to the odds of me suiting up at wide receiver for the Chiefs by the end of the year. In other words, it probably won’t happen. The far more likely scenario is the Chiefs trade for a wide receiver a tier (or three) lower in the pecking order. The names won’t jump off the page. But they might be exactly what the doctor ordered to improve the passing game for the rest of the year. The next couple of weeks could be significant in that regard. Rice was finally beginning to look like his former self when he got hurt. Can he recapture that form when he returns? That would be an encouraging sign. He brings an important element to the offense, especially as a zone beater across the middle. I would like to see the Chiefs give Allen a longer look this week, as well. Maybe that’s asking too much, but he has three receptions on four targets for 45 yards in 25 total offensive snaps over the past two weeks. He’s shown he can beat man coverage. It would be nice to see what he can produce in a larger role. Maybe that’s just not in the cards for this season, but if the Chiefs think there’s untapped potential, now is the time to find out. And he’s not replacing world beaters in the lineup. Jalen Royals and Andrew Armstrong have combined for 4 catches for 40 yards on 154 snaps, with 10 targets over the past two weeks. That’s the extent of the internal options. The truth is the Chiefs are severely lacking an outside wide receiver with size and the ability to separate against man coverage. Those are the skills Thornton brought to the table. An ability to win deep would certainly be a plus. We saw the effect of not having a serious threat on the field last week as the Seahawks completely shut down the Chiefs’ passing attack. So where could the Chiefs realistically turn their attention if a trade becomes necessary? Here are some names to keep top of mind. Colts WR Josh Downs 2026 Stats: 26 receptions, 41 targets, 307 yards (11.8 YPR), 0 TD Contract Status: 1 yr, $3.9M At this point, you’ve heard the name, and you’re probably familiar with his game. He’s small and he’s traditionally been a slot receiver for the Colts (69% slot rate this year, 79% for his career), but he’s quite good at separating against man coverage and he’s been utilized as a downfield threat in Alec Pierce’s absence (6 targets 20+ yards downfield this year). Eagles WR Dontayvion Wicks 2026 Stats: 19 receptions, 31 targets, 284 yards (14.9 YPR), 1 TD Contract Status: Technically? 2 yrs, $10.25M. But it’s the Eagles, so there are void years, and it’s a bit convoluted. But for the Chiefs, it appears it would be 2 yrs, $4.4M. I think this is the player we probably haven’t spent enough time discussing. The Eagles are in freefall, and it’s probably more than a one-year fix. Wicks is an imperfect player, but he fits exactly what the Chiefs are missing. He lines up outside roughly 70 percent of the time this year, and more than 60 percent of the time in his career. He’s been a significant deep threat for the majority of his career (9 deep targets this year, and 32 deep targets over the past three years combined). He does his best work against man coverage, as well . He’s not a big name, and he’s not a high-volume target, but he could capably fill some of what the Chiefs are missing in Thornton’s absence. He should also come at a reasonable price. Texans WR Kayshon Boutte 2026 Stats: 15 receptions, 23 targets, 194 yards (12.9 YPR), 0 TD Contract Status: 1 yr, $3.7M Boutte was already traded earlier this year from the Patriots to the Texans, and he’s seen his snap share drop significantly in recent weeks. I don’t think the Texans are willing to give up on their season just yet, but that time might be coming. Boutte is another deep threat who lines up outside the vast majority of the time (73% this year, 86% for his career). He’s also a deep threat with seven targets more than 20 yards down the field this year. His average depth of target is more than 14 yards downfield. If you want an outside wide receiver with recent playoff success who is likely to be available for a cheap cost, this might be your man. Chargers WR Quentin Johnston 2026 Stats: 8 receptions, 21 targets, 165 yards (20.6 YPR), 0 TD Contract Status: 2 yrs, $20.5M ($1.3M prorated ‘26, $18M fully guaranteed ‘27) Hear me out. I don’t think it’s overly likely, and the money is a problem. But I’m not sure Johnston is as much of a lost cause as it might seem on the surface. He had 16 total touchdowns over the past two years, and he’s shown an ability to stretch the field. That’s a huge element to bring to the table. He also lines up outside the vast majority of the time (83% outside rate this year, 87% for his career). He’s been in a disastrous situation this year with the Chargers. Maybe the Chiefs believe he could be a transition piece in the offense for the next 1.5 years? I’m open to it. He’s probably the most talented player on this list, even if he’s also arguably the most frustrating and inconsistent. Commanders WR Treylon Burks 2026 Stats: 9 receptions, 152 yards (16.9 YPR), 2 TD Contract Status: 1 yr, $1.2M Once upon a time, I was convinced the Chiefs would draft Treylon Burks. That obviously didn’t happen, but he’s developed into a decent deep target for the Commanders this year. He’s lining up almost exclusively outside (69% outside rate this year, 74% for his career), and he could be had for a relatively low price. It’s not sexy. But it could work. Colts WR Laquon Treadwell 2026 Stats: 15 receptions, 26 targets, 197 yards (13.1 YPR), 0 TD Contract Status: 1 yr, $1.3M Another former first-round bust. Maybe I’m only mentioning him because I thought he played pretty well against the Chiefs, but he’s an outside receiver with the ability to take the top off the defense occasionally. It’s not my first (or second, or third…) choice, but if stuff hits the fan, fine. Commanders WR Dyami Brown 2026 Stats: 9 receptions, 16 targets, 94 yards (10.5 YPR), 0 TD Contract Status: 1 yr, $1.2M I feel like I’ve been waiting for a Dyami Brown breakout for the past five years. It’s never really happened. I don’t think it’s coming. But he’s similar to Burks and Treadwell in that he’s an outside receiver with legit downfield chops. That’s all I’ve got. I know, it’s not an inspiring list. But Tyquan Thornton wasn’t a headline addition when he arrived in Kansas City, either. I think this is a far more realistic list of trade deadline targets for the Chiefs than some of what’s been speculated about in internet circles. I would love to see the Chiefs add Downs to the mix, but I personally believe Wicks and Boutte are probably the best fits for what this offense currently lacks.

title: Chiefs News: Self-awareness is a defining trait of Patrick Mahomes

They’re relying on Xavier Worthy as their man-beater, but nickel Nick Emmanwori easily covering Worthy on a slot fade should tell you whether he can be relied on in that role. The Chiefs desperately need a receiver who can separate against man coverage. George Pickens would be the dream trade for the Chiefs, and they should be willing to trade significant capital for him if the Cowboys put him on the market, rather than potentially losing him in free agency next year, but Jerry Jones is unpredictable. The next best option would be Downs, who could be significantly more productive in the Chiefs’ offense. Ranking the best 2026 NFL rookies: Arvell Reese, Denzel Boston, others in top 10 | ESPN 7. Mansoor Delane, CB, Kansas City Chiefs Stats: 27 tackles, 1 INT, 5 PD Drafted: No. 6 It’s almost impossible to excel as a rookie corner in the NFL. Just ask Delane, who had perfect positioning and an elite strike on Seattle’s Jaxon Smith-Njigba but still got beat for a touchdown in Week 7. Regardless, Delane has consistently been in the hip pocket of top NFL receivers; he has the physicality and ball skills necessary to develop into a premiere ball hawk. With a 20% pass breakup and interception rate (league average for corners is 15.3%) and a tight window forced on 32% of his targets (league average is 25.3%), Delane is answering the call as a top-10 draft pick. — Solak How to bet on 2026 NFL Week 8: Betting odds, game previews, tips, trends, schedule, sportsbook promos, offers | CBS Sports Chiefs vs. Broncos preview This is the second meeting of the season between these teams, as Kansas City cruised to a 31-10 win over Denver in Week 1. Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker III outgained Denver by himself (191-176), finishing with the most rushing yards in a team debut since Michael Turner in 2008. Kansas City is coming off its first loss of the season, falling to Seattle in a 20-3 final. Denver is coming off a 30-16 win over Arizona, averaging a season-high 6.7 yards per play. Quarterback Bo Nix completed 15 of 19 passes for 222 yards and a touchdown while rushing for 74 yards and another score. Months after shooting, Eric Bieniemy calls wife Mia a ‘rockstar’ | KCTV5 Kansas City Chiefs offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy shared an emotional, uplifting update on his wife, telling reporters she recently traveled out of town for an annual weekend getaway with Chiefs coaches’ and players’ spouses. “You know what, she’s doing great. She actually went on a trip this weekend. She was on the wives’ trip. She was a rockstar,” Bieniemy said. “She’s doing great. I appreciate you asking about her. Her rehab has been going great. She actually had an opportunity to come out here and hang out, and I’m sure I got on her nerves.” Around the NF L Bears acquire All-Pro DT Jeffery Simmons in trade with Titans | ESPN The Titans (1-6) are receiving 2027 and 2028 first-round picks, plus a 2027 fourth-round pick, from the Bears (5-2) for Simmons and a 2028 fifth-round pick. Simmons is the first defensive tackle in the common draft era (since 1967) to be traded for multiple first-round draft picks, according to ESPN Research. Titans general manager Mike Borgonzi said Thursday he had no intentions of trading Simmons until receiving a call Wednesday night from Bears general manager Ryan Poles, who he worked with while with the Kansas City Chiefs. The offer was the first one that made Borgonzi consider trading Simmons. Thursday Night Football: Packers hold on for 27-19 win over Panthers | Pro Football Talk A new study from JAMA Network Open by researchers at Boston University, Mass General Brigham, and the Concussion & CTE Foundation has found that an estimated 75 percent of former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had CTE. “Many cases may have been early stage at the time of death and possibly symptom free,” the paper said, via Shwetha Surendran of ESPN. That observation speaks to one of the basic realities of CTE. It’s unknown how many people have it. And it’s no surprise that the vast majority of former NFL players who die with CTE symptoms are later determined to have had CTE. June Jones, former Atlanta Falcons head coach, dies at age 73 | NFL.com June Jones, the cutting-edge coach who brought the run-and-shoot offense to Hawaii and led the Rainbow Warriors to their greatest era and an undefeated regular season that catapulted them all the way to the Sugar Bowl, died on Thursday. He was 73. In a statement, Hawaii’s football program did not list a cause of death for Jones, who coached the Atlanta Falcons for three seasons in the 1990s before his stint at Hawaii. The Honolulu Star-Advertiser cited a close family friend as saying Jones had entered hospice two weeks ago in his native Oregon. title: Dave Toub says Chiefs are trying to get Harrison Butker right
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs now employ two kickers after signing Justin Tucker to the practice squad on Wednesday. Harrison Butker, the Chiefs’ placekicker since 2017, has struggled in recent games, but the signing of Tucker was not a move to replace the three-time Super Bowl champion specialist. At the podium on Thursday, special teams coordinator […]
full_text: (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs now employ two kickers after signing Justin Tucker to the practice squad on Wednesday. Harrison Butker, the Chiefs’ placekicker since 2017, has struggled in recent games, but the signing of Tucker was not a move to replace the three-time Super Bowl champion specialist. At the podium on Thursday, special teams coordinator Dave Toub clarified that acquiring Tucker is part of a plan to get the best out of Butker going forward. “We haven’t had to do this, but we’re at the point now where every position has competition, everybody has somebody behind them that’s ready to come up,” Toub told local media. “We went out and brought in three kickers and worked them out to get somebody onto the practice squad to be ready.” Later in the press conference, Toub emphasized the Chiefs’ stance on the kicking position. “Butker is our kicker. We’re trying to get Butker right,” Toub said. “That’s what this whole thing is about.” To find the right player to be Butker’s understudy, Toub was talking with special-teams coaches around the league and assembled a trio of kickers that the team thought as “the best guys out there,” according to Toub. He had heard positive things about Tucker’s previous attempts at an NFL comeback. “He had four workouts before; we were his fifth tryout,” Toub reminded. “The word was that he was hitting the ball great, and I wanted to see it. I always thought he was a great kicker, and those two guys, him and Harrison, idealized each other when they were kicking together.” The next step was to put the tryout players through a rigorous placekicking circuit. Tucker excelled. “I made a grueling workout for these guys; I had 30 kicks: 10 extra points, seven kicks over 50, one was a 60-yarder,” Toub remembered. “He made every kick. Not only did he make them, he was accurate: 60% of his kicks were inside of a six-foot cylinder in the middle of the uprights.” “Somebody that is struggling as a kicker is not able to put the ball with that kind of accuracy on 30 kicks, so he was off the charts good,” Toub said. “That’s the reason we signed him to the practice squad.” As Toub mentioned, Butker and Tucker were two of the league’s top kickers for a stretch of time. That experience is a key reason for the move, and something Toub seems to believe can sharpen Butker’s current shortcomings. “Those two guys are collaborating now,” Toub shared. “Talking, ‘What did you go through?’” “I’m a coach, I’m not a kicking guy, I don’t speak that language like those guys do,” Toub continued. “Yesterday was unbelievable, those two guys. They were talking about issues, talking about, ‘How did you handle it,’ and it’s been great. They’re professionals… that part of it has been good.” With Tucker now on the practice field in Kansas City, Toub has already seen Butker lock in and have an impressive showing with a backup over his shoulder. “He went 10 for 10 yesterday with Tucker standing right there,” Toub said. “On a windy day, it was 28 miles-per-hour gusts yesterday and he went 10 for 10… that’s a good thing. We’re going to keep working it.”

title: Mansoor Delane learning from tough moments against Jaxon Smith-Njigba
summary: Kansas City Chiefs rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane — the sixth overall selection in April’s NFL Draft — has performed admirably early in his career, but (like the rest of the squad) ran into trouble on Sunday against the Seattle Seahawks. Seattle wideout Jaxon Smith-Njigba had his way with the entire Kansas City defense, and Delane […]
full_text: (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images Kansas City Chiefs rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane — the sixth overall selection in April’s NFL Draft — has performed admirably early in his career, but (like the rest of the squad) ran into trouble on Sunday against the Seattle Seahawks . Seattle wideout Jaxon Smith-Njigba had his way with the entire Kansas City defense, and Delane was no exception. Just before halftime, quarterback Sam Darnold found Smith-Njigba for a touchdown against Delane. The star wideout craftily beat Delane and then correctly anticipated how to hold the ball to keep the rookie from forcing a fumble. Before Wednesday’s practice, Delane vowed it would be a learning experience, especially with multiple top wide receivers on deck for the Chiefs’ secondary in the next few weeks. “It really just prepares me,” Delane remarked. “I think there’s great receivers on every team. You’ve just got to bring it, and you’ve got to prepare. They’re going to win some. You’re going to win some. So just really having that short term mentality, whether it’s good or bad, and just having an expert mentality.” Delane has already looked back to find areas for improvement, although few NFL playmakers match Smith-Njigba’s talent. “[There’s] definitely little things,” he noted. “He’s a savvy receiver. On TV, it may look like you should just do this or that, but then you line up across from him and see how it is. He’s a good player. He’s going to make plays. There’re definitely things I could have done better.” To live up to the expectations that come with his draft position, Delane asks defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo for the difficult assignments. “I think some people may get discouraged from passes caught on them,” the rookie explained. “But I told Coach Spags, ‘Man, put me in those tough situations.’ I’m not asking for a cloud. I’m not asking for cover two. Go back out there and play man and that’s what we did. A lot of teams are kind of scared to do that. But I feel like we didn’t shy away from it. So, we learned from it, but at the same time, there are going to be times in my career that I’m going to better handle that stick, and I’m definitely going to learn from that.” After Sunday’s middling results, Delane does not believe he has lost any of Spagnuolo’s trust. “I think he has the ultimate confidence in me,” Delane said of the relationship between coach and player. “That says a lot. I’m a rookie. He doesn’t care anything about that. He trusts me to go out and guard arguable one of the best receivers in the league. It’s up to me to get that job done and just instilling that confidence in him. I know after talking to him, he didn’t lose any confidence in me. He just gained it, and we’re going to go forward.” As he moves forward, Delane knows he has plenty to improve. His process is to pick one thing from his game each week and put all his effort into improving it. “I don’t look backwards too much,” Delane added. “I really try to look forward. If anything, I just take one thing a week and try to eliminate it. I don’t try to take everything. Try to narrow on one thing and really improve on that. I feel like I’m doing that. It’s inspiring to see, but every week I come up with something else I can prove. I’m just trying to get better at one thing every time.” This week will be against the Denver Broncos . Delane made his debut against Denver in Week 1 and snagged a spectacular interception off of quarterback Bo Nix on his third snap. Unfortunately, he injured his shoulder going to the ground on the play and missed the remainder of the game. Although the Chiefs dominated the Broncos to open the season, Delane knows that the now 5-2 opponent will be much more dangerous this time. All 11 defenders will need to do their part. “They’re kind of finding a little bit of a groove,” he observed. “[Head coach] Sean Payton took over playcalling. Bo Nix — I think he’s getting a little of his confidence back. He’s been in a little bit of a slump. Really, it’s just doing our one-eleventh this week and limiting those deep shots they like to take and limiting what they like to do best.”

title: Travis Kelce on Chiefs loss to Seattle: ‘You can’t be okay with being mediocre’
summary: Coming off the team’s first loss of the season, Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce addressed the game on his podcast “New Heights.“ Kelce gave credit to the Seattle Seahawks, who held the Chiefs to historically low offensive numbers; the captain of our ship here at Arrowhead Pride, Ron Kopp Jr., highlighted this in […]
full_text: (Photo by Alika Jenner/Getty Images) | Getty Images Coming off the team’s first loss of the season, Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce addressed the game on his podcast “ New Heights .“ Kelce gave credit to the Seattle Seahawks , who held the Chiefs to historically low offensive numbers; the captain of our ship here at Arrowhead Pride , Ron Kopp Jr., highlighted this in a piece following the game. Mahomes finished with 165 yards on 19 of 33 passing, posting the fifth-lowest marks of his career for passing yards per attempt (5) and passer rating (58.3). It was only the second time Kansas City has scored three or fewer points with Mahomes at quarterback. The other game was also in Week 7, in 2021, a 27-3 loss to the Tennessee Titans . “They came ready to play,” Kelce admitted, giving a special shoutout to Seattle’s fans, known as The 12th Man . “Sunday night up in Seattle, that place was rocking. The Twelves were loud, and it was a pretty frustrating game from the jump.” Diving into more detail about what frustrated the Chiefs, Kelce said Seattle played a shell defense for much of the game, relying on their defensive linemen to win one-on-one matchups. “It felt like they were playing prevent the entire time and just letting the front four cause havoc in the run game…” “We still couldn’t find a way to get the ball past the 30- or 40-yard line. We had to dink and dunk, and they forced us to be good on third downs and, essentially, fourth downs as well.” Kelce also addressed his personal performance, namely a costly penalty for an illegal formation that he was called for on the Chiefs’ opening drive. “I had another drive killer in the first f*cking drive,” said Kelce. “I got caught in motion, not knowing that the running back came up to the line with Pat. I’ve just got to get set. That killed that drive, and we were rolling, man. We were rolling that first drive, and that kind of stalled us.” One penalty doesn’t lose a game, though. Kelce said numerous factors led to the Chiefs losing to Seattle. “…it was bad technique, bad fundamentals, just okay effort. There were a lot of things—the attention to detail. And I say this because that’s what I see out of myself on film. “As a unit, we’ve got to play better together, which means making sure we’re all being accountable in every single aspect of the game. If it’s the backside of a route, be ready and on time. If it’s the called route that we’re trying to get open, be on time and where you need to be, releasing the right way and attacking the defense the right way.” Kelce added that the Chiefs’ wide receiver and tight ends need to do a better job making “The read easy for Pat (quarterback Patrick Mahomes) to get the ball out on time so the offensive line doesn’t have to strain for more than what they typically do.” After going back and watching the tape and self-scouting the team’s performance, Kelce said he was frustrated because the team missed opportunities to attack Seattle. “If we get the opportunity to play them again, I’m sure we’ll have it geared up and be fired up and ready to go. “But looking at it right now, they kind of got us, man. And it wasn’t just that scheme. Those guys were flying the f*ck around. They played very well together. They were all on the same f*cking page in terms of the gap assignments and things like that. There were very few mistakes, and the mistakes they were making, we didn’t capitalize on. It’s frustrating as hell.” “I think a lot of it is coming in with the right mentality and a togetherness that we’re not going to be denied. We need to learn from this, feel how it felt to get our tail kicked like that, and never let it happen again.” So that leaves the million-dollar question: what do the Chiefs need to do to bounce back and ensure last Sunday night’s performance was a fluke, not the new norm? “I’ll be damned if we go out there and have another f*cking showing like that. I can promise you that.” Travis shared his thoughts after the Chiefs first loss of the season pic.twitter.com/L2gg29e8yG — New Heights (@newheightshow) October 28, 2026 “We’re coming off a game where we didn’t perform well in really any phase. It’s got to fire you the f*ck up, man. You’ve got to have a nasty taste in your mouth when you lose,” said a fired-up Kelce. “You can’t be okay with being mediocre or looking around like, ‘I wasn’t the reason.’ “You’ve got to f—ing have a nasty, disgusting taste in [in your mouth],” said Kelce. “Losing in this league and find the f—ing answers. All that means is you’ve got to f—ing go to work. “I’ll be damned if we go out there and f—ing have another f—ing showing like that again. I can promise you that.”

full_text: The Carolina Panthers fired defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero on Friday following a loss to the Packers on Thursday. Evero previously spent five seasons on Sean McVay’s staff coaching defensive backs, from 2017 to 2021, prior to being hired as the Broncos defensive coordinator in 2022. Would now be the right time to bring Evero back to the L.A. Rams? BREAKING: The #Panthers have fired DC Ejiro Evero, per @JFowlerESPN . Evero has been Carolina's DC since 2023. pic.twitter.com/lMePHTYykc — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) October 30, 2026 Evero’s Denver defense ranked seventh in yards allowed in 2022, but Nathaniel Hackett’s staff was quickly disassembled after a disastrous season with Russell Wilson. The Panthers next hired him to the same job and Carolina ranked fourth in yards allowed, but 29th in points allowed. In 2024, the Panthers were dead last in points and yards allowed, but the team showed patience with new head coach Dave Canales and his staff. Carolina improved the next season as they were middle of the pack defensively in 2025 and made the playoffs. However, the Panthers have fallen to 3-4 and they gave up 59 points to the Bears in Week 1, a sting that hasn’t gone away for Evero. But would he be welcomed back on a Rams defensive staff that could use some consultation in the secondary? Trent McDuffie could return to the field this weekend against the L.A. Chargers and the Rams have made a big investment there recently with McDuffie, Jaylen Watson, and Quentin Lake. Some fans think Chris Shula needs the help. If not more than just help.

title: Does Josh Downs make sense for the Rams?
summary: Joshua Downs wants a trade away from the Indianapolis Colts, but does it make sense for the Los Angeles Rams to acquire him? Some would say, yes. Some would say, no. The dichotomy makes this a great debate. On the one hand, Downs is talented, he can stretch the field, but if memory serves, we’ve […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - OCTOBER 18: Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Josh Downs (2) during player introductions prior to the start of and NFL game between the Tennessee Titans and the Indianapolis Colts on October 18, 2026 at Lucas Oil Stadium at Indianapolis, IN. (Photo by Jeffrey Brown/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Joshua Downs wants a trade away from the Indianapolis Colts, but does it make sense for the Los Angeles Rams to acquire him? Some would say, yes . Some would say, no. The dichotomy makes this a great debate. On the one hand, Downs is talented, he can stretch the field, but if memory serves, we’ve seen the young man make some strong catches over the middle too. Though he’s not the biggest receiver, similar to Tutu Atwell. So, would Downs handle the level of run blocking the Rams might ask him to do? Also, would the Rams use Downs? It’s well-known Matthew Stafford sometimes just locks in on one player and goes from there. If Downs isn’t Stafford’s main target on a given day, how much work would he get? Can trading for Downs work? I believe Sean McVay could make it work. Is trading for Downs worth it? That’s the debate. As talented as Downs is, I am not sure he’s what the Rams need for the Super Bowl in 2026. I am not sure he truly moves the needle. I can be proven wrong. This story isn’t quite done being written just yet, but for me, more than any trade, the Rams need to win games. They have the pieces; it’s up to them to deliver. Los Angeles Rams Make Perfect Sense as Josh Downs Trade Suitor (sports.yahoo) “So far this season with the Colts, Downs has caught 26 passes for 307 yards, but has not found the end zone. Last year, he racked up 58 receptions for 566 yards and four scores. Throughout his entire 54-game NFL career, Downs has totaled 224 receptions for 2,447 yards and 11 touchdowns. At 25 years old, Downs would bring excellent slot production to the Rams’ offense. He would also be an addition both for this season and the future. Assuming Los Angeles worked out a contract extension with him, the move could pay dividends for years to come.“ Joshua Karty’s return is the full-circle flourish to Rams’ kicking saga (ramblinfan) “Perhaps the most hilarious, or tragic, for the doom and gloomers out there, aspect of Karty’s return is that he is in a sense replacing his own replacement, Harrison Mevis, who lasted all of 14 games after taking over last November. The Rams just can’t get this right. Rams re-up Joshua Karty in latest go-round of kicker carousel Grupe, their first stab at upgrading on Mevis, was waylaid by misfortune rather than mistake. Tearing his ACL on his second Rams kickoff was not the plan.“ 4 key matchups that will decide Rams vs. Chargers on Sunday (ramswire) “LT Alaric Jackson vs. OLB Khalil Mack Mack will play on the left and right side, so Warren McClendon Jr. will have to block him, too. But it’s imperative for Jackson to protect Matthew Stafford’s blindside because if Mack gets around the corner, he has the ability to attack the football and force fumbles.“ Chargers look to avoid 0-7 start in battle of LA (nbcsports) “Mike Florio details the nuggets in Week 8’s “battle of LA,” where the Chargers look to avoid their third-ever 0-7 start and Puka Nacua’s bid at history.“ Rams and Chargers share a city, not a rivalry as they head into their first meeting in 4 seasons (apnews) “INGLEWOOD, Calif. (AP) — Although the Los Angeles Rams and the Los Angeles Chargers share a stadium, they don’t share a rivalry. The NFL schedule only puts these teams together once every four years, and they have neither the long history nor the recent animus necessary to make Sunday’s meeting into a true crosstown showdown. “It’s a big town to cross,” Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford said with a grin. “I don’t run into those guys too often, to be honest with you. I don’t really want to make that drive. Nobody does.” Kyren Williams and Blake Corum are too potent for the Rams to ignore (ramblinfan) “In that game, Kyren Williams and Blake Corum combined for 192 rushing yards on 5.8 per carry, with each eclipsing 90. It was easily the run game’s most complete performance this season. In a recent interview on The Pat McAfee Show , Stafford described how his running back duo is perfectly suited for LA’s offense. “I haven’t had a tandem like Kyren Williams and Blake Corum where they both can do everything,” Stafford said. “We can call our entire offense with both of those guys in the game.” The offense continues to feature Stafford as its engine, propelling him to 1,989 passing yards, 14 touchdowns, and seven interceptions. But the Rams are also one of only two teams with two names among the league’s top 25 rushers.“ Puka Nacua admits he’s still managing his injured calf every day (ramswire) “He wound up playing and caught eight passes for 68 yards and a touchdown, but he’s not fully out of the woods yet with his injured calf. Nacua told reporters on Thursday that he’s still getting treatment and managing the injury, doing everything he can to suit up on Sundays. “After a Thursday practice, I’ll get some supplemental work, but it’s definitely something that, maintenance every day in the morning, moving some stuff in my insoles and stuff like that and working with everybody in the training room and ‘EQ’ [equipment staff] so I can go out there and play as free and confident as I can,” he said.“ ‘His Vertical Route Tree Would Complement (Puka) Nacua’ — NFL Analyst Urges Rams To Pursue Trade for Pro Bowl WR After Davante Adams’ Injury (sports.yahoo) “But now “The Athletic’s” Ted Nguyen is suggesting that trading for Brian Thomas Jr. could help swing the Super Bowl odds back in the Rams’ favor. His idea is for the Rams to send the Jacksonville Jaguars a third-round pick in 2027 and a fifth-round pick in 2028 in exchange for the one-time Pro Bowler. “The Rams tried to play it too cute in the draft and live in two timelines, taking quarterback Ty Simpson with the 13th pick when the best option this season would have been a receiver,” Nguyen argues. “Davante Adams is 33 and had hamstring issues last season — it wasn’t hard to predict he would miss games this season. Puka Nacua has had injury and off-field issues.” Sean McVay open to having 2 kickers active on game day (sports.yahoo) “Mevis lost his job this season due to the same issues, with Blake Grupe (tore his ACL in his first game) and Brandon McManus taking over since. With Karty back in the facility, and his “knuckleball” kickoff style being pointed at as a possible solution to the team’s long-standing kick coverage issues, some wonder if the Rams will entertain the idea of having two kickers on their game-day roster. Head coach Sean McVay would not close the door on the idea. “We’ll work through all different things,” said McVay. “It all depends. When you have 48 bodies and the different guys that are filling in, you have to really ask yourself, ‘Okay, does that really make sense? Does it fit?’ There are a lot of layers to it so I wouldn’t be ready to answer that question yet.” Week 8 Preview: Los Angeles Chargers vs Los Angeles Rams (lastwordonsports) “The Rams are in the midst of the easiest part of their schedule. They must capitalize on this opportunity and come away with a win this week. The Chargers are vulnerable with several problems throughout their roster. During the offseason, the Chargers hired offensive extraordinaire Mike McDaniel as their offensive coordinator. McDaniel has struggled to find success, while Star Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert has had the worst start to a season in his career. The Chargers will also be without star safety Derwin James Jr., who has missed the last three games with a hamstring injury.“ Comment od the day: Feed post of the day:

title: RAMalytics: Why the Rams are regressing on offense
summary: Seven weeks into the NFL regular season and we know these facts about the Los Angeles Rams’ offense: By design the Rams are looking for five to six yards each time they run the ball. The duo rushing scheme is intended to manufacture a lot of singles and doubles. It makes it harder to hit […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 18: Davante Adams #17 of the Los Angeles Rams runs the ball against Mack Wilson Sr. #1 of the Arizona Cardinals during the game at SoFi Stadium on October 18, 2026 in Inglewood, California. The Arizona Cardinals won 18-16. (Photo by Alika Jenner/Getty Images) | Getty Images Seven weeks into the NFL regular season and we know these facts about the Los Angeles Rams’ offense: They are old They are slow They lack explosiveness They are inconsistent By design the Rams are looking for five to six yards each time they run the ball. The duo rushing scheme is intended to manufacture a lot of singles and doubles. It makes it harder to hit triples and home runs. To be fair, this also best suits the skillsets of Blake Corum and Kyren Williams. But that was true regarding the Rams last year. That doesn’t explain their sudden offensive decline. So what does? LA stayed pat at receiver with a duo of Puka Nacua and Davante Adams. Neither player are strangers to injury, and it was highly improbable that Adams would be healthy for the full season. Even knowing that, the Rams still were stubborn about a lack of investment in a third receiver. They had a false comfortability with Konata Mumpfield and Jordan Whittington, of which neither are suitable replacements for Adams in the starting lineup. And while Nacua has been on the field of late, he doesn’t look like his normal self. Nacua is clearly not healthy. Early in the season he battled the early stages of a sports hernia, per reports. That injury hasn’t gone anywhere—it’s just being managed. It could likely be limiting his explosiveness. Nacua is also working through a calf injury that cropped up last week, although he was able to play and handle a large workoad. But the wrinkle that Nacua added to his game that made him an offensive player of the year candidate a year ago was his prowess in the deep area of the field. That is gone in 2026, likely because of injuries. Nacua has regressed to a high volume of short area passes, which is how he made his initial mark on the NFL. That is good. It’s not star-level production. Nacua’s change in role has shown symptoms across the offensive ecosystem. The deep passing attack has disappeared for the Rams. On passes that traveled at least 20 yards through the air, Matthew Stafford has completed just 7 of 25 attempts (28%) for 244 yards with one touchdown and four interceptions. This comprises just 9% of his total throws. Nacua accounts for nine of these plays (14.5% of total targets) with two receptions for 60 yards and no scores. 54.8% of his targets are coming within nine yards of the line of scrimmage. During his MVP season, Stafford targeted the deep area of the field at a 14.8% clip. He completed 48 of 106 attempts (45.3%) for 1,532 yards with 12 touchdowns and a single interception. Nacua accounted for 32 of these plays (16% of total targets) with 17 receptions, 514 yards, and four scores. 52.5% of his targets came within nine yards of the line of scrimmage. That’s a major step back for both players. But just as the Rams were comfortable running it back with an aging Adams, they did the same with Stafford. Stafford won his first MVP award nearly 20 years into his NFL career. He had never seriously been considered for the honors up to that point. A wise betting man would have said that year was an outlier and expect regression to the mean the following season. That is exactly what is happening. Stafford was operating at the best level we had ever seen from him a year ago. The hot streak is now over. Applying a 50% drop back threshold in the Pro Football Focus (PFF) database, Stafford currently ranks as the 18th quarterback in the NFL. Last season he was solidly in first place. While PFF attempts to separate individuals from the overall offensive ecosystem, quarterbacks are subject to how often they are under pressure, how well their receivers separate, and how the play caller pulls the strings in conjunction with the running game. Stafford’s regression is not entirely his fault. The receiving corps’ struggles have played a role in this consequence. But at the same time Stafford is not immune from criticism. He’s clearly not performing at the level we saw from him a year ago. Stafford’s ability to generate big-time throws has fallen off a cliff. He has declined from a 7.7% rate in 2025 to 3.1% this season. He’s putting the ball in harm’s way more often with a slight uptick in turnover-worthy plays from 3.3% to 3.8% and in negatively graded plays from 8.0% to 10.1%. Positively graded plays are also happening less frequently and have fallen from 17.2% to 14.2%. Whether Stafford can get back on track individually remains to be seen. He has his work cut out for him without Adams, and the Rams must remain committed to the run game in order to build a supporting offensive ecosystem. But the lack of receiver depth is an issue of the Rams’ own making. In some ways Stafford is paying the price for the team’s lack of investment in the position, although he’s contributing to the offensive decline in his own performance. If the Rams are going to go on a run and make the playoffs, they will need to find different ways to win. That might place a heavier burden on the defense to keep games within reach. The offense may not be capable of carrying them deep into the postseason this time around.
author: JB Scott

title: Braden Fiske feeling the Aaron Donald effect
summary: When Aaron Donald announced that he was coming out of retirement to help the Rams win a Super Bowl, there was some concern by fans that his presence may stunt the development of Braden Fiske. But over the last few weeks, it seems the only one doing the stunting and having his presence felt is […]
full_text: When Aaron Donald announced that he was coming out of retirement to help the Rams win a Super Bowl, there was some concern by fans that his presence may stunt the development of Braden Fiske. But over the last few weeks, it seems the only one doing the stunting and having his presence felt is Fiske. The former second-round pick out of Florida State who finished third in Defensive Rookie of the Year voting a couple of years ago didn’t just post his first sack of the season against the Raiders in Week 7, he has also been the most consistent force on L.A.‘s defensive line recently. In fact, Fiske is quickly rising up the leaderboard for pressures among all interior defensive linemen. Braden Fiske, shuffle step or kind of up, jab step inside and gets his right armed cocked, right arm clubs/swipes hands of g and he closes the initial stutter gets G off balanced, his head gets over his skis and you can see him in an awkward position and Fiske's hustle does the… pic.twitter.com/qLN4lSLy6b — Jim Youngblood 53 (@53_jim70721) October 26, 2026 According to Next Gen Stats, Fiske generated three pressures on 32 pass rushes against Las Vegas, good for a pressure rate of 9.4%. He also had three “stops”, which is a tackle that creates a negative play for the offense when they try to run the ball. A week earlier against the Cardinals, Fiske had a pressure rate of 17.6%, generating three pressures on 17 snaps. And three weeks ago against the Eagles, SIX pressures for a pressure rate of 23.1%. So not only does Fiske have a pressure rate of 11.9% on the season — which is pretty good — he has been especially difficult for linemen to block over the past four weeks: 87 pass rushes 13 pressures 14,9% pressure rate 1 sack 8 stops Fiskes ranks 16th among all qualified defensive linemen at 11.9% — the recently-traded Jeffery Simmons ranks 15th — but a 14.9% pressure rate alone would rank sixth! He would rank above Maxx Crosby and just behind Aidan Hutchinson. Although he has not turned those pressures into sacks yet, which does matter, there’s reason to think now that Fiske could be a viable long-term defensive line cornerstone for the Rams, something they messed up when they parted ways with John Franklin-Myers once. Fiske has primarily played defensive tackle, with just 39 of his snaps coming as a defensive end, but he has generated three pressures as an edge. He lines up on both sides of the line with similar results from either angle, and he has a 14.8% pressure rate when the Rams blitz. The Rams didn’t get to see Fiske and Donald play together when he was drafted in 2024. Now they’re finally getting to see the duo on the field at the same time and it may be even better for Fiske than for AD.
author: Kenneth Arthur

title: Was Myles Garrett a better trade for Rams than Jeffery Simmons?
summary: The Chicago Bears traded two first-round picks for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons on Thursday, with some pointing out that no such trade has worked out for a team since the Los Angeles Rams made a similar deal for Jalen Ramsey in 2019. How much did the Bears overpay for Simmons, if at all? And did […]
full_text: The Chicago Bears traded two first-round picks for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons on Thursday, with some pointing out that no such trade has worked out for a team since the Los Angeles Rams made a similar deal for Jalen Ramsey in 2019. How much did the Bears overpay for Simmons, if at all? And did the Rams do better by trading for Myles Garrett in the offseason or should they have waited until they were able to watch the season play out a little bit before making their move? Compensation Return Myles Garrett Jeffery Simmons – Jared Verse – 1st-Round Pick – 2027 1st-Round Pick – 1st-Round Pick – 2028 2nd-Round Pick – 4th-Round Pick – 2029 3rd-Round Pick pic.twitter.com/CNwLuHpsje — Polymarket Football (@PolymarketBlitz) October 29, 2026 The Rams traded a 2027 first-round pick, pass rusher Jared Verse (a 2024 first-round pick), and more to the Cleveland Browns for Garrett coming off of a Defensive Player of the Year season with 23 sacks. It was a bold move to add a superstar regardless of position — one could easily argue that edge was not L.A.’s biggest need — and could have paid off during the early portion of the season. Unfortunately, Garrett posted no stats in Week 1’s 27-7 loss to the San Francisco 49ers and has not played in the last six games. There is no clear return date in sight for Garrett, although that could change any week. When the Rams open Garrett’s 21-day window to be activated, there’s a good chance he will be ready to go by the following game given his age, experience, and amount of time off rehabbing a knee injury that he’s already had. Jeffery Simmons had 7.5 sacks on 3rd down this season. The only player with more was Myles Garrett (11.0). @Titans | #TitanUp — NFL Researcher (@NFL_Researcher) January 8, 2026 However, one could also argue that Simmons would have fit a much bigger need than Garrett and the Rams wouldn’t have had to sacrifice Verse. That is, if you think that Verse is worth keeping— which hasn’t been clear in his first season with the Browns in which he has the same number of sacks this year as Garrett . Imagine what the Rams may have looked like this week against the L.A. Chargers if they had Jeffery Simmons — although now we can’t say for sure who else they would have had. Does Aaron Donald still return? Are Kobie Turner and Poona Ford still injured? Is Jared Verse still in L.A.? Jeffery Simmons since 2025 (DT ranks): 🔹15.0 sacks (1st) 🔹23 TFL (1st) 🔹85 pressures (T-1st)* 🔹28 pressures after double team (1st)* 🔹31 quick pressures (1st)* 🔹6 turnovers caused by pressure (1st)* 🔹9.5 sacks on 3rd down (1st) *Per @NextGenStats https://t.co/SwLhxcZFmb — NFL Researcher (@NFL_Researcher) October 29, 2026 Another two trades that the Rams have not participated in during the season happened within their own division. The Seattle Seahawks acquired Quenton Nelson and the 49ers acquired DeForest Buckner, with neither team giving up more than a third-round pick. The Rams traded a first-round pick for Trent McDuffie before the draft, and a first-round pick plus more (including a conditional pick that could become a first) for Garrett. McDuffie has also missed the last two games. Would Les Snead be better served waiting for more midseason trades — as he did for Ramsey in 2019 and Von Miller in 2021 — or is it fair game to hunt the market for players all year round like open season? Such as acquiring Matthew Stafford after the 2020 season. Most QB pressures after being chipped or double teamed in 2025, per @NextGenStats : 1. Myles Garrett – 32 2. Micah Parsons – 28 3. Danielle Hunter – 21 4. Jeffery Simmons – 19 5. Christian Barmore – 17 6. Will Anderson Jr. – 16 6. Leonard Williams – 16 6. Nik Bonitto – 16 6.… — NFL Researcher (@NFL_Researcher) March 19, 2026 The Rams have a good team now, albeit one that wishes they were better than 3-4. McDuffie is trending to play this week, Garrett could return next week perhaps (although I have no proof of that), and Davante Adams may be back closer to six weeks than 10 weeks . A team with Garrett will not look like one that necessarily needs Simmons, and the Bears got no discount in trading two first-round picks to the Titans for a star defensive lineman anyway. But Chicago does know better who they are when they make the trade, and that self-awareness could help them attack their weaknesses — and Quenton Nelson (Chicago plays Seattle on Monday) — sooner than the return of Garrett. What would you prefer?

title: Dylan Parham offers reminder about Raiders’ investment on offensive line
summary: Sunday, the Las Vegas Raiders will visit the New York Jets and guard Dylan Parham. Parham left the Raiders this offseason as a free agent to sign with the Jets. Parham was the Raiders’ first draft pick in 2022, taken in the third round. Parham was at the beginning of a commitment from four different […]
full_text: (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images Sunday, the Las Vegas Raiders will visit the New York Jets and guard Dylan Parham. Parham left the Raiders this offseason as a free agent to sign with the Jets. Parham was the Raiders’ first draft pick in 2022, taken in the third round. Parham was at the beginning of a commitment from four different Raiders regimes to build the offensive line. The Raiders have used eight picks in the first four rounds of the draft on offensive linemen since 2020. They were: John Simpson (fourth, 2020), Alex Leatherwood (first, 2021), Parham (third, 2022), Jackson Powers-Johnson (second, 2024), D.J. Glaze (third, 2024), Caleb Rogers (third, 2025), Charles Grant (third, 2025) and Trey Zuhn (third, 2026). However, only Glaze and Rogers are currently starting for the Raiders. Powers-Johnson, Grant and Zuhn are currently backups while Simpson, Leatherwood and Parham are no longer on the roster. There is a thought that Zuhn may replace Rogers in the starting lineup Sunday at the Jets. So, Rogers could join Powers-Johnson players who lost their starting roles. This is not an ideal payoff for such a strong draft capital investment on the offense line. Part of the problem is that there have been so many different front offices and coaching staffs. They all have different wants and philosophies when it comes to offensive linemen, so that creates the constant need to start over. Second-year Las Vegas general manager John Spytek has been vocal about his affinity for offensive linemen and his selections of Rogers, Grant and Zuhn in the third round shows that. The key is for these young players to develop into depenndable starters so the Raiders can can spread out their premium picks to other areas in the coming years.
author: Bill Williamson

title: Raiders-Jets Week 8: 5 things to watch
summary: The 3-4 Las Vegas Raiders play at the 2-5 New York Jets on Sunday. Kickoff is at 10 a.m. PT. Here are five keys to victory for Las Vegas: Stop the run: The Rams ran right over the Raiders as they compiled 199 yards on the ground last week. That is a recipe for a […]
full_text: (Photo by Sarah Stier/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 3-4 Las Vegas Raiders play at the 2-5 New York Jets on Sunday. Kickoff is at 10 a.m. PT. Here are five keys to victory for Las Vegas: Stop the run: The Rams ran right over the Raiders as they compiled 199 yards on the ground last week. That is a recipe for a defeat. Rob Leonard’s unit must tighten the ship this week. Run the ball: Yes, this has been a focal point every week and every week it seems to be a problem area for Las Vegas. The Raiders have had the worst running game in the NFL this season. Last week, they ran the ball just 17 times. They have to establish the run at some point. Ashton Jeanty said he think the Raiders can run on the Jets because they have some players not interested in tackling. It’s time to live up to those words. Be Better in red zone on both sides of the ball: On offense, in the past two games, the Raiders converted in the red zone just three of 10 attempts. On defense, in the past two games, the Raiders allowed touchdowns on eight of their opponents’ 10 trips to the red zone. That’s another recipe for defeat. That must change this week. Be better than a bad team: The Raiders are 3-0 against teams with a combined record of 3-16. They are 0-4 against teams with a combined record of 17-9 record. The Jets are 2-5. The Raiders are better than the Jets. They need to show it. Take advantage of an Aaron Glenn weakness: Since he took over in 2025, Jets head coach Aaron Glenn’s team have been outscored 106-7 in the final two minutes of the first half. That’s a weird quirk. But it’s real. Go take advantage, Las Vegas.
