title: Defensive collapse, offensive impotence leading to Raiders’ freefall
summary: The game of football is decided in the trenches — more often than not. And the Las Vegas Raiders are habitually losing that battle. And, as a result, the team is in a four-game freefall and are 3-4 overall after a torrid 3-0 start to the 2026 season. The Silver & Black’s most recent outing […]
full_text: (Photo by Candice Ward/Getty Images) | Getty Images The game of football is decided in the trenches — more often than not. And the Las Vegas Raiders are habitually losing that battle. And, as a result, the team is in a four-game freefall and are 3-4 overall after a torrid 3-0 start to the 2026 season. The Silver & Black’s most recent outing — a 35-21 shellacking at the hands of the visiting Los Angeles Rams this past Sunday — where the team was outgained on the ground 199 yards to 48 yards, was the latest example of the ineffectiveness in the trenches. The Rams battered the Raiders at the line of scrimmage — offensively and defensively — sprinting to a 28-6 lead at halftime and the deficit threw everything into disarray for Las Vegas head coach Klint Kubiak and his coaching staff. The lack of production in the ground game reeked of not only ineffectiveness but also coaching ineptitude and the reeling Rams used the Raiders as a get-right game showcasing the balanced offensive attack and aggressive defense that Kubiak wants from his football team. “Yeah, well, we’re not going to run the ball until we stop the run. Until you make the game competitive,” Kubiak plainly said on Monday when asked about the constant theme of Las Vegas improving the run game and run defense. “You can’t be in the fourth quarter chasing points and expect to be a good run team. So, you need attempts, and in order to get those attempts, then we have to stop the run, and we have to keep our opponent out of the end zone.” In those four-straight losses, Las Vegas defense is getting sliced through like hot knife through butter allowing 656 total rushing yards while the offense has struggled to produce 223 rushing yards. The 199 yards yielded to the Rams ground game was the high mark during that span and the 72 yards the Raiders run game produced in the 30-27 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs in Week 4 being the most Kubiak’s crew produced. Through seven games, Las Vegas owns the third-worst ground game with 523 yards total and a 3.0 yards per carry average (second-worst). Only the Green Bay Packers (419 yards) and Cincinnati Bengals (487) are worse in that department — those two teams are 4-3 and 4-2, respectively, by the way. While there are fleeting moments breakaway runs, Raiders starting running back Ashton Jeanty (stats) and rookie backup Mike Washington Jr. (stats) run into the backs of offensive linemen or are taken down behind or at the line of scrimmage. The #Raiders were dominated up front. When you can't stop the run or run the ball, you can't win. pic.twitter.com/cm0C0g0mOv — JT The Brick (@JTTheBrick) October 26, 2026 Despite being stonewalled on the ground, Kubiak’s aerial attack is producing, albeit in one-dimensional fashion. Led by veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins, the Raiders passing game is the second-best group in terms of yardage (1,883) and atop the league with 16 touchdowns. The Rams have the most passing yards (1,919) and the San Francisco 49ers and Bengals are tied for second in touchdowns with 15. To showcase the imbalance that Kubiak spoke about above, Las Vegas is sixth with 266 passing attempts compared to 16th in rushing attempts with 174 totes. And the disparity in production from those two areas are crystal clear. It’s great that Las Vegas has the fifth-best offense with a total of 183 points, but the team also has the second-worst defense allowing a total of 197 points (a -13 point differential, the winless Los Angeles Chargers (-61) and 2-5 Arizona Cardinals (-66) are worst teams in this department). All of that showcases this isn’t an aberration for the Raiders. After the team’s defeat to the Chiefs, I noted Kubiak’s quickness to take ownership of the team’s shortcomings as admirable . Admitting an issue is the first step to fixing it. However, the inability to get the ground game going remains a glaring liability. Even considering there would be growing pains with a rookie head coach in Kubiak and his chosen defensive coordinator Rob Leonard (who is also a neophyte at his post), not being able to run the ball and stopping opponents from doing is a total collapse that exceeds realistic expectations. This highlights a disconnect in coaching, player execution, and overall roster quality. Of that trio, the first two are within Kubiak’s and his coaching staff’s control while the third can be truly bolstered next offseason with another round of free agency and draft. Sure the general manager John Spytek can explore the trade market before the November 10 deadline, but the Raiders roster issues in Year 1 of the Kubiak era requires more than just that. “Well, no one’s coming to help us. We’ve got to figure it out ourselves as a coaching staff with the players, and we have to complement each other as well because to we’ve got to start the game a lot faster offensively,” Kubiak said in the postgame press conference after the loss to the Rams. Great punch out by JJ Pegues 🔥 LARvsLV on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/ulY8ligD9N — NFL (@NFL) October 25, 2026 Accountability is key and it’s present in both the Raiders coaching staff and roster. “Absolutely, yeah. And there’s conversations like that every game, whether you’re winning and losing. There’s always hard conversations at halftime, making adjustments, holding people accountable. That’s part of every team,” middle linebacker Nakobe Dean said after the loss to the Rams. “For sure, for sure, I got a lot of belief. I got a lot of faith in this team,” Dean added. “We got a lot of great players. We just got to put it together. We got to play as a team. We got to play as one. We can’t be all individual mercenaries out there.” The taking action to change the behavior and fixing specific problems remains an issue. Opponents continue to load the box to stymie the Raiders ground game and daring the team to beat them over the top — which Las Vegas hasn’t consistently done even though it’s gotten quality production from tight end Brock Bowers and wide receiver Tre Tucker. Communication issues on defense compound a young Raiders secondary as tight ends, deep routes, and short passes in the flat are wide open too often. There there’s poor tackling technique and angles (Pro Football Reference charts Las Vegas with 41 missed tackles, eighth most int he league and a 8.5 percent missed tackle rate as a team) that make the soft zone coverages even more ineffective. And because of the consistent shortfalls, tempered expectations are in order. The luster of the 3-0 start is gone and reality has set in like heavy fog. Three victories and four losses in the initial seven games is progress for a rookie head coach, so kudos to Kubiak. And while his expectations from his football team are elevated and gargantuan, this is Year 1 of his tenure. And the Raiders are no paragon of quality depth and talent roster-wise — I don’t think anyone will say otherwise (and if you do, can I have a sip of that Kool-Aid?). “Yeah. I think from our perspective as players and coaches, that’s not something that’s on our mind. What’s on our mind is win the next game, and we’ve played very talented teams and played much more competitive games than that, being the Chiefs and the Bills,” Kubiak responded when asked about this not being an overnight rebuild and did the last four loses show there’s a gap that needs to be made up. “Yesterday, when you start the game that slow, you put yourself in position to be behind that much, you don’t give yourself a chance to win.” "Fernando [Mendoza] is gonna play at some point, it's not gonna be this week." The ultra-productive Cousins remains the starting quarterback and Kubiak continues to seek offensive…

title: Emerging rookie Omar Cooper Jr. will test Taron Johnson in slot for Las Vegas Raiders-New York Jets Week 8 key matchups
summary: If a postseason elimination game in Week 8 exists, the contest between the Las Vegas Raiders and New York Jets is it. The 3-4 Raiders and 2-5 Jets are only separated by a game and both teams are on the outside looking in at the AFC playoff picture, meaning neither club can afford another loss […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images If a postseason elimination game in Week 8 exists, the contest between the Las Vegas Raiders and New York Jets is it. The 3-4 Raiders and 2-5 Jets are only separated by a game and both teams are on the outside looking in at the AFC playoff picture , meaning neither club can afford another loss to stay “in the hunt” at the halfway point of the season. So, the three key matchups below will be crucial to keep any (albeit slim) playoff hopes alive. Johnson vs. Cooper While wide receiver Garrett Wilson is still the Jets’ top option in the passing game, leading the team with 37 catches for 444 yards and three touchdowns through seven games, Wilson’s production has significantly decreased over the last two weeks. He’s logged just six catches for 70 yards in the last couple of contests combined. Part of the reason for that is rookie wideout Omar Cooper Jr. returned from injury. After suffering a sprained ankle while hauling in his first NFL catch (a 30-yarder) and just five snaps into his professional debut, Cooper has been on a tear since returning from injured reserve in Week 6. He had six catches for 103 yards and a touchdown against the New England Patriots and then went for five, 115 and one versus the Miami Dolphins last Sunday. According to Pro Football Focus , the Indiana product has spent 67.8% of his pass snaps in the slot this season, where seven of his catches (58.3% of his season total) and 188 yards (75.8%) have come from. Additionally, his 5.37 yards per route run from the slot ranks third among NFL wide receivers who have at least six targets on the inside. Granted, that’s where missing four games is a slight advantage, as that figure could come down with a bigger sample size. But the overall point is that Cooper has been a problem for opposing nickelbacks. Meanwhile, the Raiders have a veteran nickel in Taron Johnson, who has been stingy in slot coverage this season. Of corners with at least 41 coverage snaps on the interior, he ranks fifth in yards per coverage snap allowed at 0.63, giving up 10 catches on 16 targets (62.5%) for 96 yards and a touchdown, per PFF . That being said, Johnson has benefited from a few off-target throws, recording just one PBU and logging a subpar 54.0 coverage grade . Where this matchup could get really interesting is after the catch. Despite missing time, Cooper ranks seventh among slot receivers with 111 YAC and second in YAC per reception (15.9, minimum six targets) and has forced three missed tackles, according to PFF . Johnson is 15th among nickels in total YAC allowed ( 58 ) and is typically a sure tackler, recording his first miss of 2026 in Week 5. However, he has four failed tackle attempts in the last three games. While Wilson is the name people recognize most in the Jets’ receiving corps, Cooper is the hot hand right now, which makes Johnson’s impact on Sunday even more important. Bowers vs. Fitzpatrick Brock Bowers’ impact on the Raiders’ offense doesn’t need much explanation. He missed the first two games of the season and still leads the team in targets (52) and receptions (34) while trailing wide receiver Tre Tucker for the team lead in receiving yards (474 to 455) and touchdowns (four to three). That’s led to the tight end getting the ‘WR1’ treatment from defenses, where Las Vegas’ opponents often put their best coverage defender on him. For New York, that player is versatile defensive back Minkah Fitzpatrick. The nine-year veteran has made five Pro Bowls and been a first-team All-Pro three times throughout his career and is still playing at a high level. On 148 coverage snaps this season, he’s only been targeted nine times and has yielded just five receptions, per PFF , with a PBU and an interception thrown in the mix. However, he is prone to giving up explosive plays in coverage, allowing 122 receiving yards for 24.4 yards per catch, including 20-, 37- and 42-yard grabs. Granted, Fitzpatrick has only given up on catch to a tight end — an 18-yarder to Colston Loveland in Week 4 against the Chicago Bears — and the Jets rank 13th with 0.186 EPA per target to tight ends this season, per Sumer Sports . But Bowers is not a typical player for the position, and New York is coming off games where Hunter Henry had four catches for 48 yards, four first downs and a touchdown, and Greg Dulcich went for five grabs, 85 yards and five first downs. Part of the issue for Gang Green, though, is that none of Henry’s and Dulcich’s targets came against Fitzpatrick. In other words, expect to see the two perennial Pro Bowlers line up across from each other often in Week 8. Jeanty vs. Sherwood Of course, the Raiders’ run game is struggling, ranking second to last in the NFL with negative 0.27 EPA per rush, according to Sumer Sports . That likely isn’t changing against a Jets defense that currently has the eighth-best EPA per rush at negative 0.12 . Still, a matchup between a running back and a linebacker can be a big one on Sunday with the implications it has in the passing game. Ashton Jeanty has almost as many receiving yards as rushing yards so far this year ( 312 to 328 ) and currently leads all running backs in receptions (34, tied with Christian McCaffrey), receiving yards and receiving touchdowns (three). He’s also the most targeted (43) back in the league and is tied for seventh with Jahmyr Gibbs in yards per route run (1.91), according to PFF . Meanwhile, Jamien Sherwood has been a quality coverage linebacker in New York this season. He has a solid 65.5 PFF coverage grade that ranks 25th at the position and is tied for 20th with a seven percent forced incompletion rate. Additionally, Sherwood has given up 25 or fewer receiving yards in five out of seven games . However, he has yielded 236 yards on the campaign, with over half (127) coming in Week 3 against the Detroit Lions. The former college safety had an especially tough time against Gibbs, who hauled in five catches on five targets for 47 yards against him, per PFF . Lions’ backup running back Sione Vaki also had an 11-yard catch versus Sherwood in that contest, for good measure. Also, the matchup extends to a pass protection battle. Sherwood has registered 12 pressures on 49 pass rushes — the third-most among off-ball linebackers — and Jeanty has given up three pressures on 37 opportunities . However, the latter has been much better in that department lately, allowing just one pressure in the last four games while recording three PFF pass-blocking grades in the high 70s to low 80s three times during that stretch. In other words, this matchup has a high variance of outcomes. In full disclosure, Tyler Linderbaum vs. T’Vondre Sweat and DJ Glaze vs. David Bailey were also considered key matchups. However, according to Eric Allen of the Jets’ website , head coach Aaron Glenn said Sweat is week-to-week with a knee injury that caused him to exit last week’s game early, and Bailey is dealing with a “lingering” groin injury that could keep him sidelined on Sunday. Neither player participated in Wednesday’s practice.

title: Week 8 game at Jets is critical for Raiders
summary: While explaining why he is sticking with veteran Kirk Cousins as his starting quarterback, Las Vegas Raiders coach Klint Kubiak pointed out the team is still in the AFC playoff mix. To remain in the mix, the Raiders must win at the New York Jets on Sunday. After starting the season 3-0, the Raiders have […]
full_text: (Photo by Candice Ward/Getty Images) | Getty Images While explaining why he is sticking with veteran Kirk Cousins as his starting quarterback, Las Vegas Raiders coach Klint Kubiak pointed out the team is still in the AFC playoff mix. To remain in the mix, the Raiders must win at the New York Jets on Sunday. After starting the season 3-0, the Raiders have dropped four straight game. Falling to 3-5 at midseason would be staggering for the Raiders for several reasons. The Jets are 2-5 and aren’t a good team. The Raiders, whose three wins this season have come against teams with a combined 3-16 record, must take advantage of this schedule break. Their next three games are at the San Francisco 49ers, at home against the Seattle Seahawks and at the Denver Broncos. Those three teams are a combined 15-6. There is little room for error in this stretch. The Raiders’ schedule does ease down the stretch, but the key is for Las Vegas not to create a hole they can’t dig out of. There are currently nine teams in the AFC with running records. Seven teams advance to the playoffs. The Raiders are the only team in the conference at 3-4. Six teams have two or fewer victories in the AFC. If the Raiders want to stay close the playoff chase, they must win at New York. Dropping to 3-5 after a 3-0 start would be devastating for a team and it could propel the team into becoming trade sellers before the November 10 deadline. So, for a lot of reasons, this is a crucial week for Kubiak’s team.

title: Miami Dolphins vs. New England Patriots: Three Reasons Why
summary: Miami Dolphins fans have enjoyed a post-win week that is always extra enjoyable when it comes against the Jets. But the time has come to put away that excitement and focus on another division opponent: The New England Patriots. For a few seasons, the Pats were a doormat, which they honestly deserve after 2 decades […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - OCTOBER 25: Malik Willis #2 and Caleb Douglas #7 of the Miami Dolphins react after winning the game against the New York Jets at MetLife Stadium on October 25, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images Miami Dolphins fans have enjoyed a post-win week that is always extra enjoyable when it comes against the Jets. But the time has come to put away that excitement and focus on another division opponent: The New England Patriots. For a few seasons, the Pats were a doormat, which they honestly deserve after 2 decades of dominance. But they rebounded last year with a shocking Super Bowl run. That run could maybe be explained by smoke and mirrors (schedule, backup QBs faced, etc.) but make no mistake, the Pats are not a doormat right now. Does this mean the Dolphins have no chance? Absolutely not. 3 REASONS FOR HOPE THE DOLPHINS ARE BACK HOME This may seem like a cop-out reason. I have used it in previous home games and in fairness, playing at home is an advantage. But Joe Robbie Hard Rock Stadium has typically been a house of horrors for the Patriots. The Dolphins have hosted the Patriots 61 times in franchise history, including playoffs. The Pats have won in Miami 18 times . That’s a 0.295-win percentage. This isn’t simply a result of the Dolphins being good back in the 70s or when Dan Marino was under center. Since 2000 – the Belichick and Brady era up until the Vrabel era – the Pats have won in Miami 10 times in 26 contests (0.385-win percentage). Brady and the Pats won 9 of those, even including 2008 when Matt Cassel was playing for an injured Brady. In 2000, the Pats finished 5-11. They did not have a losing record again until 2020 when they went 7-9. In that span, the Pats averaged 12.2 wins every season, meaning an average of 3.8 losses per season. You could almost bank on one of those 4 annual losses to be against the Dolphins in Miami. Of course, the circumstances are different this season. The Dolphins are rebuilding and the Pats are coming off a SB run. On the surface, this seems like an easy W for the Pats. But in Miami… the Dolphins have as good a chance as any. The Pats just do not like it there. THE OFFENSE MAY BE FIGURING THINGS OUT I don’t want to make too much of the performance against the Jets. It is the Jets after all. But the Dolphins put up 377 yards at 5.5 yards per play against a stingy Jets defense that allows only 4.9 YPP (and that’s after the Dolphins). The Dolphins did it on the road too which is important because the offense has struggled on the road. In 2 home games, the Dolphins average 330 yards per game. In their 3 road games prior to week 7, the Dolphins averaged 247 total yards per game. That average was boosted by a 77-yard garbage time TD against the 49ers. The run game has been the engine driving the offense with Ollie Gordon II taking over for an injured De’Von Achane. He is averaging 4.7 YPC and has scored a TD in each of the last 4 games. Malik Willis is adding to that formula with some designed runs and key scrambles. Willis is 99 yards away from breaking Fiedler’s record for most rushing yards by a QB in a season for the franchise. But Willis also looked like a competent QB passing the ball against the Jets, which was a surprise to me. The Jets have a really good pass defense and given Willis’ struggles in prior games, I was expecting the worst. But he played really well. The Pats defense is decent against the run. They allow 3.9 YPC, which is tied for 12th best. They kept Josh Allen in check in their contest against the Bills with 5 attempts for 4 yards, so they can handle running QBs. But their pass defense is not as daunting, certainly not as good as the Jets statistically. While the Jets allow 6.7 YPA, the Pats are 20th at 7.4 YPA. They have a pressure percentage of 22.2%, which is 18th highest, but they only produce a hurry at a rate of 6%, which is 8th lowest. They blitz at a rate similar to the Jets (36.5 for NE, 36.4 for NYJ). But Miami possibly developed an answer for the blitz against the Jets. Perhaps that carries over. The Pats aren’t a bad defense by any means, but the matchup for Miami isn’t necessarily bad either. THE PASS RUSH WILL GET HOME THIS WEEK I have posted the tweets about Chop Robinson and NextGenStats has him tops in the league with a pressure rate of 23.4%. This graph shows that not only is the pressure rate high, but no one gets to the QB as fast as Chop . The issue is the sacks aren’t there. He’s close but that only counts in horseshoes, hand grenades, and nuclear bombs. This week, he’ll get a OT combo of Will Campbell and Morgan Moses. I don’t have access to all the fancy stats i.e. I ain’tagonna pay for it, but from what I can find, Campbell is having a good season. He’s not allowing pressures at a high rate (I’ve seen numbers like 5.6%). RT Morgan Moses on the other hand is parting the Red Sea for defenders, allowing a pressure rate of 14% . He will have his hands full with Robinson. The Pats have a good IOL in terms of pass protection with center Jared Wilson and guards Ben Brown and Alijah Vera-Tucker all ranked top 20 in pass block win rate. But both AVT and Brown were injured and missed time with injuries. Brown could be back, but AVT is now on injured reserve. Something has to give. I dislike making predictions, but I think Chop has his breakout game for this season with at least 2 sacks. BUT EVEN… if the pass rush doesn’t get home, the pressures could create some turnovers. The Pats are tied for the most INTS thrown with 8. In any case, I have a feeling the pass rush finally gets to it this week. It’s only a matter of time before it does. 3 REASONS FOR CONCERN PASS DEFENSE I don’t need to keep reminding you about the issues with Miami’s pass defense. Everyone knows about the awful completion percentage allowed. The Jets are a mid-level passing offense but still produced against the Dolphins. The Pats are a top 10 passing offense in both total yards, yards per game, yards per attempt, completion percentage, and passer rating. It’s not a question of whether the Pats passing game will produce, but rather how much they will produce. The Pats acquired AJ Brown from Philly and he will be an issue for whatever CB is facing him. But in the 3 games he has played so far, he only has 9 total catches on 20 targets. He may be due for a breakout game, but thus far, he has been quiet. The Dolphins did well against Garrett Wilson last week. The problem will come from RB Rhamondre Stevenson and – cover your eyes Dolphins – TE Hunter Henry. Stevenson is 3rd in targets with 24 and has 20 catches for 204 yards and a TD. He averages 9.4 yards after catch per reception with an average depth of target (ADOT) of 0.8 yards. He’s essentially getting a 1st down every time he catches the ball. Henry will be another TE thorn in the Dolphins’ flesh unless they get something figured out before Sunday. Henry is 2nd in targets with 31. He has 26 catches for 296 yards and a TD. He averaged 6.6 yards after catch per reception with an ADOT of 6 yards. The Pats spread out their targets fairly evenly, but they’ll most certainly attack the Dolphins with those 2 players. Don’t rule out rookie TE Eli Raridon either. He has 12 catches on 16 targets and 2 TDs this season. His target share has started going up. DeMario Douglas is the top target for the Pats with 34. He has 23 catches, 256 yards and 3 TDs. He works primarily in the slot thus will face rookie Chris Johnson most of the game. Johnson has played well in recent games, but he will be tested. Doubs and Hollins will also be factors. Summing it up, the Pats are going to throw the ball and have success. The real question is how much the Dolphins can limit the damage. RUN DEFENSE The Pats’ passing offense will be a problem, but they’ll present a problem on the ground also. The Pats are 8th in total rushing yards (854) and 11th in rushing yards per game (122.0). They are 22nd in…

title: Ollie Gordon: ‘Hafley definitely tried to connect with us more’
summary: The Miami Dolphins reset the franchise this season, from the front office through the coaching staff and onto the roster. The reset has brought with it learning curves, struggles, and growing pains. The team started the season 0-5, with talk that they could be the first team to finish a season 0-17. Last Sunday, they […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - OCTOBER 11: Ollie Gordon II #0 of the Miami Dolphins celebrates during an NFL football game against the Cincinnati Bengals at Hard Rock Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Miami Dolphins reset the franchise this season, from the front office through the coaching staff and onto the roster. The reset has brought with it learning curves, struggles, and growing pains. The team started the season 0-5, with talk that they could be the first team to finish a season 0-17. Last Sunday, they ended that talk with a solid win over the New York Jets, with every aspect of the team working together and showing their potential. Running back Ollie Gordon II, a second-year player, started the year as a depth player but has thrust himself into a starring role following an injury to De’Von Achane. Earlier this year, he sat down with former Dolphins tackle Terron Armstead on “The Set with Terron Armstead” podcast, and discussed the situation with the team. Released this week, the discussion included a comparison of first-year head coach Jeff Hafley and former head coach Mike McDaniel. “Haf has definitely tried to connect with us more,” Gordon said. “Every team meeting, he’s up in front of us, he is talking. He’s sitting in offensive meetings. He’ll sit halfway through, he goes to defense, he’ll come back. He puts his two cents in, which is good, you need that. He’s not just a one-sided coach. Obviously he was a defensive guy before, that’s his background, but he comes in, he’s like, ‘If I were scheming against y’all, I would do this and this. So I need y’all to make it look like this.’ I feel like that helps alot, especially coming from a defensive guy. “He’s lined up against every offense you can in this league, so it’s like he knows what he is talking about. I definitely feel like he is trying to be more connected to us and make us connected as a team.” Gordon also shared his three “welcome to the NFL” moments: “I feel like one was being on the field with [linebacker] Bobby Wagner when we played the [Washington] Commanders, bro. As a kid, I watched him. I watched the league, you know what I am saying? All of them. I wanted all of them [the Seattle Seahawks ’Legion of Boom’ defense of the 2010s]. [Safety] Earl [Thomas], [safety] Kam Chancellor, [cornerback] Richard [Sherman]. Being able to be on the field at the same time as him, I feel like that was huge. Just like to little me, like ‘Damn, you’re really on the field with Bobby Wagner.‘” Armstead, after pointing out that Gordon did not mention a hit or a specific play, but just being on the field with Wagner as a moment he remembers and made the NFL real to Gordon, said, “I love that, for real. People be acting like they are too proud or got too much ego to be like a fan of somebody. First time I played Terrell Suggs, same thing. Like seeing these guys on the other side that are legends, and still actively playing. Jared Allen, Julius Peppers, I’m like ‘Dog, this is dope.’” View this post on Instagram Gordon went on to his second and third moments, saying, “Two, the Baltimore game, me and my coach [running back coach Eric Studesville] got into it after I slipped…It was one of those where everyone is a grown man in the party. You can’t talk to one person crazy and if you get talked to crazy, you get a reaction from the other person. I feel like, that was my first time really just getting into it with a coach.” Gordon added, “I ain’t going to lie, that was so bad. I think I blacked out. I don’t even remember…We was cool, though, we was cool right after. We talked at halftime. We talked after the game. We was good.” For his third moment, Gordon turned to the team’s Week 10 game last year, when the Buffalo Bills visited Miami. “We ran a little outside zone,” the running back explained, “When I got the ball, [Bills defensive end Joey] Bosa was just looking at me. Bro must have just picked me up and flipped me over. Oh my God. My life flashed before my eyes and when I opened my eyes, I was on the ground.” Gordon went on to add that he thought the hit from Bosa was payback for earlier in the year when the running back scored his first career touchdown, running through the Bills’ defense – including Bosa. What do you think of Gordon’s three “welcome to the NFL” moments? Do you think Hafley is connecting with the players and having the players connect with each other better than McDaniel did?

summary: The Miami Dolphins, coming off their first win in 2026, face a second-straight AFC East division rival this weekend. full_text: Miami Gardens, FL - November 24: New England Patriots QB Drake Maye has his pass knocked down by Miami Dolphins LB Chop Robinson in the fourth quarter. (Photo by Matthew J. Lee/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images The Miami Dolphins, coming off their first win in 2026, face a second-straight AFC East division rival this weekend. Having dispatched the New York Jets in Week 7, Miami returns to South Florida to host the New England Patriots in a late-afternoon Week 8 contest. The Dolphins moved to 1-5 on the season with their victory, using their Week 6 bye week to make adjustments and continue the growth of the league’s youngest team and, ultimately, land the first victory for head coach Jeff Hafley. Now they will look to upset the Patriots, who fell to 4-3 this year with a Week 7 Thursday night loss to the Chicago Bears. The Patriots at Dolphins game is one of only two games in the late-afternoon slot – but the Kansas City Chiefs at Denver Broncos game is nearly a national broadcast with Miami-New England relegated to local networks. Where will the Patriots vs. Dolphins game air on TV? The game is on CBS with Andrew Catalon, Logan Ryan, and A.J. Ross on the call. The current plan is for Miami, West Palm Beach, and Fort Myers to pick up the game in Florida, while the New England region, from Connecticut and Rhode Island through Massachusetts, Vermont, and New Hampshire, and across Maine getting the broadcast. Otherwise, the country will see the Chiefs and Broncos. Broadcast plans can still be adjusted, with local CBS affiliates shifting the game they will air, but for now, it is an extremely limited region for the Dolphins-Patriots contest. What other games will I see in Florida? 1 p.m. Eastern time slot CBS will air the Buffalo Bills at Baltimore Ravens game to start the day in South Florida, including Miami, West Palm Beach, and Fort Myers, up through Tampa. The rest of the state, north from Orlando and across the Panhandle, will see the Indianapolis Colts at Jacksonville Jaguars game. The FOX broadcast plan is more broken across the state. Miami will see the Las Vegas Raiders at New York Jets game. West Palm Beach is slated to see the Minnesota Vikings at Detroit Lions game, while the majority of the rest of the state will have the Atlanta Falcons at Tampa Bay Buccaneers game. Jacksonville will not have a game on FOX to avoid the conflict of the local broadcast on CBS. The western end of the Panhandle will get the Arizona Cardinals at Dallas Cowboys game. 4:05/4:25 p.m. Eastern time slot We covered the FOX plan for the late slot when discussing the Dolphins game. CBS does not have the doubleheader, this week, but Jacksonville will have the Los Angeles Chargers at Los Angeles Rams game. 8:20 p.m. Eastern time slot – Sunday Night Football The Sunday Night Football game this weekend will feature the Philadelphia Eagles at Washington Commanders game.

full_text: SEATTLE, CO - OCTOBER 15: Christian Haynes #64 of the Seattle Seahawks runs out of the tunnel prior to an NFL football game against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on October 15, 2026 in Seattle, Colorado. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Wednesday, the Miami Dolphins claimed offensive guard Christian Haynes off waivers from the Seattle Seahawks despite the Baltimore Ravens announcing earlier in the day that they were the team to claim the former third round pick. With Miami being higher on the waiver priority list, Haynes is heading to sunny South Florida. Haynes, drafted in the third round of the 2024 NFL Draft, started five games for Seattle this season, but was deemed expendable after the Seahawks traded for star offensive guard Quenton Nelson — formerly of the Indianapolis Colts — earlier this week. Over his three-year career with Seattle, Haynes has played in a total of 31 games. To make room for Haynes, the Dolphins waived rookie guard DJ Campbell — the 200th pick (6th round) of the 2026 NFL Draft out of Texas. Campbell had not played in a game for Miami this season as he’s been a healthy scratch for the club each week. With starting left guard Kadyn Proctor currently in concussion protocol, the Dolphins add Haynes to an offensive guard group that also includes starting right guard Jonah Savaiinaea and reserve linemen Caedan Wallace and Jarrett Kingston. We will continue to keep you updated on all things Miami Dolphins as the team prepares to welcome the New England Patriots to Hard Rock Stadium this Sunday.

title: Vikes Views: Who Ya Got? Minnesota Vikings at Detroit Lions
summary: The undefeated Minnesota Vikings will have their biggest challenge of the year as they head to the Motor City to take on the Detroit Lions. It will be strength against strength when the high-powered Lions offense is on the field against the best defense in the league. Series Record: 82-45-2 Road Record: 37-27-1 Largest Win: […]
full_text: Sep 25, 2011; Minneapolis, MN, USA; Minnesota Vikings defensive end Brian Robison (96) sacks Detroit Lions quarterback Matthew Stafford (9) in the third quarter at Mall of America Field. The Lions defeated the Vikings 26-23 in overtime. Mandatory Credit: Marilyn Indahl-USA TODAY Sports | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The undefeated Minnesota Vikings will have their biggest challenge of the year as they head to the Motor City to take on the Detroit Lions. It will be strength against strength when the high-powered Lions offense is on the field against the best defense in the league. Series Record: 82-45-2 Road Record: 37-27-1 Largest Win: 34-0, November 9, 1980 Largest Defeat: 45-7, December 12, 1981 Streak: W2 The Vikings are giving up a league-low 12.3 points per game, 4.9 fewer than the second-best Kansas City Chiefs. The Lions rank 26th in the league, allowing 27.5 points per game. The Lions have the 2nd highest scoring offense in the league with 30.7 PPG. The Vikings are 24th with 20.8 PPG. The Vikings boast the best kick return and punt return averages in the league. Pair that with the best kicker in football, and special teams have become a real advantage. The Lions rank first in offensive success rate on first down (50%), while the Vikings rank 32nd (29.2%). Motown legends The Four Tops will play a halftime show. Justin Jefferson has been a Lions killer throughout his career, averaging 107 yards per game and a 72% catch rate when targeted.. However, he has averaged just 53 YPG in the last four meetings. Unfortunately, we won’t get to see Kerby Joseph reunited with Justin Jefferson this week. The modern rivalry of the NFC North has been fun the last few years. It was nice to have the two annual wins penciled in back in the day, but I do enjoy it now that the Lions are an actual NFL team. It’s a clash of styles for two familiar foes. One of the best offenses in the league will face the definitively best defense in the league. Something has to give on Sunday. Either the Lions prove they can move the ball against an elite defense, or the Vikings continue their march toward becoming the most feared defense in football. Everyone seems to be on the Lions, either because the believe in them, or the Vikings are “due” for a loss. I’m not picking anything based on who is “due” anything. I know the Viking defense is due a turnover twice a game. They’re due another 2nd half shutout. I’m not picking this team to lose until I see them face an offense they can’t stop. We’ll get to enjoy watching them against the two best offenses in the league the next two weeks. I’m taking them to win this week, if I’m right, they’ll be my pick next week too. Vikings 20 – Lions 13

title: How the Vikings Can Neutralize Jahmyr Gibbs and Upset Detroit
summary: How can the Minnesota Vikings beat the Detroit Lions? Simple—exploit Jahmyr Gibbs. On the latest episode of The Real Forno Show, host Tyler Forness and producer Dave Stefano broke down the Vikings’ key to victory, a wild NFC North trade ahead of the deadline, and why Brian Flores’ defense could be the ultimate difference-maker on […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - OCTOBER 11: Jahmyr Gibbs #0 of the Detroit Lions warms up during the NFL game at State Farm Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. The Lions defeated the Cardinals 45-21. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images How can the Minnesota Vikings beat the Detroit Lions? Simple—exploit Jahmyr Gibbs. On the latest episode of The Real Forno Show , host Tyler Forness and producer Dave Stefano broke down the Vikings’ key to victory, a wild NFC North trade ahead of the deadline, and why Brian Flores’ defense could be the ultimate difference-maker on Sunday. The show opened with blockbuster news: the Chicago Bears acquired DT Jeffrey Simmons from the Tennessee Titans for two first-round picks and a fourth. Forness questioned the fit within Dennis Allen’s read-and-react scheme: “If Simmons comes in and it’s just Jeffrey Simmons, it’s not gonna matter that much.” The Bears still lack edge rushers, raising questions about whether the move translates. Meanwhile, the Vikings have been reportedly aggressive in the run up to the deadline, with names like Maxx Crosby and Jalen Carter circulating. “If you bring in Jalen Carter, that’s become the centerpiece of your defense,” Forness said. “That is the guy that you are building everything around.” He emphasized that such a move wouldn’t be for 2026 alone—it would be a long-term foundational piece, especially with Andrew Van Ginkel and Kyle Van Noy hitting free agency. Forness was blunt on the quarterback front: only Daniel Jones and Kirk Cousins, both familiar with Kevin O’Connell’s system, make sense as trade targets. “You’re not trading for great players at this point. You’re trading for somebody who you hope can steer the ship.” On J.J. McCarthy’s departure, he added: “He got himself traded. The Vikings didn’t do it because they wanted to give up on him. He earned it.” The heart of the episode centered on neutralizing Gibbs in pass protection. Last Christmas, the Vikings forced Gibbs into a career-high 15 pass-protection snaps—over 35% of his total—resulting in seven pressures and a sack. “They made it so Gibbs was basically ineffective because of their blitzing and how they attacked,” Forness explained. With Van Ginkel, Blake Cashman, Ivan Pace Jr., and Dallas Turner matching up on him, the plan is straightforward: make Gibbs block, or take him off the field entirely. Stefano noted the broader impact: “By having him pass block, he’s not out in their patterns either.” Flores’ defense, refined over three seasons, has reached what Forness called his “opus” and a “pile driver onto a steel chair.” Stefano captured the confidence: “Our defense does. They know what they’re doing. The question is, how quickly can Goff figure it out? And I don’t think anybody’s figured it out this season.” Forness agreed: “I do think that this defense is good enough to win a Super Bowl on their own.” Key Points: Gibbs exploitation : Vikings will blitz in the 70–85% range, forcing Gibbs to pass-protect or leave the field Flores’ finalized defense : Three years of refinement into a system nobody has solved Trade deadline : Maxx Crosby and Jalen Carter as long-term defensive cornerstones; Daniel Jones as affordable QB insurance McCarthy’s exit : Talent was never the question—”He got himself traded” Offensive key : Kyler Murray must “take a deep breath, play more relaxed, and trust Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison” Lions’ defensive weakness : 30th in EPA per play, 31st in explosive play percentage allowed Prediction : Vikings favored by 3–3.5; Forness picks Minnesota: “I think they’re gonna be able to take down Goff” Listen: View Link Or on your favorite podcast aggregator. Watch: The Vikings’ defense has yet to be solved, and if Flores’ unit can again turn Jahmyr Gibbs into a liability, Sunday could be a statement win. For the full breakdown—trade deadline analysis, quarterback rumors, and complete Xs and Os—listen to The Real Forno Show , a Minnesota Vikings podcast from Vikings 1st & SKOL. Fan with Us!!! Tyler Forness @TheRealForno of Vikings 1st & SKOL @Vikings1stSKOL and A to Z Sports @AtoZSportsNFL , with Dave Stefano @Luft_Krigare producing this Vikings 1st & SKOL production, the @RealFornoShow found at the @BleavNetwork . What do you think? Can the Vikings exploit Gibbs and prove they’re the team to beat in the NFC North, or will Jared Goff finally find the answers?

title: Five Good Questions with Pride of Detroit
summary: While we haven’t gotten that many opportunities to do so this year, this week we’ve gotten the chance to gather some intel on the Minnesota Vikings’ opponent for this week from the folks who run the SB Nation site that covers them throughout the season. I got the opportunity to exchange Five Good Questions with […]
full_text: While we haven’t gotten that many opportunities to do so this year, this week we’ve gotten the chance to gather some intel on the Minnesota Vikings’ opponent for this week from the folks who run the SB Nation site that covers them throughout the season. I got the opportunity to exchange Five Good Questions with Ryan Mathews from Pride of Detroit, SB Nation’s home for everything about the Detroit Lions. You can see my answers to the questions that he sent me over at POD (or on the front page here). Here are the questions that I sent over to him, along with his responses. 1) It seems like every time we talk about the Vikings and the Lions, the subject of Dan Campbell’s aggressiveness on fourth down comes up. This past Sunday, he chose to go for it on a 4th-and-1 from his own 24-yard line in a 17-17 game with five minutes left in regulation, and the Lions didn’t convert. They dodged a bullet when the Packers missed the go-ahead field goal, and ultimately won the game. Are Lions’ fans still fans of Campbell’s aggressiveness or do they feel he veers into recklessness too frequently in these situations now that he’s been the head coach for a while? In the moment, it felt incredibly reckless, even by Dan Campbell’s standards. It was a long yard to gain, and with the way the offensive line was having trouble keeping Packers defenders out of the backfield, the play call felt uninspired at best. But after hearing Campbell’s explanation, it’s hard to argue with his rationale: Detroit didn’t want to punt and run the risk of letting Green Bay eat the clock and score without having a chance at rebuttal. Considering the Lions’ offense was moving the ball all day long, it makes a lot of sense to put the onus on that side of the ball to keep them in the game. However, the issue I took with that particular drive was the sequence of play calls prior to going for it on fourth down. Jahmyr Gibbs arguably reached the line to gain on first down, but Campbell decided not to challenge the play–and in his defense, overturning the spot of the ball doesn’t happen all too often. But after going to Gibbs again on second and third down, the latter being a short pass, it felt like poor play-calling choices if the plan all along was going for it on fourth down that drive. In fact, I took a bigger issue with a different fourth down Detroit went for earlier in the game. At the tail end of the third quarter and from the Packers’ 6-yard line, Detroit was up by three points and decided to go for it on fourth-and-5. Going up six at that point in the game, and forcing Green Bay to find the end zone to take the lead with only a quarter to go felt like a better decision. 2) The Lions’ defense has had significant issues this year, particularly against the pass, where they’re 32nd in the league in both yards allowed and touchdown passes allowed. Do you think this is more of a function of the personnel they have in the back end of the defense or are there other reasons that they’ve had problems stopping teams through the air so far? With the secondary, it’s been a mix; a little bit of this and a little bit of that. Injuries completely ravaged the safety position at the start of the season. Detroit were already without Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph, but not long after, both Avonte Maddox and Thomas Harper were sidelined with injuries. Detroit essentially ran out of contingencies after Week 4, and after both injuries and disappointing play took their toll, the Lions were desperate enough to turn to rookie fifth-round nickel cornerback Keith Abney II–he played nearly 60 snaps at deep safety against the Cardinals and did a pretty good job. Good enough he played 34 snaps, this time in more of a box safety role, against the Packers last week despite the return of Brian Branch. Branch’s return last week was a seismic shot in the arm for their defense as a whole. He picked up an interception and was his usual self in run defense, recording three run stops according to Next Gen Stats–tied for second among Lions’ defenders in Week 7. Kerby Joseph did return to practice on Wednesday, but don’t expect him to play in this one. Detroit usually gets their players at least a week before they return them to the field. In short, much of Detroit’s shortcomings on defense stemmed from miscommunications, misunderstanding of personnel, and missed opportunities from the secondary. Cornerback play could have been better, and the Lions were forced to shake things up at CB2 after Rock Ya-Sin’s injury, but much like the safety room, it’s healing and performing much better in recent weeks–even if that means going from 31st in EPA/play on defense in the first four weeks to ranking 18th in EPA/play over their last two games. Throw in some positive turnover differentials and Lions fans couldn’t have imagined seeing this kind of improvement more than a month ago. 3) The Vikings come into this one sporting the best defense in the league by most measures, but the Lions have been able to have a measure of success against them in recent years. How do you think Drew Petzig and company are going to go about trying to attack Brian Flores’ group and trying to solve them this time around? Earlier in the week, Flores had some incredibly complimentary words to share about Jared Goff: “Command of the offense, cadence, his ability to just extract information from the defense with shifts, motions, cadence, and his ability to gather that information and then make the correct reads and throws, is high level.” “Statistically, he’s been one of the best quarterbacks, not even statistically, period. He’s been one of the best quarterbacks in the National Football League over, you know, a good amount of time. And so, yes, he’s grown quite a bit. That’s what you expect, as guys get more time under their belt. I think he’s one of the best in the league and they’ve got a great skill group and he knows how to, you know, distribute the ball to all of them.” It hasn’t all been perfect with Goff and Petzing despite the numbers, and that might sound privileged considering they rank third in EPA/play and second in success rate on offense, but there’s still real room for this offense to work through some of their kinks. It isn’t all perfect along the offensive line as Detroit reintroduces Cade Mays at center, and the ground game is still missing some of those home-run plays from Jahmyr Gibbs. But there is something that Detroit found a lot of success in doing last week: crossing routes and working the middle of the field to open up the shots outside the numbers. Those kinds of long-developing routes require the offensive line holding up in pass protection, and they helped hold the Packers to the 24th-lowest pressure rate in Week 7. The key matchup here, in my opinion, is Goff & Mays vs. Flores. Against the best coach in football, it’s a fair handicap match. Mays got a full load of snaps, hopefully knocked off some of the rust in the process, and is up to the challenge of sorting through the eye candy Flores puts in front of him. 4) Give us one player on each side of the ball for the Lions that fans of the Vikings might not be familiar with that you think will be a big contributor to any success that the Lions are going to have on Sunday. Detroit’s offense is full of household names, so it’s a little more difficult to give you an under-the-radar sort of player who’s expected to be a big contributor on that side of the ball. Here’s the name of a player who will certainly play some snaps on offense as the team’s RB2 and serve as a four-core special teamer: Sione Vaki. He comes on in a lot of third down situations as a pass blocker, but he is liable to get a touch or two just to keep the defenses honest and not completely keying in on what Detroit’s called. For the defensive side of the ball, the aforementioned Keith Abney II has been intriguing over the past couple of weeks. His safety play has been mostly sound, he’s a willing tackler in run defense, and…

title: Week 8 Preview: Begin the Gauntlet
summary: The Minnesota Vikings head to Ford Field this week for a pivotal NFC North matchup against the 4-2 Detroit Lions. A win could put the Vikings in an early stranglehold on the NFL’s best division, especially since they’d get two of their three division wins on the road. A loss would give skeptics more fodder […]
full_text: The Minnesota Vikings head to Ford Field this week for a pivotal NFC North matchup against the 4-2 Detroit Lions. A win could put the Vikings in an early stranglehold on the NFL’s best division, especially since they’d get two of their three division wins on the road. A loss would give skeptics more fodder to call the Vikings “frauds” for another week. They’d also be buoyed by the fact that the Vikings’ next three opponents have a combined 15-5 record. Yeah, this is a big one. VIKINGS ON OFFENSE I vented about this earlier this week, so there is no need to rehash the grievances. For the fourth straight week, the Vikings offense will face another statistically awful defense – albeit one that is getting healthier. Safety Brian Branch returned last week against the Packers, and Kerby Joseph’s 21-day practice window after returning from the PUP list has apparently opened, too. He may still be a week or two away from game action, however. Regardless, this Lions defense is anything but good. They are dead last (32nd) in total yards allowed per game, last in passing yards allowed, and 26th in points allowed per game. They’re also no better than 25th in red zone conversion allowed, success rate allowed, and EPA per play. If there are bright spots, they’re a respectable 12th in rushing yards allowed and have gotten to the quarterback as often as the Vikings this season, with 21 sacks. That surprised me, Aidan Hutchinson, or not. What’s frustrating is that there is clear merit to the argument that the Vikings’ offense is “close.” Big plays in the passing game have been missed, either by missing downfield shots or by failing to finish them. And yes, some of it has to do with Kevin O’Connell’s deliberate transition to a more run-oriented, time-of-possession attack in 2026. Asked to explain Justin Jefferson's low production, Kevin O'Connell notes several reasons but starts with: "I think in the past we're throwing the ball a thousand times." Indeed, the Vikings rank: No. 4 in designed run % (43.3) No. 31 in dropbacks (198) — Kevin Seifert (@SeifertESPN) October 28, 2026 But none of that matters. The official ledger is what it is, and it’s putrid. There couldn't be two more different teams in the NFL 😭 MIN Vikings: 6-0 | 31st in Total TDs LA Chargers: 0-6 | 32nd in Total TDs pic.twitter.com/mKQJa1e6FM — DraftKings Sports (@DKSports) October 28, 2026 And here’s one more Warren Sharp post to drive the point home: Vikings in the red zone: #32 in % of drives reaching the red zone (21.5%) #32 in % of drives reaching goal-to-go (7.7%) #32 in red zone EPA per play (-0.33) #30 in red zone scoring rate (78.6%) — Warren Sharp (@SharpFootball) October 28, 2026 It’s got eerie vibes, like a reversal of what we went through with the defense in 2022. Sure, things were ugly, but give it time. Look at our record! Once the defense figures it out, it’ll all be fine. Yeah, sure. Last time I checked, the goal is to win a Super Bowl, not make the playoffs and bow out 6-3 to the Seahawks, 49ers, or Rams in the wild-card or divisional round. And right now, as the calendar turns to November, that’s exactly what we’re looking at. The Vikings need to wake up and finally put 30+ points on the board against someone. Will they do it? As I noted in my last write-up, I’m officially in the “I’ll believe it when I see it” mindset. I’m done predicting a turnaround and looking like a fool in these weekly previews. To quote Michael Scott: “Fool me once, strike one. But fool me twice…strike three.” So we’re in a holding pattern. We’re facing another terrible defense. The weather won’t be a factor, and early in the week, the offense looks nearly fully healthy again. We’ll see. Hopefully, the one week I don’t predict it will happen is the one when it actually does. VIKINGS ON DEFENSE As usual, this is the main event. Early on, Brian Flores struggled against a Ben Johnson-led Lions offense. The Vikings were 0-4 in those games, with the Lions never scoring fewer than 30 points and averaging 404 yards per game. Once they separated, he got the better of both the Lions’ offense and Ben Johnson in Chicago. Last year in Detroit, Flores’s strategy clearly focused on stopping Jahmyr Gibbs and David Montgomery first. It worked. The Lions managed only 65 yards on 20 carries (3.25 per carry). Jared Goff threw for 284 yards and two TDs, but he was under duress all day and was sacked five times for 44 yards in the wrong direction. The Lions were 5-for-17 on third downs. Flores mixed up the pressures and kept Goff off rhythm all game. Then, at U.S. Bank Stadium in Week 17, the Lions were playing for their season, and Flores unveiled his masterpiece before a nationwide audience. That says something, given how this season has gone so far. With no help on offense, the Vikings’ defense dominated a game unlike any I can remember. Neither Gibbs nor Montgomery managed more than 2.5 yards per carry. Goff was perplexed and pummeled. He was sacked five times and threw two INTs. Three fumbles accompanied this. Overall, Flores’ unit forced six turnovers, and the Lions didn’t make the playoffs. Too bad. Just as I conceded earlier this week that I should at least listen to the national media’s talking-head skepticism this time, the consensus view I’ve seen is that the Lions will expose the Vikings in this one. That would be fine if the previous two games I just detailed hadn’t happened. The narrative in this series has clearly shifted. As bad as the Vikings’ offense has been, I’m fairly sure they’ll surpass the 161 total yards (51 passing/65 yards on one Jordan Addison scoring run alone) we saw in Week 17. Listen, the Lions’ offense is unquestionably dangerous, if not as good as it was under Ben Johnson. They’re top five in points per game (30.7), yards per game (397.3), passing yards per game (282.3), yards per play (6.0), success rate, pass EPA per play, and red zone TD rate. They’re really good. If anyone can drop 21+ on our D and force our offense to look at least mediocre to win, it’s them. But I can’t shake what happened in that Week 17 game last year, and this Vikings defense is even better now. Which leads me to… PREDICTION If the Vikings lose this one, cries of “fraud” and predictions that 6-0 will turn into 6-4 before Thanksgiving will be everywhere. KOC and the offense have to be pissed off and fed up with the criticism and negative vibes. They’d better be. The desire to drop 30+ points has to be overwhelming. But being angry and wanting to prove the haters wrong is one thing. Actually doing it is another. As much as I want it to happen and as much as the fanbase needs it to, I’m not budging from my position: “I’ll believe it when I see it.” That’s the bad news. The good news is that defense and special teams matter, too. And that’s what I believe will be the difference in this one. The offense does enough, aided by advantageous field position the D/ST gifted. Will the Thrill (who else?) wins it as the clock expires. Minnesota Vikings: 17 Detroit Lions: 16

Injury designation definitions: Probable = the league defines a Probable injury designation as a 75% or greater chance of playing. Historically, 95% of players designated probable are active and played on game day. Questionable = the league defines a Questionable injury designation as being ‘uncertain’ of whether the player will play or not. This replaces the former definition of having a 50% chance of playing. Historically, 70-75% of players with a Questionable injury designation were active and played on game day. Doubtful = The league defines a Doubtful injury designation to mean the player is unlikely to participate in the game. In practical terms, teams use the designation when a player has less than a 50% chance to suit up, and active game appearances from this designation remain rare. Players with this designation are not active on game day and league rules prohibit them from playing. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images I am bewildered as to why so many people (writers, bloggers, podcasters, fans, etc) are down on the Vikings mainly because the offense is failing to score enough points for their liking. I contend that the Vikings are actually doing an excellent job running their offense especially considering the injuries they have had to navigate whilst trying to incorporate Kyler Murray into the offense. They are not turning it over and they have one of the top time of possessions in the NFL thus far. This is allowing their defense to stay well rested and wreak havoc. But they get not credit for any of that. Here are some numbers for time of possession and rushing yards per game … Team | TOP | TOP Rank | Rush Yds/G | Rush Rank | Past SOS | REM SOS | Games Played Chicago Bears | 35:30 | #1 | 154.29 | #1 | #31 | #21 | 7 Minnesota Vikings | 32:43 | #2 | 119.33 | #12 | #24 | #26 | 6 New York Giants | 32:32 | #3 | 116.71 | #15 | #30 | #31 | 7 Arizona Cardinals | 32:15 | #4 | 96.00 | #23 | #6 | #5 | 7 Indianapolis Colts | 31:59 | #5 | 117.57 | #14 | #19 | #16 | 7 Tampa Bay Buccaneers | 31:55 | #6 | 146.43 | #3 | #10 | #8 | 7 Jacksonville Jaguars | 31:29 | #7 | 112.83 | #18 | #13 | #27 | 6 Seattle Seahawks | 31:21 | #8 | 113.71 | #17 | #12 | #2 | 7 (Note: TOP is Time Of Possession; for SOS ranks, 1 is the hardest and 32 is the easiest.) Also, the Vikings defense ranks #1 in the NFL for the opponent’s average starting field position. Opposing offenses are forced to start their drives at an average of their own 25.3-yard line, This is helped by the dudes that put their foot on the ball. Through 6 games, the Vikings have punted 27 total times, pinning their opponents inside the 20-yard line on 10 of those opportunities (37.04% of their punts). This does not take away from the offense prioritizing clock management and not turning the ball over in their own territory. … seems to me that KOC is actually doing an outstanding job keeping things afloat while dealing with the injuries. The defense is fantastic but they also are getting helped by the offense keeping the ball longer and not giving up short fields too often. Now some might argue that other teams have had to deal with injury too. Not like the Vikings though. Minnesota Vikings Kyler Murray QB — left early in Week 1; missed Week 2. Jordan Mason RB — injured his thumb in Week 1; missed Weeks 2, 3, 4 and 5 Christian Darrisaw LT — left Week 4 with a concussion; missed Week 5. T.J. Hockenson TE — left Week 5 after three snaps with a concussion; missed the next game, with the Week 6 bye in between. Justin Jefferson WR — left Week 3 with an ankle injury; missed Week 4. Jordan Addison WR — missed Week 5 with a hamstring injury. Jauan Jennings WR — missed Week 2. Donovan Jackson LG — suffered a season-ending knee injury in Week 4. The only other team to come close has been the 0-6 Chargers Los Angeles Chargers David Njoku TE — reported absences in Weeks 3–7; exact game-by-game status needs verification. Kayode Awosika LG — reported absences in Weeks 3 and 5–7. Joe Alt RT — reported absences in Weeks 4–5. Tyler Biadasz C — reported absences in Weeks 4–5. Rashawn Slater LT — reported absences in Weeks 5–6. Ladd McConkey WR — left Week 1 early; reported out in Week 6. Tre Harris WR — left Week 5 early; reported out in Weeks 6–7. Omarion Hampton RB — reported out in Week 3. For me, when you take all of this into context, the fact that the team is undefeated is outstanding work. I realize that the wailing and gnashing of teeth will continue on in regards to the JJ McCarthy trade. I do not think it will ever die down this season and probably not for at least one or more future seasons. If he stayed, the odds of him playing this year were low. He would have had to surpass Wentz as the backup? If he did not play then what would his trade value have been in the 2027 offseason? Should they have gotten more than a 5th? Well yeah. Why not? But from what team? What team would have traded more for him now? It’s easy to say but harder to identify the team willing to give up more knowing that he was injured often (including this 2026 preseason) and had fallen to third string. The best thing is that JJ McCarthy now has a chance to play and try to put his game on tape so that he is able to secure a future contract. I’m OK with the return but always want more in trades. What will the Vikings do in 2027? Well, if not Murray, then they could try for Mac Jones. Deshaun Watson is likely going to be released due to his contract and he is doing well this year. Daniel Jones could get released too. That is possibly four options there. Could Lamar Jackson be on the trade block? That might be the dream scenario. Overall, I think the team is headed in the right direction. I think they will have a decent QB for next season and right now my money is on Murray returning. I would not mind that if he plays a little better the rest of the way. A short 2 yr deal plus maybe bring in Anthony Richardson to back him up. Now you know why I am not GM eh? News Alert The Bears traded two first round picks for Jeffrey Simmons! Wow! I love it! Looks like Jonathan Taylor is not going anywhere either. According to Shefter, the Colts do not “inherently” want to trade Taylor Schefter: Colts owner doesn't want to trade Taylor Would you trade a 2027 2nd, 2027 5th, and a 2028 3rd for Taylor? I would without hesitation. Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason are both free agents and there are no good backs as free agents next year either. The team will likely have to spend a first or second to get a decent back in the draft. I’d rather have Taylor if possible. If the Vikings do trade for him before the game this week they would owe him about 5.3M in salary for the rest of the season.. If they wait until after this game and before the next game (makes the most sense now) then they would owe him 4.8M in salary for the rest of the season. summary: With the NFL trade deadline coming up on Nov. 10, the rumor mill is starting to work overtime. According to a report by Albert Breer of Sports Illustrated, the veteran defender “could be had” via trade in […]
full_text: With the NFL trade deadline coming up on Nov. 10, the rumor mill is starting to work overtime. And one member of the New England Patriots is among the names recently mentioned: defensive tackle Christian Barmore. According to a report by Albert Breer of Sports Illustrated, the veteran defender “could be had” via trade in the coming two weeks: The Patriots are deep in the AFC race, but veteran DT Christian Barmore could be had, having played only 41.9% of the team’s defensive snaps, falling behind Milton Williams and Cory Durden in the team’s rotation. As noted in the excerpt, Barmore has been on the field for 41.9% of the Patriots’ defensive snaps this season — 13th most on the team overall and third among defensive tackles behind the aforementioned Milton Williams and Cory Durden. In those snaps, he has registered six tackles, three sacks and a forced fumble. His 12 combined quarterback pressures are ranked second among New England’s interior linemen behind only Williams’ 14. Whether or not that production is living up to his $17.1 million salary cap number is up for debate, however. Fact is that New England, currently ranked near the bottom in available cap space, could create significant savings by moving on from the 27-year-old: depending on the timing of a hypothetical trade, as much as $8 million could come off the Patriots’ books this year, plus almost $41 million the next two seasons. Whether that is enough for the team to put Barmore on the trade market will be seen — something that also is true for potential compensation. The Patriots getting the same haul the Titans received for fellow DT Jeffery Simmons, who was traded to Chicago for a package involving two first-round draft picks, is doubtful. The Patriots will travel to Miami this weekend to play the Dolphins.

full_text: After enjoying a weekend off, the New England Patriots are back in action this Sunday. Their opponent coming out of the mini-bye is a familiar one, at least on paper: the Miami Dolphins. However, these are not the same Dolphins that lost both of their games to the Patriots in 2025. Led by new head coach Jeff Hafley, they have overhauled significant portions of their roster and staff. Are they better off as a result? So far, the record doesn’t say so. That said, unlike the Patriots, the Dolphins are entering Week 8 off a victory — their first of the season. Still, according to FanDuel Sportsbook , the Patriots are seen as seven-point favorites entering the game. Will they live up to that status? Or will the Dolphins manage to defend their home turf? Let’s find out what Pats Pulpit’s staff and community think. Patriots vs. Dolphins score predictions Bernd Buchmasser: The Dolphins are not as bad as their 1-5 record would suggest, but they still have some shortcomings across the board and are simply a less talented team than their opponent this week. Even a shorthanded Patriots team playing on the road should therefore be able to come away victoriously, especially after 10 days of rest. title: Patriots vs. Dolphins weather forecast for NFL Week 8
summary: The last time the New England Patriots traveled to Florida, they were soundly beaten 35-6 by the Jacksonville Jaguars. One of the contributing factors to that loss appeared to be the team struggling with the heat and humidity. At least one of the two might not have that big an impact come Sunday’s game against […]
full_text: The last time the New England Patriots traveled to Florida, they were soundly beaten 35-6 by the Jacksonville Jaguars. One of the contributing factors to that loss appeared to be the team struggling with the heat and humidity. At least one of the two might not have that big an impact come Sunday’s game against the Miami Dolphins. According to NFL Weather , temperatures at Hard Rock Stadium will not exceed 78°F during the Week 8 contest between the two division rivals. The National Weather Service , meanwhile, projects highs near 82°F for the day. What will differentiate that game from the Jaguars one, however, is the precipitation. Whereas that Week 3 contest was played in sunny conditions, this one won’t: the chance of rain has been calculated at 80% with showers and thunderstorms an option. In addition, wind gusts of up to 26 mph are projected for the area (although in-stadium conditions may vary). All in all, however, the weather could have an impact on the contest — as could the Patriots’ conditioning. “We have to be conditioned,” said head coach Mike Vrabel this week. “The better that we play, the more we possess the ball, the fresher we’ll stay defensively. Hopefully we get the receivers into a rotation. The backs, we rotate. I don’t think that the offensive linemen will necessarily rotate. We may play a couple guys based on who’s available. That remains to be seen. The edge guys, we rotate. We try to rotate along the defensive line. We like to have our best players available to help us win.” Kickoff between the Patriots and Dolphins on Sunday is scheduled for 4:25 p.m. ET.

full_text: After a mini-bye following Thursday Night Football, the New England Patriots are ready to get back on the field. That will take place in Miami with a divisional matchup against the Miami Dolphins. But first, let’s get into this week’s edition of the #PostPulpit Mailbag. What moves do you expect before the trade deadline. I know we did a lot for receiver group in the offseason but do you see adding another body considering WR1 and WR2 aren’t really panning out as expected? – sumeetw I’m not expecting much from the Patriots at the trade deadline. They’ve invested heavily in both wide receiver and offensive guard from a financial and draft-capital standpoint, so it would be tough to see another significant investment there — like Josh Downs or previously being in the Quenton Nelson market. They should also get healthier with Alijah Vera-Tucker, Mack Hollins and Romeo Doubs all on injured reserve, while the players filling in for them have largely held things together. If the Patriots do make a move, I’d expect a fringe or depth addition in exchange for late-round draft capital. Perhaps they look to add another run-stuffing defensive tackle, a blocking tight end or more depth on the defense. Hey Brian. They’re not sexy names, but what are your thoughts on trading for Grover Stewart or Dalvin Tomlinson? After moving on from Tonga in the offseason, no one has really stepped up to fill his void on the roster. Durden has been underwhelming in my opinion. I’m not expecting either guy to be Tonga, but they could use a solid experienced pro to anchor the middle on early downs. – Pat in Agawam A run-stuffing nose tackle would be on our list of targets due to some inconsistent play from the current group, led by Cory Durden who might be at his best in the rotational role he held last season. Players like Stewart or Tomlinson fit that mold and both make sense as targets as neither would require a significant investment in terms of draft capital or money. Among the backup OL guys that have been in the mix, which have actually performed the best? Lomu is pretty obvious, but not a true backup. Have any of the others done well enough to be called a pleasant surprise or to be in line as backups again next year? – ed.liebfried None have been perfect, as expected, but everyone has shown intriguing flashes and helped hold things together. We’ve written plenty about Lomu, but Ben Brown did not allow a quarterback hit in any of his three starts, while Matt Pryor’s size allows him to drop anchor and move bodies along the interior. Walter Rouse has also shown intriguing traits at left guard, including some impressive moments in 1-on-1 pass protection. His awareness against stunts will need to continue to improve, but the 25-year-old, who is relatively new to the position, could develop into a reliable top backup or spot starter. Would it be crazy to grab a free agent coverage linebacker for a playoff run? Matt Milano? Bobby Okereke? Your Ad Here? Maybe if we only picked them up for half a season we could afford someone good and “well rested.” It doesn’t necessarily have to be another coverage linebacker, but I would be in favor of looking for a playable third linebacker that can allow New England to play more base defense. New England is bottom 10 in success rate against heavy personnel grouping due to Marcus Jones’ size or inconsistent play from the third safety in big nickel. Finding another linebacker to play true base defense could be an answer to slowing those groups down. With only 5-6 designated-to-return spots, it’s getting tougher to choose who comes back. If we think their cap number is a good proxy for value during a playoff run, it would be: -AVT -Mike Onwenu -Romeo Doubs -Reggie Gilliam -Mack Hollins -Player to be named later And I guess Harold Landry III is a freebie? How would you allocate the spots? – WannaBe Pats GM The Patriots currently have six return designations remaining, having used two on A.J. Brown and Marcus Bryant. They would receive two additional designations if they make the playoffs. Brenden Schooler does not count toward the total, and neither would Harold Landry if he returns. Among the players currently on injured reserve, Alijah Vera-Tucker, Mack Hollins and Romeo Doubs seem like clear-cut locks to return when healthy. Mike Onwenu would join that group, though his timeline likely puts his return in the playoffs. New England would also likely want to bring back Gilliam, but his availability remains uncertain after he was hampered by a knee injury throughout the season. That would leave three or four return designations for the remainder of the regular season, with no other players currently on injured reserve — including Greg Van Roten, Dell Pettus and Khalil Jacobs — appearing to be immediate priorities. That’s all for this week’s #PostPulpit mailbag. If you have questions you’d liked to be answered next week, submit them online in our weekly submission post on the Feed. Make sure to follow @iambrianhines and @PatsPulpit as well.

title: Patriots coaches not ringing alarm bells over A.J. Brown
summary: A.J. Brown’s career with the New England Patriots is off to an underwhelming start. Despite him missing four weeks due to a high ankle sprain, averaging only three catches per game, and being a no-show at practice on Thursday, however, his coaches are not willing to sound the alarm. Quite the opposite is the case. […]
full_text: A.J. Brown’s career with the New England Patriots is off to an underwhelming start. Despite him missing four weeks due to a high ankle sprain, averaging only three catches per game, and being a no-show at practice on Thursday, however, his coaches are not willing to sound the alarm. Quite the opposite is the case. The Patriots remain high on the 29-year-old. “It’s been a small sample size for A.J,” said wide receivers coach Todd Downing on Thursday. “I think there’s been a lot made about a couple of weeks. My hope, and his hope, and everybody’s hope is that he gets a little bit of traction. I’m not worried about where A.J. is at at all. Certainly haven’t had the results that we had hoped for, but that doesn’t mean that they aren’t right around the corner.” Brown joined the Patriots via trade with the Eagles this offseason, and showed some promise early in his tenure with the team. However, his regular season debut in Seattle was cut short when he sprained his ankle in the early third quarter. New England subsequently sent him to injured reserve, with his highly-anticipated return to the field happening in Week 7 against the Jets. That game, however, was a struggle. There was some improvement four days later against the Bears, but the numbers still have not looked the part. Besides catching just six passes on 14 targets for 53 combined yards in his two games back, Brown’s knee injury has now reportedly also “flared up.” After practicing in a limited capacity on Wednesday, he did not take part in Thursday’s session. This puts his outlook for Sunday’s game against the Dolphins in question. Long-term, however, the Patriots remain confident in his potential and ability to contribute. “He’s played eight quarters in almost two months and had four practices. I’m certainly in the mode of, ‘This is a process of building into our best football,’” offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels said. “We’ve seen that with pretty much every player that’s come here starting last year and then obviously we’ve seen it this year with different guys. “I think there are things that we can work and do better, and certainly his health is going to be a big part of that. When they tell us we can do A, B and C, we’ll do A, B and C. And if there’s some element of a thing that we will need to wait on, then we’ll do it. Love his attitude and his approach. He’s been here working his tail off to put himself in a great position to help our team, and I know he’s going to do that.”
