title: Should the Steelers be buyers at the trade deadline?
summary: The NFL trade deadline this year falls on Nov. 10 at 4 p.m. EST. The league has already seen a handful of big-name players moved, with All-Pros such as Quenton Nelson, Jeffrey Simmons, and DeForest Buckner among the headliners. While we know there is a certain segment of the Behind the Steel Curtain readership who […]
full_text: Photo by Rich Storry/Getty Images | Getty Images The NFL trade deadline this year falls on Nov. 10 at 4 p.m. EST. The league has already seen a handful of big-name players moved, with All-Pros such as Quenton Nelson, Jeffrey Simmons, and DeForest Buckner among the headliners. While we know there is a certain segment of the Behind the Steel Curtain readership who will roll their eyes and voice their displeasure in the comment section about the topic, it would be malpractice if we didn’t have an introspective conversation about the trade deadline now that we’ve reached that crucial period of the NFL calendar. Additionally, we hope those previously mentioned commenters will appreciate that we, writers of the Read & React column, are, in our opinion, more measured in our trade-season analysis. You won’t find fantastical trade scenarios and over-the-top pleas for the Pittsburgh front office to acquire our favorite fantasy football stars. Instead, we’ll examine if a trade makes philosophical sense for the Steelers in this phase of their roster cycle, and then discuss players whose names are already being connected to the Steelers at positions of interest. Should the Steelers make a trade? RB: I’ve always been a believer in the “never say never” philosophy when it comes to making trades — and I believe that Omar Khan is too, given that the Steelers are seemingly always highlighted in reports about teams calling around the league to check on player availability. But once again this year, while the Steelers’ record is too good to be a seller on the trade market, the roster isn’t Super Bowl-ready enough to be much of a buyer, either. And in 2026, I’d say that argument is stronger than ever given that Pittsburgh’s roster has proven surprisingly deep — there’s a good foundation for future seasons here, and trading away future capital to fill some holes this year makes even less sense than usual. Where the Steelers do have a legitimate need at midseason — defensive back and wide receiver — I’m just not sure if there’s an good deal out there for the team. At cornerback, Alontae Taylor comes with a monster cap hit while Charvarius Ward and Donte Jackson are both 30 and likely one-year rentals. Tariq Woolen might be the most interesting name given he’s 27 and could still develop into a quality starter, but he would probably cost more than expected in terms of draft picks; he’s also had a streaky season, to put it kindly, with the Eagles so far after wearing out his welcome in Seattle. Meanwhile, at wide receiver, Marvin Harrison Jr. going to the Texans for a 2027 second-round pick earlier this season showed exactly what the trade market will be for underperforming but talented receivers — namely the Jaguars’ Brian Thomas Jr. Ladd McConkey would be a great get as he could go on to be a long-term piece for the Steelers, but he would cost a lot in terms of draft compensation if he’s even available in the first place. Josh Downs is probably the most realistic and interesting trade target I’ve heard floated for the Steelers this season, but an Adam Schefter report says the Colts want a third-round pick in return . If and when Downs gets traded, it will likely be for less, but the fact that’s even the initial price tag is steep for a player who might be a one-year rental himself and has proven to be a very good but limited role player through the first three-and-a-half seasons of his career thus far. Frankly, I just don’t think any of these players greatly increase the Steelers’ championship odds this year. And most wouldn’t raise the odds for next year either, especially considering the draft capital that would be required to add them to the roster. Pittsburgh has largely made the most of its draft picks as of late as well, with its 10-man class in 2026 already looking like it has revitalized roster depth with names such as Germie Bernard, Robert Spears-Jennings and Gabriel Rubio settling into contributor roles early in their careers. If the Steelers can land their quarterback of the future in the next few years (big if, I know, but a necessary one) and keep a similar hit rate on drafts, this roster could be on a Super Bowl trajectory sooner than expected. So why try to jump the gun with another trade? Especially when the Steelers’ deadline acquisitions as of late have been the largely uninspiring list of Kyle Dugger, Mike Williams and Preston Smith. Every trade is different, but generally, the players who go for a Day 3 pick are cheap for a reason. Depending on how long-term Michael Pittman Jr. and Roman Wilson’s injuries are, and how confident the Steelers are that Jamel Dean will be healthy for the majority of the remaining season, I would not be shocked in the least if Khan, who has proven himself to be a highly aggressive GM, makes a move. But unless that trade will be for a player the Steelers are confident will be a better long-term investment than the resulting lost draft pick would be — keep the value of a rookie contract in mind as well — I don’t think it’s worth pursuing. Good players are just too expensive, and the Steelers aren’t a trade away from contending in the first place. If the deal is good enough, of course Khan should inquire, but the current landscape does not look like an ideal one for a team like the Steelers to be wheeling and dealing ahead of the deadline. That said, if Pittsburgh flips a sixth- or seventh-round pick for a band-aid roster solution this week, I won’t be losing any sleep. RP: Ryland did a good job setting the table for me on this discussion. If you’ve been paying attention to this website’s comment sections, or following the social media accounts of BTSC writers, you’ve likely seen my take. I’ve been staunch in my opinion about this since trade chatter first started in training camp: the Steelers should not trade away 2027 picks or 2028 draft picks to “make a run” this season. Criticize my fandom if you must, but I’ve consistently said I don’t believe the 2027 Steelers are legitimate contenders. Before the season, I predicted they would make the playoffs, but much like recent seasons, I see them as a team that could potentially get out of Wild Card weekend, but I’m dubious about their prospects to advance much further. As such, I’ve been watching this season with the longer view in mind. The Steelers entered the season with 11 rookies making the roster, and 29 players who are 26 years old or younger have appeared on the active roster this season. That’s a significant amount of youth on the roster, and the organization should be trying to develop as much of that talent as possible. That means getting those young players on the field and is argument number one for why I don’t think the team should be buyers, or at least aggressive ones, at the deadline. The three positions the Steelers have most been linked to in trade rumors this season — wide receiver, cornerback, and safety — are also positions where Steelers’ rookies have been asked to step into playing time already this season. Among them, receiver Germie Bernard has most cemented his role on the team with 291 snaps played this season. While trading for a complementary receiver might be of interest to the team in the short term, I wouldn’t be in favor of trading for a player who could significantly eat into his snap share with a mid-season acquisition. Safety Robert Spears-Jennings (150 snaps) and cornerback Daylen Everrette (168 snaps) were each asked to step up early this season as well. Spears-Jennings was a pleasant surprise in the absence of DeShon Elliott, but with Elliott’s return last week, the rookie’s 47% snap rate was his lowest in four weeks. Will Spears-Jenning’s role be reduced even further as the veteran continues to ramp up in his return from injury? While that in and of itself isn’t necessarily a negative, I would like to see him continue to earn some playing time. Those are valuable reps that could pay dividends in 2027 when starter Jaquan Brisker is once…

full_text: (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Cleveland Browns edge rusher Jared Verse isn’t backing down from his comments about Cam Heyward and the Pittsburgh Steelers ahead of Sunday’s AFC North matchup. The Cleveland Browns linebacker recently found himself at the center of a war of words with Heyward after describing the Steelers as “dirty.” Heyward responded by making it clear that Verse’s comments had not gone unnoticed. “Those are words that were said and they will be addressed,” Heyward said, according to Around The NFL . I'm not worried about nobody they got on their team. We out there to go dominate. About to make Pittsburgh ours on Sunday." https://t.co/hjGHgaIAdZ — Dan Labbe (@dan_labbe) October 29, 2026 The young pass rusher made it clear that his focus remains on competing and making a statement on the field. “We out there to go dominate,” Verse said. “About to make Pittsburgh ours on Sunday.” The comments add another layer of intensity to a rivalry that already has plenty of history. title: Steelers RB Jaylen Warren isn’t a secret anymore
summary: Jaylen Warren’s arrival into the discussion of top running backs may have surprised some at the national level. For Pittsburgh Steelers fans who have watched him going on five seasons now, the only surprise is that it didn’t happen sooner. Warren has always been an explosive player, even as an undrafted rookie where he totaled […]
full_text: Photo by Jeff Dean/Getty Images) | Getty Images Jaylen Warren’s arrival into the discussion of top running backs may have surprised some at the national level. For Pittsburgh Steelers fans who have watched him going on five seasons now, the only surprise is that it didn’t happen sooner. Warren has always been an explosive player, even as an undrafted rookie where he totaled just under 600 yards from scrimmage on 105 touches. Despite few talking about him on a national level, he topped 1,000 scrimmage yards in his second season, recording 784 rushing yards and 370 receiving yards in 2023. He missed two games in 2024 but was on pace for 998 total yards that season, as well, and continued his ascent in 2025 with 1,291 total yards and eight touchdowns. And while it looked as if the Steelers were still hesitant to go all in on No. 30 as a true, unquestioned featured back – the signing of Rico Dowdle signaled they would run back another 50-50 split backfield – an injury to Dowdle opened up more opportunities for Warren, and he has taken full advantage of those chances. Warren is currently seventh in the NFL in rushing yards (561) and second in the league in yards per carry of all running backs with at least 50 touches (5.5). Additionally, his 294 yards receiving are second among running backs, trailing only Ashton Jeanty. However, he has 10 fewer receptions than Jeanty and is only 18 yards behind him. Warren’s 12.5 yards per reception leads all running backs, nearly two yards ahead of second-place Emanuel Wilson. In terms of scrimmage yards, Warren is fourth in the NFL, only Bijan Robinson, Jaxon Smith-Njigba, and Jahmyr Gibbs. His efficiency has been off the charts, as well, ranking second in total EPA among all running backs with Christian McCaffrey being the only name in front of him, Over the Steelers’ three-game win streak, he ranks third in the NFL in rushing yards, as well as EPA per rush, and his 10 impact plays are the fourth-most in the NFL in that span. Warren’s ascension into stardom has led to the Steelers finding both a groove and an identity on offense. While their passing game is far from the most explosive in the NFL, having a firework like Warren has seen that gap bridged. Pittsburgh’s success rate during their three-game win streak is eighth in the NFL, and they are one of 12 teams with a positive total EPA over that span. Warren is more than just a net positive for Pittsburgh, he’s the heartbeat of their offense. And while Aaron Rodgers will prance into the Hall of Fame, Pittsburgh will go as far as Warren’s legs will take them. Let us know what you think in the comments . title: What kind of Seattle Seahawks fan are you?
summary: (Editor’s note: The following is a guest discussion post by Field Gulls commenter Kasey McKillip) I don’t mean how passionate you are, how many games you attend, or whether you regard a loss as a personal affront requiring several hours of silence. I mean something more revealing: when you encounter a number, which Seattle Seahawk […]
full_text: (Editor’s note: The following is a guest discussion post by Field Gulls commenter Kasey McKillip) I don’t mean how passionate you are, how many games you attend, or whether you regard a loss as a personal affront requiring several hours of silence. I mean something more revealing: when you encounter a number, which Seattle Seahawk appears in your mind? When you see 54, do you immediately think of Bobby Wagner, or does Grant Feasel get a look in? When you see 3, is it Russell Wilson without a moment’s hesitation, or have you already moved on to Nick Emmanwori? Richard Sherman would seem to have 25 pretty well locked up, unless you harbour an inexplicable affection for Robert Blackmon. And 24? Come on. Is there even a discussion? Marshawn Lynch played just 83 regular-season games for Seattle, but longevity has never been the only way to measure a football player. Some people occupy a roster spot. Others occupy a permanent location in your imagination. The same principle applies to 37 and Shaun Alexander, 29 and Earl Thomas, and 31 and Kam Chancellor. These aren’t merely numbers attached to men who played football. They are shorthand for entire periods of your life, complete with victories, disappointments, arguments and the occasional moment when you were convinced the Seahawks were about to ruin your entire weekend. Then there’s 89, which presents a legitimate dilemma. Brian Blades or Doug Baldwin? Both are perfectly defensible answers. You could make a case for either, and the interesting part isn’t necessarily which player you choose. It’s what your choice reveals about the games you watched, the teams you remember and the particular version of the Seahawks that lives inside your head. Number 4 is another curious case. Perhaps you remember Trent Dilfer’s time in Seattle. Perhaps, like me, your mind now goes straight to Michael Dickson, whose punting has somehow made a position most people barely think about into something worth watching. And 16? It will take some getting used to seeing somebody else wear it. Tyler Lockett leaves behind the kind of legacy that makes a jersey number feel less like an item of sporting equipment and more like an inherited family possession. Because that’s what these numbers become. Players are temporary custodians, doing their best to represent a number before eventually passing it along. Every new player adds another chapter, whether that chapter becomes legendary, forgettable or something that only one person in your friendship group remembers. Perhaps 1 takes you back to the seasons when Warren Moon was in Seattle. Maybe 5 conjures Charlie Frye. These aren’t necessarily the names that appear in highlight packages or feature prominently in conversations about the franchise’s greatest players. They’re simply the names your memory has decided to keep. And that, I think, is the beauty of following a football team for years. The longer you watch, the more complicated these associations become. Numbers accumulate histories. Memories overlap. A jersey can connect you to a championship, a terrible season, a favourite player or an afternoon spent watching a game with someone who is no longer around. Some numbers, of course, have been retired altogether: 45 for Kenny Easley, 71 for Walter Jones, 80 for Steve Largent and 96 for Cortez Kennedy. Their achievements have made the numbers inseparable from their names, leaving the Seahawks with no intention of asking someone else to fill those jerseys. Which brings me back to the original question. What kind of Seahawks fan are you? The answer might have very little to do with how loudly you cheer. It might be found in the numbers you recognise, the players you remember and the names that surface before you’ve even had time to think. Join the conversation! full_text: Week 8 of the 2026 NFL season ends with the Seattle Seahawks taking on the Chicago Bears, but it starts with a Thursday Night Football game that could be relevant to the Seahawks in the postseason race. The Carolina Panthers are 3-3 and reeling after a horrific loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Damien Lewis and Jaelan Phillips are out, while Taylor Moton ain’t back for another year after breaking his fibula. Carolina’s offensive line is banged up and they’re down both starting cornerbacks Mike Jackson Sr. and Jaycee Horn. But other than that, the Panthers are in good shape because the NFC South is its usually horrible self. It was a tough loss for the 4-3 Green Bay Packers against the Detroit Lions on Sunday. Questionable officiating, awful kicking woes, and the usual set of dropped passes led to the Packers falling 20-17 to Detroit. They started out 1-2, looked much improved over their three-game winning streak, but in the daunting NFC North they’re playing catch-up given their 1-2 division record. How this game affects the Seattle Seahawks I know you probably don’t care about Wild Card seeding in Week 8, but we’re here to provide information. There’s a really good chance that the NFC South winner will finish with a worse record than the NFC West winner, and the runner-up won’t be in the Wild Card chase. We can almost bank on multiple NFC North teams reaching the playoffs, so the Packers losing would matter to some degree. If the Packers lose, this is what the standings would look like : 1. Minnesota Vikings (6-0) 2. San Francisco 49ers (6-1) 3. New York Giants (4-2-1) 4. Carolina Panthers (4-3) 5. Chicago Bears (5-2) 6. Detroit Lions (4-2) 7. Seattle Seahawks (4-3) 8. title: Mike Macdonald confirms Grey Zabel move to right guard following Quenton Nelson trade
summary: The Seattle Seahawks will have six-time All-Pro and eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson in their lineup when they play the Chicago Bears on Monday night. Of course, that means an incumbent starter will be heading to the bench soon. Mike Macdonald told reporters on Thursday that Nelson, a career left guard, will assume the […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks will have six-time All-Pro and eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson in their lineup when they play the Chicago Bears on Monday night. Of course, that means an incumbent starter will be heading to the bench soon. Mike Macdonald told reporters on Thursday that Nelson, a career left guard, will assume the same position in Seattle. Grey Zabel, who was touted for his positional flexibility coming out of college, will make the switch over to right guard. That leaves Anthony Bradford, who just returned from injury last week against the Kansas City Chiefs, as the odd man out of the lineup moving forward. “It’s not an easy situation,” Coach Macdonald said regarding Bradford’s benching. “I thought Anthony played really good football for us, and he has. He’s earned a significant role on our team—a starting level role. It’s one of those ‘through, not around”‘ type of things with AB that is not easy. “There’s really no way to sugarcoat it—and I think he believes us when we say this about how much we love him. The guys love him in the locker room, he’s a fantastic teammate. We don’t expect him to be jumping [for] joy in this situation because that’s not realistic. He’s going to be a great teammate, he’s going to stay ready, and we know how this league works; you’re a play away from him playing every play again. It’s not an easy situation but he’s a tough cookie and the guys will have his back, as well.” Zabel made three starts at right guard while at North Dakota State back in 2020. He has not played any right guard snaps in the NFL, but he otherwise has started at every position on the offensive line except center. While Bradford is heading for the bench in the midst of a contract year and some of his best football to date when you include the back-end of last season, Seattle’s guard depth has strengthened through the Nelson trade. Should anything happen to Nelson, Zabel could return to LG and Bradford to RG, or if something happens to Zabel then Bradford slots in at RG instead of ( the since waived ) Christian Haynes or rookie Beau Stephens. full_text: Zach Charbonnet was activated off the PUP list ahead of Week 7 and now, more help is on the way for the Seattle Seahawks’ backfield. Rookie first-round pick Jadarian Price has had his three-week practice window to return from injured reserve opened by the Seahawks, the team announced on Thursday. Price initially suffered a chest injury in Seattle’s Week 2 win over the Arizona Cardinals, and then ultimately went on IR with the same injury ahead of its Week 4 win against the L.A. Chargers . Head coach Mike Macdonald told media on Monday that they would open Price’s practice window ahead of Week 8, and now the rookie tailback is officially back practicing and trending toward a return. Prior to his injured reserve stint, Price had rushed for 119 yards on 28 carries across three games, adding four catches for 21 yards through the air. In his absence, Emanuel Wilson has taken on the lead role in the Seahawks’ backfield, rushing for 403 yards on 111 carries, with George Holani adding 108 yards on 36 carries. In a search for any kind of dynamic element in the running game, the team even turned to Velus Jones Jr. in Sunday’s win over the Chiefs, but the receiver-turned-running back was able to muster just eight yards on five carries — despite an 11-yard rush. Jones later left the Chiefs game with an injury . Seattle’s been loosely connected to trade talks surrounding Indianapolis Colts star Jonathan Taylor, but with both Charbonnet and Price nearing returns, it will have a runway to see if it can spark its running game prior to the Nov. 10 trade deadline.

Trade: Titans are trading All Pro DT Jeffery Simmons to the Chicago Bears, per sources. — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) October 29, 2026 In exchange for the 29-year-old Simmons, the Titans are receiving 2027 and 2028 first round picks, as well as a fourth round pick in ’27, while sending a ’28 fifth round pick back to Chicago. Fresh off a career-best 11 sacks in 2025, Simmons and the Titans agreed to a three-year, $105.8 million extension over the summer. In seven games this year, he has totaled four sacks and six tackles for loss on a struggling team. Across 106 games in Tennessee, Simmons posted 46.5 sacks and 72 tackles for loss while making three All-Pro teams and four Pro Bowls. Now, Simmons will join a high-flying Bears team that looks like a bona fide threat in the NFC, provided they can get even average play out of their defense — and the biggest splash of the Ben Johnson era will be a massive boost in that regard. The trade comes just days before Chicago takes on the Seahawks in primetime, and days after the defending Super Bowl champs made a splash of their own. Now, in Quenton Nelson’s debut , he’ll have an immediate chance to prove his value to a contender as he lines up across from one of the league’s best defensive tackles — and a player he knows well from years battling in the AFC South. title: John Lynch on Mike Evans’ Achilles injury: ‘I think the idea is you’ve just got to quiet that thing down’
summary: The San Francisco 49ers are hopeful to get a handful of reinforcements back at practice next week. One of those players expected to return in the near future is Mike Evans, who missed Week 7 with multiple injuries. It didn’t make sense to play Evans on a short week with the bye coming up. According […]
full_text: (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers are hopeful to get a handful of reinforcements back at practice next week. One of those players expected to return in the near future is Mike Evans, who missed Week 7 with multiple injuries. It didn’t make sense to play Evans on a short week with the bye coming up. According to general manager John Lynch, “Mike’s been working tirelessly.” On KNBR, Lynch said, “He’ll continue to do that. He’s on a great plan, and I think the idea is you’ve just got to quiet that thing down. We dealt with that with Christian [McCaffrey] last year — remember, he had that bilateral. We talked about that a lot, and fortunately, with Mike, it’s just on the one side.” Lynch continued, saying, “he’s dealt with it some throughout his career, but it got to a point where it was really inhibiting his ability to play. At that point, you’ve got to take him out and try to quiet the thing down. Making good progress on that. We need to continue, and Mike will be tireless in his efforts to do that.” Lynch wouldn’t commit to saying Evans would be back at practice next week. He did say, “Mike, he’s a pro. Mike’s going to attack that, and it’s hard for Mike to miss. He doesn’t like doing it, but he also understands the big picture: That we need him right, and we’ll make sure that he is before he returns.” The 49ers face two subpar defenses in the Raiders and Vikings in Weeks 9 and 10, before the schedule turns into two to three playoff teams in the Vikings, Seahawks, and Giants. If you need to give Evans another week or two, then so be it. Ideally, it’s only one. You should be able to get by the Raiders without Evans. Dallas’s defense is lousy enough that maybe even the Cowboys, too—although you’ll need to score against that offense. But the Vikings present a unique challenge, and the Seahawks are the Seahawks. We’ll see how patient the 49ers are with Evans, and if he misses any more time at all. They have to be smart and understand Evans was signed to do what he’s been doing all season, but that won’t matter if he’s not on the field come January.

title: Do the 49ers have the resources for another trade deadline splash?
summary: The 49ers have already filled one significant need ahead of the trade deadline, making a move that made perfect sense in reuniting with defensive tackle DeForest Buckner. San Francisco sent a fourth-round pick to the Indianapolis Colts to bring back the player who was selected by the 49ers with the seventh overall pick in the […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - OCTOBER 11: General Manager John Lynch of the San Francisco 49ers gestures after the game against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on October 11, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Alika Jenner/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 49ers have already filled one significant need ahead of the trade deadline, making a move that made perfect sense in reuniting with defensive tackle DeForest Buckner. San Francisco sent a fourth-round pick to the Indianapolis Colts to bring back the player who was selected by the 49ers with the seventh overall pick in the 2016 draft. That is a very reasonable price for a player who has four sacks and who was tied for 10th in pressures among defensive tackles entering Week 8. But it leaves the 49ers with limited capital with which to address their remaining issues as they plot a run at the Super Bowl. In an ideal world, the 49ers would probably like to add another wide receiver and an edge rusher to their 53-man roster before the Nov. 10 trade deadline. However, with only six picks remaining in the 2027 draft , they may not have the resources for another splash trade. The 49ers still hold their first, second and third-round picks next year. They also have their fifth-round pick and a sixth-rounder acquired from the Baltimore Ravens and a seventh-rounder acquired from the Kansas City Chiefs. San Francisco has put a lot of emphasis on getting younger in recent years, and each of their last three drafts have netted them players who have either established themselves as starters or made a significant impact playing in a rotation. As such, the 49ers may be reluctant to use too many of their remaining 2027 selections in another trade, especially as they do not have the luxury of projected compensatory picks on which to fall back. Of course, that does not necessarily prohibit the 49ers from making another move. Veteran edge Khalil Mack has been named as a potential target and, as a 35-year-old edge rusher on a 0-6 team in the final year of his contract, it likely would not take much to prise him from the Los Angeles Chargers. But if the 49ers want to make a more eye-catching move by pursuing a wide receiver like Garrett Wilson or a dominant edge such as Maxx Crosby, it could cost them multiple first-round picks and several more selections in next year’s draft. At 6-1 after a largely impressive effort on both sides of the ball through seven games, the 49ers look to be in a position to push their chips into the middle of the table with an all-in trade. However, they will be well aware of the risk of doing so, and the potential damaging knock-on effects of having limited draft picks if such a move does not work out. By trading for Buckner, the 49ers have once again shown they are willing to do the deals to try to put the team over the top in the hunt that for that elusive sixth Super Bowl title. Yet the Niners also need to think carefully about the future and, given the position a blockbuster trade could put them in come next April, San Francisco’s next swing before the deadline may have to be more conservative than many will want.
author: Nicholas McGee

title: The Niners are not expected to trade for a star receiver, per insider
summary: The San Francisco 49ers started their bye week with a splash, trading for DeForest Buckner to add another veteran to their defensive tackle room. The move wasn’t too costly, as the 49ers sent a 2027 fourth-round pick for the 32-year-old defensive tackle, who is in the final year of his contract. On Thursday, we saw […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 19: Head coach Kyle Shanahan of the San Francisco 49ers leaves the field after a win against the Washington Commanders at Levi's Stadium on October 19, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Lachlan Cunningham/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers started their bye week with a splash, trading for DeForest Buckner to add another veteran to their defensive tackle room. The move wasn’t too costly, as the 49ers sent a 2027 fourth-round pick for the 32-year-old defensive tackle, who is in the final year of his contract. On Thursday, we saw the Chicago Bears make a major move, trading two first-round picks and more for Tennessee Titans star defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, positioning themselves as a top contender in the NFC alongside the 49ers. This deadline could end up being a busy one, with the Super Bowl race feeling quite open overall. The 49ers are at the top of the board, as they’re the current Super Bowl favorites. And they might not be done yet after the Buckner deal, with potential needs at edge rusher, wide receiver, and even cornerback. However, a trade for a star wide receiver doesn’t seem likely, according to NBC Sports Bay Area’s Matt Maiocco. Speaking on KNBR, Maiocco addressed the possibility of the 49ers going after Garrett Wilson or another star receiver following the Bears move for Simmons. “The player that I’ve heard the fans are clamoring for that would be along the lines of a Jeffery Simmons would be maybe on the other side of the ball: wide receiver Garrett Wilson, where you would have to give up a lot because he’s under contract for a while,” Maiocco shared on Thursday. “But he’s also under contract for a while at a salary up around $30 million a year.” Instead of a splash like that, the insider suggested a smaller move like San Francisco’s trade for Keion White last year that allows the 49ers to keep their draft capital and remain balanced. “I think that what the 49ers could do would be something similar to what they did last year in getting Keion White,” Maiocco continued, “where you don’t necessarily know too much about the player, but he’s on a fixed salary for this year and the next, and maybe he’s fallen out of favor or doesn’t fit a new coach’s scheme. “So, I could see where something like that would happen, but with as many high-priced players as the 49ers have on the team now, currently, and who remain under contract to the team for years to come, I don’t see them adding another 30-plus or $25 million player and giving up the first-round draft picks. I think the 49ers value those first-round draft picks.” Earlier in the season, I was against the idea of the 49ers going after a wide receiver on the trade market. After all, following their returns from injury, the 49ers are expected to have Mike Evans, Deebo Samuel, De’Zhaun Stribling, Christian Kirk, Jordan Watkins, and Jacob Cowing as their roster room. Is it an elite room? No. But that group of players could be good enough for the 49ers high-octane offense, with Evans as the clear No. 1. The big question is health, and whether Evans needs a better complementary piece, such as Brian Thomas Jr. It feels like the top priority for the 49ers next is an edge rusher. Perhaps the 49ers go the cheap route there again and look to develop a younger player, but that room definitely feels like an area to add ahead of the deadline.

title: Should the 49ers offer the Jets a Jeffery Simmons deal for Garrett Wilson?
summary: One of the best players at his position signed a three-year, $105.8 million extension this past summer. That player was traded Thursday morning to the Chicago Bears in exchange for a 2027 and 2028 first-round pick. The Titans also sent a fourth-rounder this year, while the Bears sent back a 2028 fifth-rounder. It’s a deal […]
full_text: (Photo by Sarah Stier/Getty Images) | Getty Images One of the best players at his position signed a three-year, $105.8 million extension this past summer. That player was traded Thursday morning to the Chicago Bears in exchange for a 2027 and 2028 first-round pick. The Titans also sent a fourth-rounder this year, while the Bears sent back a 2028 fifth-rounder. It’s a deal you make when Jeffery Simmons just turned 29. The Bears are telling you they believe Simmons will provide more value than the three picks they dealt away over the next three years, at least. Could the San Francisco 49ers pry away Garrett Wilson from the New York Jets? The situation is similar. The Jets are 2-5. Wilson signed a four-year, $130 million contract extension in July 2025. The selling point to the Jets The Jets will incur a dead cap if they trade Wilson. According to Over the Cap, trading Wilson would cost $6.75 million in dead money through 2029 and $4 million in 2030. Jets fans will cite that as a primary reason the Jets won’t part ways with their budding star receiver. There’s the other side of the coin: the cap space you save. You’d save $16.5 million in 2027, and over $29 million during the next two years. This was Wilson last Sunday: A frustrated Garrett Wilson has some words for Geno Smith on the @nyjets sideline as he's been a non-factor with the Jets trailing the winless Dolphins 21-14. Smith appears unmoved. pic.twitter.com/esmJHlbXi7 — Glenn Naughton (@JNRadio_Glenn) October 25, 2026 On Wednesday, Wilson said he didn’t want to be traded, but he does want to win. Offensive coordinator Frank Reich described Wilson’s frustrations as “ a healthy tension ” on Thursday. From a long-term perspective, it seems silly for a team projected to use one of their first-round picks in 2027 on a quarterback to trade away a top-flight receiver like Wilson. The Jets haven’t had any problems moving the ball in their last two games against divisional opponents. Rookie Omar Cooper Jr. has back-to-back 100-yard receiving games. Their other first-rounder, Kenyon Sadiq, isn’t the most dangerous tight end on the roster. That goes to the second-rounder in ’25, Mason Taylor. The Jets already have three first-round picks in the ’27 draft. Adding another would give them the ammunition to at least attempt to replace Wilson. You’re reminding them they can move the ball without Wilson while selling them on the value of buying two first-rounders to replace him. It’ll also open up cap space down the line for a team that’ll already have the third-most next year with over $85 million — and that’s with Wilson’s contract on the books. Why the 49ers should be aggressive buyers Trent Williams is 38. George Kittle is 33. Mike Evans is 33. DeForest Buckner is 32. Christian McCaffrey is 30. You don’t know how much longer Nick Bosa’s body will hold up. We’re a year removed from the ultimate Ironman, Fred Warner, missing double-digit games because of a freak accident. He turns 30 in November. The 49ers brass would be foolish to think this iteration of the 49ers — arguably the best of the decade — will hold up for another 20+ game season after this year. It’s a haughty assumption, especially from a team that was robbed of a Super Bowl appearance after their quarterback sustained a fluke injury in the NFC Championship Game earlier this decade. I’ve been a staunch advocate for the 49ers to avoid trading for a run-of-the-mill receiver. Josh Downs doesn’t make you a Super Bowl contender. Wilson is a needle mover. He surpassed 1,000 yards receiving in his first two seasons with Zach Wilson throwing him the ball. If that isn’t enough of an argument, then I’m not sure what would convince you that he’s the real deal. I could clip together Wilson running out routes where he breaks the cornerbacks’ ankles, releases off the line of scrimmage with the defensive back hopping the opposite direction of Wilson, or him making acrobatic catches down the field. There isn’t a route Wilson can’t run. Wilson becomes the future of the 49ers. Like the Bears — if we’re acting under the guise of the deal being multiple first-rounders — the Niners are banking on Wilson producing more —albeit far more expensive — than their two first-rounders in the next two years would. But you’re paying for that by acquiring Wilson at this contract. You get to skip past the “teach this guy how to play football” phase. There is no learning curve. You’re getting one of the best players at his position with the skill set you’d create in a lab for a Kyle Shanahan offense. The 49ers have fallen on hard luck before signing Evans. Swinging for the fences on Wilson would help the team wash their hands of the Brandon Aiyuk disaster, provide peace of mind without having to hold their breath in the future to see if Ricky Pearsall stays healthy, and take pressure off De’Zhaun Stribling to replace Evans down the line. The 49ers’ first-round draft history under this regime doesn’t come close to Wilson’s caliber. You’re removing the guessing game with a win-now player who also provides stability at a position you’ve whiffed on in recent years. It’s a rare NFL opportunity for a team like the Niners to capitalize on a player entering his prime who is visibly unhappy. It’s a big if, as there are plenty of uncontrollables for the 49ers. Everybody has a price.
author: Kyle Posey

title: Ranking the NFC Contenders with the 49ers: The Bears are all-in
summary: What a few days in the NFL world, specifically the NFC. The San Francisco 49ers welcome back an old friend in DeForest Buckner, Seattle welcomes the NFL’s best guard, and now the Bears send two first-round picks for DT Jeffrey Simmons in a clear “all-in” move. What was once an NFC West arms race has […]
full_text: Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images What a few days in the NFL world, specifically the NFC. The San Francisco 49ers welcome back an old friend in DeForest Buckner , Seattle welcomes the NFL’s best guard , and now the Bears send two first-round picks for DT Jeffrey Simmons in a clear “all-in” move. What was once an NFC West arms race has become an NFC arms race. With the conference pretty wide open, this is the best opportunity for any team that believes they are close. I am going to attempt to rank the NFC contenders at 12:55 PM EST. Let’s hope some other news doesn’t break before this is published. Now, in my humble opinion, there are four NFC contenders. San Francisco, Seattle, Chicago, and Minnesota. I would be remiss if I didn’t include the lone undefeated team in the league. San Francisco 49ers I’m open to criticism for being biased, but I still truly believe in this team as the best in the NFC and the league. Kyle Shanahan is still the coach; the defense has Raheem Morris, and Nick Bosa is returning with Buckner. Chicago’s move today gives me the sense that Khalil Mack is closer than ever to becoming a 49er. Offensively, Mike Evans, Deebo Samuel, and Demarcus Robinson are returning. Additionally, I expect the 49ers to add another receiver to the fold. The caliber of receiver is up in the air. Will the 49ers add a high-floor receiver to bolster their depth, or is a high-end receiver who blows the doors off defenses on the way? One way or another, the health of the returning 49ers and the experience of the core, with a 6-1 start, have the 49ers still in the driver’s seat. Seattle Seahawks You may not like to hear this, 49ers fans, but the margin between the 49ers and Seahawks is closer than you think. I held this opinion before the Nelson trade. Look, don’t let the numbers confuse you; Minnesota is statistically the best defense in the NFL, but Seattle is the real best defense in the NFL. Getting their running game going with the return of Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price will alleviate the need to rely on Sam Darnold. Oh, that JSN guy is pretty good. On any given day, Seattle’s defense can choke off an opposing offense. It is imperative that the 49ers add another playmaker for their potential third meeting in January. Expect Seattle to round into form right in time for a run down the stretch. Monday’s game against Chicago just got a hell of a lot more interesting. Speaking of…. Chicago Bears The cheat code for the Bears is the cheap contract of Caleb Williams. The ascending quarterback allows the Bears to swing big on Simmons. They have receivers, an offensive line, and one of the top play callers and designers in the NFL, Ben Johnson. Simmons is a game wrecker and an opportunistic defense that can create turnovers. The only reason the Bears are third is that they are still a notch below both Seattle and San Francisco defensively. Plus, Seattle and the 49ers have experience winning deep into January. Last season was a good first step for Chicago, and clearly the organization believes that is the beginning of something special. Rightfully so, by the way. I just have more faith in the two NFC West teams come January. Minnesota Vikings You can’t leave the Vikings off this list, but the reason they are fourth on this list is the scuffling offense (what happened, KOC? Thought you were the QB whisperer), and the defense is on a heater against offenses that are less than stellar. Until this offense can produce anything valid, they will remain low on this list. Is the remedy a trade for Jonathan Taylor? It’s better than nothing. I’m also not sure adding Josh Downs will help the passing offense. I mean, if you’re having issues getting a top-three receiver like Justin Jefferson the ball? One small secret about Minnesota’s defense is their explosive play rates. The defense is tenth overall at 6.5%, which is very solid. On the ground, Minnesota has allowed ten-yard runs at a 9.9% rate. That’s 13th in the NFL. The pressure applied by their blitzes and Brian Flores’ excellent defensive mind can’t be discounted. However, those gambles leave them vulnerable to big plays. It’s up to the offense to execute and decipher the pressures coming.
author: Jason Aponte

title: The biggest benefit for the 49ers from the DeForest Buckner trade
summary: The San Francisco 49ers made a splash this week with the trade for Indianapolis Colts defensive tackle DeForest Buckner, six years after the two sides made the same move back in 2020. Buckner, now 32, is still a productive defensive tackle, having 31 tackles, 20 pressures, and four sacks this year. Buckner is three years […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 20: DeForest Buckner #99 of the Indianapolis Colts sacks Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs during the second quarter of an NFL football game on September 20, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers made a splash this week with the trade for Indianapolis Colts defensive tackle DeForest Buckner, six years after the two sides made the same move back in 2020. Buckner, now 32, is still a productive defensive tackle, having 31 tackles, 20 pressures, and four sacks this year. Buckner is three years removed from his last Pro Bowl, but he’s already matched his sack total from a season ago and has been healthy this year, giving the 49ers depth. Immediately, the thought is that the 49ers can pair Buckner and Osa Odighizuwa together, giving San Francisco two quality veteran interior pass rushers. But could this deal actually help both players in a different way? Through seven games, Buckner has the fourth-highest snap count among defensive tackles at 353. Only Jeffery Simmons (435 snaps), Jalen Carter (419 snaps), and Alim McNeill (363 snaps) have played more. Buckner has been on the field for 82 percent of Indianapolis’s defensive snaps, which would be the second-highest share of his career after his rookie season. Who’s fifth on that list? Osa Odighizuwa, who has 346 snaps in seven games. Odighizuwa has played in 74 percent of the 49ers defensive snaps, also the second-highest rate of his career. With a ton of younger players in the rotation, the 49ers have leaned on Odighizuwa a ton to be available this season. He’s still posted 21 pressures, good for 10th among interior defensive linemen. Where this move could really help both players is allowing San Francisco to rotate more, as they now have another body in the defensive tackle room that can soak up a good number of snaps. This isn’t to say that the 49ers should cut Odighizuwa or Buckner’s snaps dramatically, but having them fresh for the playoffs should be the No. 1 priority. With Buckner in the fold, the 49ers now have him, Odighizuwa, Gracen Halton, James Thompson Jr., and Sebastian Valdez as their top current defensive tackles. CJ West could also return at some point, but there was a clear need for a defensive tackle who could take some of the load off Odighizuwa and balance out the snaps more. We also know that the 49ers will kick in some of their edges, such as Mykel Williams or Keion White, on passing downs, spreading out the snaps even more. But San Francisco now has two quality pass rushers on the interior that can soak up snaps and keep each other fresh. The rotation also allows for the continued development of the team’s young defensive tackles and gives the team some much-needed depth up front. Good move all around, and there could be more coming in the front seven.

title: Star defensive tackle goes to NFC contender after 49ers trade for DeForest Buckner
summary: The San Francisco 49ers got the trade deadline kicked off with the defensive line market, trading for Indianapolis Colts defensive tackle DeForest Buckner for a 2027 fourth-round pick. With the trade, the 49ers were reunited with Buckner, 32, whom they traded to Indianapolis back ahead of the 2020 NFL Draft for a first-round pick. In […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - OCTOBER 18: Jeffery Simmons #98 of the Tennessee Titans celebrates after sacking Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts during the fourth quarter of the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on October 18, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers got the trade deadline kicked off with the defensive line market, trading for Indianapolis Colts defensive tackle DeForest Buckner for a 2027 fourth-round pick. With the trade, the 49ers were reunited with Buckner, 32, whom they traded to Indianapolis back ahead of the 2020 NFL Draft for a first-round pick. In the final year of a two-year, $46 million extension he signed in 2024, the fit made a ton of sense, given the 49ers’ hope for extra depth and pass-rush help on the defensive line, as Buckner now joins Osa Odighizuwa as the main pieces on the interior. Now, the 49ers weren’t the only team reportedly interested in Buckner, as the Chicago Bears were also looking for a defensive tackle. And after the 49ers kicked off the market, the Bears made a major splash on Thursday morning. According to The Ringer’s Tom Pelissero, the Bears are trading two first-round picks and a fourth-round pick to the Tennessee Titans for star defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. It marks the second straight year that an elite defensive tackle on a poor team was flipped for significant draft capital after Quinnen Williams was traded from the New York Jets to the Dallas Cowboys last year. The official compensation is a 2027 first-round pick, a 2028 first-round pick, and a 2027 fourth-round pick for Simmons and a 2028 fifth-round pick. Moreover, it bolsters one of the top contenders in the NFC. The Bears were seen as the team with the eighth-best Super Bowl odds heading into Thursday, and that is now sure to change following the Simmons trade news. Simmons, 29, has long been one of the best defensive tackles in the NFL, but there was speculation about whether the Titans would actually move him. So far this year, he has had 24 pressures, 20 tackles, and four sacks, while recording 20 defensive stops, per PFF. If anything, the move reinforces that this trade deadline could be a wild one, with the Super Bowl race feeling quite wide open to a ton of teams this year. After the 49ers trade for Buckner, it doesn’t feel like they’re done yet either, as San Francisco could still use edge rusher help and potentially another wide receiver or cornerback, given their injuries. We’ve now seen three blockbuster trades this week: Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks, Buckner to the 49ers, and Simmons to the Bears.

title: To sell, or not to sell, that is the question.
summary: Welcome to the the midway point of the NFL season. This is the fun time where teams that are good are supposed to go out and add to their roster, while the bad teams have fans and pundits saying they need to start unloading talent to acquire draft picks and begin the preparations for next […]
full_text: TAMPA, FL - AUGUST 22: Tampa Bay Buccaneers General Manager Jason Licht talks along the sidelines before the Preseason game between the Kansas City Chiefs and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on August 22, 2026 at Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Cliff Welch/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Welcome to the the midway point of the NFL season. This is the fun time where teams that are good are supposed to go out and add to their roster, while the bad teams have fans and pundits saying they need to start unloading talent to acquire draft picks and begin the preparations for next season because this season’s hopes and dreams are finished. So which team are the Tampa Bay Buccaneers? Bad? Yes. Out of contention? No. The decision of whether or not to be sellers cant be talked through without mention of the NFC South. Since the departure of Tom Brady, the NFC South has been NFC South-ing at a high level. The division has only had one double-digit victor since 2021 and hasn’t won a postseason game since 2023. This year’s rendition of the South, has Tampa Bay in third place with just two wins after seven games— The difference between the third place Buccaneers and the second place Falcons? This Sunday’s game. Carolina remains out in front, however, Tampa has the current tiebreaker over Carolina and all of ther other division games to go. The ineptitude of the NFC South makes Jason Licht’s decision difficult. It would be sincerely simple for Tampa to throw in the towel at 2-5 if they were in the NFC West, the NFC North, or even the NFC East. Each of those divisions would have the Buccaneers in third or tied for last needing to work all the way to a winning record in order to compete. That is just not necessarily the case in the NFC South— There’s a fairly decent chance a team with a record closer to, perhaps even below, .500 snags the divison crown. The Buccaneers would need quite a turn around down the stretch to finish with a winning season, but seven wins? That feels possible and because those seven wins are a possibility, it may hold Jason Licht back from moving any major pieces at this year’s deadline.

title: How to win, how to lose: Tampa Bay Buccaneers versus Atlanta Falcons week 8 game preview
summary: The 2026 Buccaneers will not die. After starting our 0-4 and being (rightfully) written off. They are less than two games out of first place with a tiebreaker over the NFC South’s top-ranked Carolina Panthers and a matchup against the only other team ahead of them this week in the Atlanta Falcons. “Pressure is a […]
full_text: Oct 22, 2023; Tampa, Florida, USA; Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield (6) runs with the ball against the Atlanta Falcon in the fourth quarter at Raymond James Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Nathan Ray Seebeck-USA TODAY Sports | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con The 2026 Buccaneers will not die. After starting our 0-4 and being (rightfully) written off. They are less than two games out of first place with a tiebreaker over the NFC South’s top-ranked Carolina Panthers and a matchup against the only other team ahead of them this week in the Atlanta Falcons. “Pressure is a privilege.” Billie Jean king How can the Buccaneers win? Pressure Micheal Penix. The Atlanta Falcons are 3-4 on the season, however, they are 3-2 in games where Michael Penix starts. Penix hasn’t been the immediate, no doubt answer the Falcons hoped he would be when they drafted him with the eighth overall pick in the 2024 NFL draft, but he has been a sign of hope at quarterback for the organization, in limited action. Penix has only played in 19 games across three NFL seasons—He sat most of his rookie season and he has missed 12 career games due to injury. The 2026 version of Michael Penix has done a phenomenal job protecting the football, Penix has thrown nine touchdowns and has just one interception so far this season. The Falcons’ QB has been good, not great. The delineation comes from the clear hole that currently exists in his game. The ability to deal with pressure. Michael Penix has simply been a different player when he is under pressure. When facing no pressure, Penix looks like an all-star— +0.62 EPA per dropback, which is a mark that’s good for 2nd best in the entire league. Under the gun, it’s been a different story— Penix has a significnat dip in EPA, checking in at -0.82 per dropback. There is no starter who has posted a lower overall EPA in 2026, than Penix under pressure. Penix has gone 1-16 when pressured this year— He is the only starting passer with a completion rate under 30%. This makes the gameplan clear for Tampa Bay. Pressure Penix and he will struggle, give him time in the pocket and he will test Tampa’s coverage. One of Atlanta’s clear keys to victory, this week and moving forward, will be protection of Michael Penix. Penix has proven to be a completely different plyer when he has a strong pocket to work with versus when navigating breakdowns in protection. This may be tied to his injury history or it may just be a part of his story as a payer. Either way, for Tampa Bay to advance to 3-5, it must be a part the story Sunday. “Progress is impossible without change, and those who cannot change their minds cannot change anything.” George Bernard Shaw How can the Buccaneers lose? Try to duplicate last week’s performance. Last week, the Buccaneers played football like they were the 2009 New York Jets. While it was a fantastic win and quite a game to watch, that style of play is not going to be sustainable back-to-back weeks. The Buccaneers can certainly run the football and lean on their offensive line but the imbalance of 49 runs to 11 passes won’t consistently win in the modern NFL. Baker Mayfield’s thumb will be tested against the Atlanta Falcons. Last week, Tampa was aided by a Carolina turnover frenzy (4) and no caught the Panthers by surprise with their unwavering dedication to the run. This week, the Falcons will have no illusions about what Tampa Bay is doing and what they are trying to be. The Bucs’ offensive line is getting a lot of credit for rounding into shape and becoming what many with a vested interest in the Buccaneers hoped they would be. Even if that is true, a near 50-rush attempt game, for the second consecutive week, is not a viable path to victory. The Falcons rank fourth in the league in rush defense. Jeff Ulbrich’s group only allows an average of 88.9 yards per game. That doesn’t mean the Buccaneers can’t get their running game going this week, but it does mean Baker Mayfield will need to do more than hand the ball off for Tampa to take victory. The Buccaneers should be proud of what they accomplished last week and take that performance’s mentality into this week, as well as the rest of their season, however, they will have demonstrate that they understand mentality does not equal gameplan.

summary: Each week I write a preview post on Fridays. Earlier in the week, I was thinking about the mismatch that the Cincinnati Bengals offense poses for the Tennessee Titans defense. Earlier in the week, I was thinking about the mismatch that the Cincinnati Bengals offense poses for the Tennessee Titans defense. That was when Jeffery Simmons was still on the Titans. Now that Big Jeff has been traded to the Chicago Bears, that mismatch is astronomical. Joe Burrow and the Bengals are 5th in the league in passing and 4th in the league in points scored per game. The Titans are 26th in the league against the pass. With Simmons in the middle of the defense, there was at least some hope that the Titans could create enough pressure to keep Burrow from having a career-type day. How are the Titans going to do that now? They aren’t. The Simmons trade should open up snaps for Femi Oledajo and Keldric Faulk on the defensive lines. They are two young players that the Titans spent high draft picks on in hopes of them being able to disrupt the quarterback. We haven’t seen that from either of those guys to this point. It is time for them to step up. If the Titans are going to have a chance to win this game, they are going to have to be able to keep pace with the Bengals offense. The Bengals pass defense hasn’t been very good allowing 233 yards per game. Cam Ward has probably heard people talking this week about how the Simmons trade means they have given up on him. If he wants to quiet that talk, he needs to come out and have a big day against a pretty soft defense. The Titans opened as 10.5-point underdogs at FanDuel . That number moved to +11.5 when the trade was announced yesterday. I just don’t see a way where they are going to be able to cover, much less win this game. Now, he just hit on the picks he acquired. In the bigger picture for the Titans, this trade tells me that Borgonzi has already decided Cam Ward is not the answer at quarterback. The only reason to trade Simmons is if he thinks the Titans aren’t going to be able to compete before Simmons starts his decline. The only reason he would feel strongly enough about that to actually make the trade is if he had given up hope that Ward is going to turn into a franchise quarterback. To me, Borgonzi made the right call here. Crazier things have happened than Ward being able to turn it around, but we have seen nothing through his first season and a half in the league that would give us hope that he can develop into a franchise quarterback.

full_text: The Colts dealt superstar guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks earlier this week. The Commanders did not make a play for him. Washington general manager Adam Peters was clear about that in his weekly (paid) interview with 106.7-FM The Fan on Friday morning. He addressed the NFL trade deadline and several other topics during the interview, including receiver Antonio Williams, cornerback Amik Robertson and the state of the Commanders coming out of their bye week. Also, Peters revealed that receiver Terry McLaurin is having Friday surgery to repair a torn patellar tendon. Here are the highlights from that interview – the full session can be found below – as Washington steamrolls into a vital Sunday night matchup with the Philadelphia Eagles. On the NFL trade deadline We’re looking at everything. Any position on our team where we can make our team better for the present of the future, we’re always going to look into that. Whether it’s wide receiver of any other position that you can think of, we’re going to look for us to get better. There aren’t a lot of opportunities to do this. There are times where teams are looking to move on from guys you’re interested in and those are opportunities where you can make a move. On Antonio Williams First and foremost, I want to give a shout out to Terry. He’s having surgery today. For all those who do so, please say a prayer for him. He’s a big part of what we’re doing and what we’ve done. I just want to send him some love here today. Moving forward with Antonio, every single day he does something special in practice that shows you what kind of talent he has, what kind of instinct he has as a receiver. The sky’s the limit for him. With Terry going down, that creates more opportunities for others and people will have to step up. We’re still hoping and expecting that Antonio will do that. He’s definitely capable of that. On the Amik Robertson and his guarantee We went out and signed Amik for a reason, because he’s a straight dawg. He’s a very good player. He has the utmost confidence and has an edge and an attitude and impacts a defense. I love that he’s on our team. Listen, that’s the mindset you want. For sure that’s bulletin board material if you do subscribe to that, but I’ve always said that, if you need bulletin board material to get ready for a division game on Sunday night, then – all the material and motivation – that’s kind of a problem, you know? On Chig Okonkwo We’ve high hopes for him. He had a slow start because he got hurt, and now we’re seeing what that’s going to look like within our offense. We really haven’t seen the full extent of what he can do within our offense in terms of catching and running. We’re going to continue to give him those opportunities. With Terry down and other guys that have been down, that gives other guys opportunities in terms of Antonio and Chig – and we think we can get even more from Chig. On Steve Wilks When that opportunity came about, it was a no brainer. It’s something we had talked about and it came into fruition. He had some other obligations with (Appalachian State), where he had some commitments. He wasn’t working in the league this year, so we thought it was a great opportunity. We looked into a number of different possibilities for this role and he was the best fit. … Within the short time he has been here he has aquitted himself well, which I knew he would. He has fit in seamlessly. … Having an extra set of hands is always good and we’re thrilled that he’s here.

They need to limit the self-inflicted mistakes and drive-killers if they want a chance. The bye week was supposed to be about more than rest. Over the last three weeks before the break, Washington committed 33 penalties, 16 on offense, including seven false starts. Getting to 2-4-1 with a divisional road win on Sunday night doesn’t fix the season — but it changes the entire conversation. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE ESPN Ranking the best 2026 NFL rookies: Arvell Reese, Denzel Boston, others in top 10 We polled five NFL analysts and reporters — Matt Bowen, Kalyn Kahler, Jeff Legwold, Jordan Reid and Ben Solak — to form a consensus ranking through Week 7. T-1. Sonny Styles, LB, Washington Commanders Stats: 46 tackles, 1 sack, 1 INT, 1 FF Drafted: No. 7 Styles’ speed is what made him a top-10 pick, and he has put it on full display this season. In Washington’s only win , he went stride for stride with Seattle running back Jadarian Price to break up a deep pass. Later in the third quarter, he caught up with tight end Eric Saubert and stripped the ball at the goal line — though Saubert recovered it for a touchdown. (He also had his only interception in that game.) Styles even made a strong debut, trucking Eagles running back Saquon Barkley on his way to sacking quarterback Jalen Hurts. Styles has 13 tackles in Washington’s past two games, which suggests he’s only improving as his rookie year continues. — Kahler To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Last Man Standig (paywall) Commanders 2027: Who stays, who goes and what the defense still needs Get past Sonny Styles and there are more questions than answers with Washington’s defense next season including decisions on pending free agents Daron Payne and Frankie Luvu, and salary-cap Outlook: The 2026 season might mark the end of the line for Payne in Washington. There’s always the chance a new deal with the 2018 first-round pick gets worked out, but players with options generally aren’t keen on taking a pay cut to stay with the same team. And I don’t see Washington — or any team — matching Payne’s $22.5 million average annual salary. Though his pass-rushing stats haven’t popped as hoped, Payne remains a mountain of a man against the run. That’s why he’ll draw interest if Washington becomes a seller ahead of the trade deadline. If Payne goes, Washington has a massive hole to fill. Kinlaw has been fine. But fine enough to justify a $16.9 million cap charge? The bigger question is what this group looks like without both Kinlaw and Payne. Newton’s status as a former second-round pick probably keeps him around for depth. We haven’t seen enough to project tangible upside. He’ll have roughly half a season to show what he’s got after Washington opened his 21-day practice window, approximately 11 weeks following pectoral surgery. Settle’s $9.7 million cap hit makes him a viable restructure candidate. For more from Ben Standig, click here The Athletic (paywall) The Commanders’ first-year coordinators were both risks. When does the payoff arrive? The struggles of these Commanders don’t completely fall at the feet of new offensive coordinator David Blough and new defensive coordinator Daronte Jones. But with a game against the Philadelphia Eagles that could alter coaching careers coming up Sunday night, both assistants are being examined. All spring and summer, their plans and strategies sounded interesting. In practice? “We would love for it to be perfect right now,” Blough said Thursday. “We know that’s not the case.” “Inconsistent,” Jones said. This was Quinn’s choice and Quinn’s risk. He stripped former defensive coordinator Joe Whitt Jr. of his play-calling duties during the 2025 season and fired him thereafter, eventually hiring veteran defensive assistant Jones away from the Minnesota Vikings to do a job he hadn’t performed at the NFL level. The organization wanted a more collaborative offensive staff that might design a system that could take some of the burden off quarterback Jayden Daniels, so it moved on from offensive coordinator Kliff Kingsbury and elevated Blough, who began the 2025 season as the assistant quarterbacks coach and was not even four years removed from his career as a backup quarterback. If Quinn had hired and empowered first-year coordinators in Year One of his tenure and the team was 1-4-1 and the on-the-job training was difficult but necessary, fine. But he didn’t. He installed them in Year Three, and not only handed them the keys but allowed them to build the cars from the ground up. What you have, then, is a work in progress on both sides of the ball at a time when the Commanders can’t afford to take baby steps. Through six games, Blough’s offense ranks in the bottom half of the league in both yards per play and points per game. Jones’ defense is ranked 22nd in yards per play and 31st — next-to-last — in points allowed per game. That’s some combination of “meh” and “oh no!” with the season — and therefore the future of Quinn and the entire coaching staff — in the balance. full_text: It sure looks like the Commanders are going to play Sunday night’s game without Javon Kinlaw . The defensive tackle missed his second practice of the week while dealing with a knee injury. That’s a big deal, considering his impact on the Commanders interior defensive line to this point. There’s always hope that he can recover in time to play the Eagles, and Charles Omenihu ’s return to practice activity theoretically offers some depth if Kinlaw can’t go. Receiver Stefon Diggs was back at practice , as head coach Dan Quinn previously announced, after some veteran rest and despite hand and hamstring issues. That’s a plus for the Commanders, especially with Terry McLaurin out for the season . Tight end John Bates missed a second day with a shoulder issue. Not having him available on Sunday, if we get that far, is a sneaky big deal considering his role as a blocker in the pass and run games. Receiver Treylon Burks went from limited to a DNP, which is a bad sign for an already banged up pass-catching corps. Also center Nick Allegretti popped up on the injury report with a back issue. title: Tyler’s Take: Grading Commanders GM Adam Peters’ 2024 NFL draft class
summary: Editor’s note: HH analyst Mark Tyler uses input from Commanders analyst Grant Mitchell, who offers quality content you can find on Twitter (@FullCommandShow) and on YouTube (@FullCommandShow) I’ve always said that you can’t grade a draft class for at least two full seasons. full_text: Editor’s note: HH analyst Mark Tyler uses input from Commanders analyst Grant Mitchell, who offers quality content you can find on Twitter ( @FullCommandShow ) and on YouTube ( @FullCommandShow ) I’ve always said that you can’t grade a draft class for at least two full seasons. With Adam Peters’ 2024 draft class , we now have two full seasons and six games to evaluate. With that said, the grading of the 2024 class is now pretty fair game… I saw this tweet from my friend Grant Mitchell from the Full Command Show and it got the old gears a turning… This is a trend on the internet right now, so, Adam Peters draft picks revisited Tell me what’s wrong pic.twitter.com/9iyBRRl2X1 — Grant Mitchell (@FullCommandShow) October 28, 2026 There is a LOT of RED on this 2024 list! I reached out to Grant to get a more detailed take on his colors. Unlike Grant, I cannot yet fairly give my grades for the 2025 or 2026 draft classes, so I kept this article about the 2024 class. Grant’s Color Code : Green : Objectively good draft pick Yellow: Average — leaning slightly in good/bad direction or unproven Red: Bad pick Commanders 2024 Draft Class Jayden Daniels (RD1 – pick 2) Jer’Zhan Newton (RD2- pick 36) Mike Sainristil (RD2 – pick 50) Ben Sinnott (RD2 – pick 53) Brandon Coleman (RD3 – pick 67) Luke McCaffrey (RD3 – pick 100) Jordan Magee (RD5 – pick 139) Dominique Hampton (RD5 – pick 161) Javontae Jean-Baptiste (RD7 – pick 222) I like to color-code using the Scot McCloughan system. This article I wrote in 2022 outlines that color-code (with some of my own added). You all remember the great Scot McCloughan, right? We learned some good thing, and some not so good things, from his tenure in Washington. One thing I took from Scot, that I still follow today, is his color coding system for players (which I have added to). Below is a excerpt from a 2016 interview with Bleacher Report where he describes his team-building mentality and his color scheme: You don’t always need the biggest, fastest, strongest guys. You need football players who understand that it’s a team philosophy and, you know what, we’re fighting together. Blues are like perennial Pro Bowl players. Reds are like really good football players. So, if you’re lucky, you have four or five blues, and hopefully one of those is your quarterback. If you have another 30 who are reds, starters, solid backups, core special teams guys, then you have a chance. That’s how you build your roster. That’s how you build a team. That comes from this and this (points to his head and heart). It’s not about speed guys and the ESPN guy, the prettiest guy running around making plays. It’s a football player. You get enough football players, they’re going to fight together. Taking the McCloughan approach, and adding a few colors of my own, I have color coded our current roster, done intentionally before free agency and the draft, to see where we currently sit per the McCloughan/Tyler way. Tyler’s Take Key Blue – Pro Bowl Player Red – Quality Starter Orange – Average Starter Yellow – Backup Purple – Incomplete/No longer on team Jayden Daniels (RD1 – pick 2) – RED (potential to become BLUE) Jer’Zhan Newton (RD2- pick 36) – YELLOW Mike Sainristil (RD2 – pick 50) – YELLOW Ben Sinnott (RD2 – pick 53) – YELLOW Brandon Coleman (RD3 – pick 67) – YELLOW Luke McCaffrey (RD3 – pick 100) – YELLOW Jordan Magee (RD5 – pick 139) – YELLOW Dominique Hampton (RD5 – pick 161) – PURPLE Javontae Jean-Baptiste (RD7 – pick 222) – YELLOW Out of nine draft picks, six being in the top 100, I have just one RED. Everyone else, with the exception of Dominique Hampton (who was cut) is what I’d call a backup (even though Coleman is currently a starter). Coleman is the one player from 2024 that you can argue could be considered an ORANGE, but even if he was listed as one, that shade would be a VERY LIGHT shade of ORANGE. Mitchell and Tyler’s comparison Grant and I discussed our grading systems a bit and I thought it would be interesting to see where we agreed; and maybe where we differed. Jayden Daniels: Both Grant and I agree that Jayden was a really good pick and one with high expectations. Grant feels he’s there, while I still believe he’s knocking on the doorstep. Jer’Zhan Newton: Both Grant and I agree that Newton was a bad pick and the colors show that. When a player taken with the 36th overall pick can’t even be a quality starter, that pretty much sums it up. Mike Sainristil: Mikey was awful in 2025 and that has carried over to his benching in 2026. Grant and I both agree — he’s not even average. Ben Sinnott: Grant lists him as average, where I have him in my categorization as a “backup.” There is probably not a lot of disparity here between our grades, but I tend to be a bit harsher given he was drafted with the 53rd overall pick in the draft. Brandon Coleman: Grant mentioned to me how poorly Coleman is at pass blocking (which I agree with), but he’s great in run blocking. I do not use the word “great” and Brandon Coleman in the same sentence, so we differ a bit here. I do think we’d both agree that he’s FAR from a RED, and in an ideal situation, probably a quality backup. Luke McCaffrey: Grant has Luke as a bad draft pick, and seeing how Adam Peters used a top 100 draft pick on him, I would have to agree. I colored him YELLOW, which is a backup, but that shade may lean more towards lemonade YELLOW versus what you see in the sky on a bight, summer day. Jordan Magee: I think Grant and I are both in alignment here that Magee is no more than a backup and that’s okay, because every team needs these types of players with fifth-round draft picks. Unfortunately, Magee can’t seem to stay healthy. Dominique Hampton: Hampton was released by the team. Not much more to say here. Javontae Jean-Baptiste: Nothing special to see here. Jean-Baptiste is a situational backup. Grant : C- Would be a D, but they found the franchise QB. Mark : C- When you have six top 100 draft picks and come out with just one quality starter (a player who was essentially gift-wrapped for you), that’s not a good look.

full_text: The Washington Commanders have come back from their bye week and head into a fourth division game despite the fact that its just Week 8. They are hosting the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday Night Football in a game that will have big consequences for the loser. If the Commanders win, they still have a chance in a weak NFC East . Lose and the calls to fire head coach Dan Quinn get too hard to ignore. That will also affect first-time coordinators Daronte Jones and David Blough who have both had a lot of questions about their first season in their roles. During the bye week it was reported that the team had brought in former head coach Steve Wilks to advise on defense, a plan that has been in the works since training camp. Daronte Jones said they felt the team could use his resources and knowledge as they install a new scheme in Washington. Jones didn’t bring any assistants with when forming his coaching staff, and how has an experienced coach to advise as he continues his growth as a coach. One of the big issues with Washington’s defense has been an inconsistent pass rush, and the inability to play two good halves in the same game. David Blough has had his own concerns as he installs an offense in only his third year in coaching. The Commanders coordinators addressed all that and more in their Thursday press conferences. title: Commanders News: RT Josh Conerly Jr is good – and getting better
summary: The Daily Slop – 29 October 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff.
