full_text: The Daily Slop – 29 October 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles ESPN Why Commanders believe they aren’t done yet in the NFC East The Washington Commanders’ hopes of climbing into the NFC East race focuses on a variety of factors: The NFC East isn’t good; the schedule eases up; Jayden Daniels is healthy and playing well. What they need to provide legitimate hope, though, is something that hasn’t occurred nearly enough: wins. As Washington returns from its bye week, it does have renewed belief despite a 1-4-1 record heading into Sunday’s game against the Eagles (2-5). But in the next seven weeks Washington plays only two teams that currently have a winning record — the Giants and Cincinnati. Also, Washington has first-year coordinators on both sides of the ball; if they hired the right people — and have the right players — they should improve as the season progresses. [O]f the 10 teams that have played only six games, Washington has committed more penalties than all but two. Here’s why that matters: 25 of their 69 drives this season have featured at least one penalty; the Commanders have scored a touchdown on two of those series. With 11 games remaining they still believe they have a chance — and the next three games will be pivotal as divisional games between Philadelphia and New York are sandwiched around a conference one vs. the Rams. “We certainly know what’s ahead over the next three games,” Quinn said. They also haven’t lost faith in who they have. because only one team has a winning record — and is on its third quarterback — it provides at least the illusion of hope for others. But the Commanders also know that’s not enough. “We have to take care of our business,” Ekeler said. “As much as we can look at the division, it all comes back to us. We’ve got to win our games. It’s great for us [that no one is pulling away], but we’ve got to win now. I guess that’s a positive, but it won’t matter until we take care of business.” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Bullock’s Film Room (subscription) Commanders Film Review: Josh Conerly Jr. Development Coming out of college. Conerly was a very athletic tackle prospect with a ton of upside due to his movement skills, but he lacked the lower body strength and technique to anchor against NFL caliber power rushers. During the offseason, I wrote about how Conerly developed over the course of last season and with the Commanders having had a bye week, I figured it was time to check in again with how that development is going. I’m going to break this post into two sections, the first looking at his work in the run game and the second looking at his pass protection. He’s at different levels in both aspects so I wanted to break them up to discuss each aspect of his game separately. Run game While the Commanders overall run game hasn’t been as productive as they’d like, Conerly has been playing at a high level. Some of the blocks he’s made in the run game have been excellent, even if they go unnoticed a lot of the time. The Commanders have shifted to more of a zone blocking scheme in the run game this year and Conerly has pulled off some outstanding blocks on the back side of zone runs, which is where the biggest runs can hit. During the offseason, Commanders offensive coordinator David Blough mentioned using Conerly as a weapon and I wrote an article showing some examples of how the Lions used star offensive tackle Penai Sewell as a weapon when Blough was in Detroit. One of those examples was a run play with Sewell pulling on a tackle pull play. A few weeks ago, we saw Conerly do the same thing. Overall, Conerly has been far better than I expected him to be in the NFL as a run blocker. Coming out of college, he was a little passive as a run blocker, but he showed plenty of promise last year in this area and he’s only gotten better this year. He’s a scheme-diverse talent that is athletic enough to create movement and reach blocks on zone runs, but also powerful enough on double teams and down blocks to be effective on gap scheme runs too. Pass protection The biggest question for Conerly early in his career was always going to be how he dealt with power. You could see coming out of college that he lacked lower body strength and technique to handle power. That carried on into his rookie season, where he did develop his technique to find some answers but he still got overpowered more than you’d like. title: NFL trade deadline grades: Jeffery Simmons, DeForest Buckner, Quenton Nelson
summary: Did the Bears give up too much to go all-in with Simmons? How did the Colts do in their DeForest Buckner and Quenton Nelson deals?
full_text:
NFL analysts Ben Solak and Seth Walder are grading deals ahead of the 2026 trade deadline , which is Nov. 10 at 4 p.m. ET.

 When grading trades, we evaluate them for each team based on on-field impact, cap implications, draft compensation and effects within the context of a team's overall short- and long-term outlooks. How confident are we in knowing if this is a good or bad decision? And how big is the impact of this decision? Both questions play a role in our grades, though a low-impact decision can still receive a strong or poor grade. Even with lower stakes, clear-cut wins or losses still matter.

 Here are our evaluations for the first deals of trading season, including the massive blockbuster sending  Jeffery Simmons to Chicago. Check back through the deadline for grades on the biggest moves.

 

 
 Jump to a trade: 
 Simmons |  Buckner |  Nelson 
 Harrison  |  Jurgens 
 Porter | McCarthy 

 
 

 

 Titans trade DT Simmons to Bears 
 Bears get:  DT Jeffery Simmons , 2028 fifth-round pick 
 Titans get: 2027 first-round pick, 2027 fourth-round pick, 2028 first-round pick

 Bears grade: C 
 Titans grade: A

This trade is extremely fun. The Bears were already an enjoyable and fascinating team with legitimate Super Bowl aspirations. And now they've added one of the game's truly elite defensive players. They also gave up a lot to do so.
 The Bears enter Week 8 as ESPN Football Power Index 's seventh-best team, with an 80% chance to reach the playoffs and a 13% chance to reach the Super Bowl. When quarterback Caleb Williams has played this season, their offense has produced 0.14 EPA per play, which would be fourth-best in the NFL. Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen has also been working miracles -- without major turnover luck this time -- but there was a clear need for reinforcements on the defensive depth chart. And now the Bears have landed the best defensive tackle in the league, period.

 Simmons has four sacks this season, despite having his pass rush opportunities limited by being on a bad team. He leads all interior linemen in pass rush win rate and ranks fifth in pressure rate. His run stop win rate is above average. And it is hardly a fluke: Simmons ranked second in pass rush win rate (and above average in run stop win rate) while recording 11 sacks last year in a season in which he might have merited Defensive Player of the Year consideration if not for Myles Garrett  setting the single-season sacks record.

 Simmons is a force and a massive upgrade at an area of weakness. The Bears had been playing 33-year-old Grady Jarrett (who has zero sacks but a solid pass rush win rate) alongside veteran journeymen Kentavius Street , Neville Gallimore and James Lynch . Simmons is an entirely different level of player.

 So, Simmons absolutely makes sense for the Bears, and in general, I am strongly in favor of Chicago making deadline additions this season. But there is a compensation limit where a trade ceases to make sense, and I think the Bears ran past it.

 

 Simmons joins a small fraternity of non-quarterbacks to be traded for multiple first-round picks in recent years: edge rushers Micah Parsons and Khalil Mack , offensive tackle Laremy Tunsil , safety Jamal Adams and cornerback Sauce Gardner . The results have been mixed at best for the acquiring team and Simmons, at 29 years old, is the oldest of these players at the time of the deal (Mack was the previous oldest, as the Bears acquired him as a 27-year-old in 2018).

 Simmons is under contract through 2030. Assuming that contract is untouched, he will cost $27 million in 2027 and $29.8 million in 2028, with the 2028 base salary becoming fully guaranteed the year prior. That is below what Simmons would make on the open market, but it's still a decent-sized contract for Chicago to take on.

 The money saved on Simmons' contract compared to what he would make as a free agent will not reach the expected surplus value of a first-round pick. Even accounting for the high levels of uncertainty in the NFL draft, first-round selections can deliver massive value for NFL teams -- stars on very affordable contracts. The 2027 pick will likely be toward the end of this year's draft, and it seems hard to imagine that 2028 won't be a late first-rounder, too. But I caution against making such strong assumptions -- the Colts didn't think the first-round picks they sent to the Jets last year in exchange for Gardner were going to be as good as they're turning out.

 That is the main reason this is a winning trade for the Titans. Tennessee isn't going anywhere this season, and there is little point in keeping Simmons for a few meaningless wins down the stretch while his trade value diminishes. He's a pillar of the organization, but getting that type of draft capital for a 29-year-old player jump-starts the next phase of the team. The question wasn't whether Simmons should be traded, but what they could get in exchange. And they got a great return.

 Defenders of the Bears will rightly say surplus value alone isn't everything. The objective isn't to have the highest WAR per dollar; it's to win the Super Bowl. And this move increases the Bears' chance to win the Super Bowl in 2026. Maybe in 2027, too. But it likely hurts their odds from 2028 through 2031.

 There are quality defensive players out there who could have improved the Bears' defense while costing them less -- edges Josh Sweat or Yaya Diaby , defensive tackle Daron Payne  ... maybe even bringing back Mack. I would have preferred one of those moves. They might have gotten two of those players for less than they gave up for Simmons.

 

The Bears know they are contenders now, which is why they should go for it. But they gave up too much for a (relatively) older player. Given the player, the need and the situation, it's a move I want to like. But I don't think it can be justified in exchange for two first-round picks. -- Walder 
 
 

 Colts trade DT Buckner to 49ers 
 49ers get: DT DeForest Buckner 
 Colts get: 2027 fourth-round pick

 49ers grade: A- 
 Colts grade: B-

 As soon as the Colts emerged as a team that might engage in a trade-deadline teardown, it wasn't hard to see the dots connecting Buckner back to the 49ers. That became a reality Tuesday.

 Though his numbers have dipped, Buckner, 32, can still help the 49ers get after the quarterback. He has four sacks this season, but his pass rush win rate ranked in the 45th percentile among defensive tackles, alongside a 69th percentile pressure rate. That is a drop from last season, when he was in the 90th and 88th percentile in those metrics, respectively. However, that 2025 performance is a positive sign for what he could bring to the 49ers the rest of this season.

 Extra pass-rushing help will be welcome in San Francisco, which ranks 19th in pass rush win rate. The 49ers have been without Nick Bosa , who has been out because of  a calf injury since Week 3 but is expected to return soon. Their pass defense is the only one of their major units (run and pass on offense and defense) that ranks outside the top seven in EPA per play (13th).

 I'll admit I'm a little surprised the 49ers made this move considering they already have Osa Odighizuwa as a pass-rush-first defensive tackle. But he can play next to Buckner -- especially on passing downs. Also, San Francisco's rash of defensive line injuries makes any help welcome.

 

 This type of roster-bolstering move makes sense for San Francisco. The 49ers are the Super Bowl favorites, according to ESPN's Football Power Index . In fact, they are the favorites by a lot , with the FPI giving them a 23% chance to win the Super Bowl (every other team is below 11%). Adding Buckner to reinforce those chances is worthwhile.

 The cost was also quite reasonable. The 49ers are surrendering a fourth-round pick and taking over the prorated remainder of Buckner's $13 million salary, assuming his contract is untouched. While compensatory picks are never a guarantee,…

title: Jeffery Simmons traded to Bears: Does dealing multiple first-round picks work?
summary: The Bears' aggressive move for Simmons marks the 10th time in the past decade that a team has traded multiple first-round picks for a star player. But the hit rate isn't great.
full_text:
On the day an NFL team trades two first-round picks for a superstar player, there is only one winner. Fans are thrilled. Most (but not all) NFL observers are excited. Getting a proven player at a position of need for some unsure, abstract things that aren't even due until the future feels great. It should!

 The Bears trading two first-round picks for Jeffery Simmons makes a lot of sense. Chicago has a great offense and a defense that could use some help. Simmons is a true shop-wrecker, the sort of pass-protection magnet whom coordinator Dennis Allen and the Bears didn't have and had sought for years. There's no question that the 2026 Bears are better with him in the lineup.

 The hit rate on these deals in the modern era isn't great. Success isn't binary, but there's more risk in these deals than it might seem at first glance. The sure thing isn't always so. Those picks that feel guaranteed to land in the bottom half of the first round don't always fall there. And the significant investment a team makes in one star limits what it can do elsewhere, often creating hidden restrictions as it tries to build a successful roster in the years to come.

 That shouldn't preclude the Bears from making a move for a star player, but it should inform how confident we should be that the deal will work out. Simmons was the highlight while watching Titans tape over the past couple of years, but he wasn't single-handedly elevating a defense that ranked 31st in DVOA before the trade. Can he be enough of a difference-maker for the Bears to justify this sort of trade?

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 For the Titans, this is an acknowledgment that they're not close to winning with Simmons, but does this haul transform their team? Is there any reason to believe that the Titans can take advantage of this sort of trade to find the next Simmons in the draft? Does this deal portend that they're about to restart their rebuild?

 Let's take a balanced perspective on this deal. Does this shift the balance of power in the NFC toward Chicago? Was it already there? Will we look back at this move as the one that pushed the Bears into the Super Bowl? It's possible. We might also see it as the latest in a series of overly aggressive in-season trades from Chicago general manager Ryan Poles that didn't land the difference-maker he wanted. But let's go through history to get some perspective.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Have similar trades worked? 
 Will the Simmons trade work? 

 
 

 The (modern) history of the two-first-round-pick trade 
 The Bears, of course, kicked this all off. When the league moved to its current slotted draft structure in the summer of 2011 and drastically increased the value of first-round picks, we saw teams really hoard Day 1 selections. Teams used first-rounders to move up and down the board for rookies during the draft, of course, but there were only a handful of deals where a team traded even one first-round pick for a veteran player -- and they were almost all disasters.

 The Raiders traded one for Carson Palmer, who was there for 25 games. Darrelle Revis lasted one season with the Bucs. Percy Harvin caught 23 passes for the Seahawks (although he returned a kickoff for a touchdown in the Super Bowl while Seattle was already up by multiple scores). Trent Richardson lasted two seasons with the Colts. Sam Bradford started 17 games for the Vikings. Jimmy Graham tore his patellar tendon and wasn't as impactful with the Seahawks as he had been with the Saints, who landed a more impactful veteran in Max Unger on the other side of the deal. Brandin Cooks was dealt away after one season with the Patriots and then spent two years with the Rams before being shipped off for second- and fourth-round picks. Those trades were all messes.

 

 That didn't stop the Bears from making a massive trade just before the start of the 2018 season. Hoping to land Vic Fangio a franchise defender, general manager Ryan Pace authorized a massive outlay for a superstar in the prime of his career. The Bears sent a package of picks , highlighted by their first-round selections in 2019 and 2020, to the Raiders for Khalil Mack . That's kicked off a flood of trades with teams sending multiple first-rounders (or the draft capital equivalent) for franchise players.

 How have those moves worked out? Let's run deal by deal to see. Keep in mind, though, that evaluating these trades isn't as simple as looking at the players each team landed. There's an enormous cash difference between the two sides, with the team adding the star both paying a top-level talent and foregoing the ability to add cost-controlled talent around that player in the draft. The team getting the picks isn't assured of anything, but given how much less those picks cost over the next four years of their pro careers, the hit rate doesn't have to be quite as high. Those teams also get extra money to spend elsewhere on their roster in free agency.

 And from each team's perspective, once the trade is done, what the other team's players do doesn't matter. The Titans want these picks to land as high as possible, but if they land a franchise quarterback with one of these selections, they won't care what the Bears do. If Simmons struggles in Chicago, it won't suddenly be a good trade for the Bears if the players the Titans draft don't pan out. And we obviously don't know whom the Bears would have picked (or what other veterans they could have used the picks to acquire) if they hadn't made the deal.

 We have to evaluate these trades from each side relative to what their expectations should be at the time of the deal. In this case, we're evaluating from the perspective of the team that shelled out the draft capital to land the superstar. I'll mention the players, though, and I'll try to guess where the team getting the draft picks might have invested their savings in free agency.

 

 Khalil Mack   to the Bears (2018) 
 Bears got: Mack, second-round pick, conditional late-round pick 
 Raiders got: Two first-round picks, third-round pick, sixth-round pick

 Bears picks became: TE Cole Kmet , OL Arlington Hambright 
 Raiders picks became: RB Josh Jacobs , CB Damon Arnette , WR Bryan Edwards 
 Surplus Raiders cash became:  OT Trent Brown 

 Why the deal should have worked: Mack was the sort of superstar that isn't available in free agency. A 27-year-old edge rusher who hadn't missed a game as a pro, Mack had been a first-team All-Pro twice and won Defensive Player of the Year two years before the trade. He was coming due for a new contract, and new Raiders coach Jon Gruden didn't think Mack was worth the largest deal in football for a non-quarterback, a contract Mack quickly landed as part of the trade with Chicago.

 Why it shouldn't have worked:  The Bears couldn't have felt they were a superstar edge rusher away from being Super Bowl contenders. They were coming off a 5-11 season and had just hired Matt Nagy as their new coach. They were excited about  Mitchell Trubisky , of course, but the QB had spent most of his rookie season on offensive training wheels. Pace couldn't count on those picks landing in the bottom half of the first round.

 

 Did it work? In Year 1, yes. Mack's best game with the Bears was his first, as he absolutely terrorized Aaron Rodgers  and the Packers on national television, forcing a fumble and producing a pick-six. The Bears blew a late lead in that game, and Mack missed three matchups over the rest of the season, but his 12.5 sacks were good enough to earn him another first-team All-Pro nod, and he finished second in the Defensive Player of the Year balloting. At 12-4 and with Mack leading one of the best defenses in the league, it felt like an easy victory.

 Things sort of steadily declined from there. Mack lasted three more seasons in Chicago and battled injuries, including a foot problem that cost him 10 games in 2021. He was a good player but didn't eclipse 10 sacks or earn a first-team All-Pro…

title: Fantasy football buzz: Despite win, can you trust Packers' running game?
summary: Jordan Love and the Packers continue a one-dimensional attack. Will the running game ever get right?
full_text:
Everything that happens in the NFL has additional context when viewed from a fantasy football perspective. From position battles to injuries and so much more, the news cycle will constantly affect player values.

 Our fantasy football buzz file, with contributions from our ESPN fantasy writers and our NFL Nation reporters, aims to provide fantasy managers with the intel they need as news breaks around the league.

 

 Oct. 30: Packers' ground game cause for concern 

 By Adam Rank 

 Jordan Love throws multiple touchdown passes. Matthew Golden looks good. I mean, Christian Watson left and arrived back at Lambeau Field from an ambulance in a move that would make Triple H say, "no way this is real." And yet, I get a note from my editor (a Packers fan, mind you) complaining about the (lack of a) Green Bay Packers running game. 

 I mean, the Milwaukee Brewers just won the World Series , but we need to focus on the Packers' rushing attack? Well, I guess that is the best place to start.

 

 The Packers won the game despite rushing for just 66 yards . They have been held to fewer than 90 rushing yards in all eight games, the club's longest streak in the Super Bowl era. The Packers' 485 rushing yards are the fewest by any team through eight games since the 2019 Bengals. I mean, what in the name of Eddie Lee Ivery is going on here?

 The short answer is the offensive line is bad. The playcalling is bad. I mean, you think the guy who favored Dion Lewis over Derrick Henry when he was offensive coordinator in Tennessee  was ever going to have a solid running game in Green Bay? It's just the facts.

 And it's not going to get much easier in the coming weeks, either. The New England Patriots , Minnesota Vikings and Los Angeles Rams aren't great matchups. It's not until the New Orleans Saints in Week 13 that the schedule softens for Josh Jacobs . If you kept him on your roster all this time, you're likely going to be compelled to start him, but the matchups aren't ideal.

 Some other notes from Thursday night: 

 

 
 Love has accounted for multiple touchdowns in all eight games this season, but this was his first game of the season with three touchdown passes. He's a set-and-forget quarterback moving forward. It is wild to think he wasn't drafted as a QB1 this year. 
 Watson is nearing ace territory this season. He recorded his 12th reception of 20-plus yards, second in the league behind  Jaxon Smith-Njigba . 
 Golden is also a must-start, but he registered two drops Thursday. Love has seen 20 drops by his receivers this season. I feel like that total would double if you counted the number of interceptions that are dropped. Or maybe it just seems that way to me, a Bears supporter. 
 Is the " Bryce Young as a QB1" era over already? Well, for starters, the Carolina Panthers need to do a better job of protecting him. He was hit. A lot. I'm not rushing him back into my lineup next week against the Denver Broncos . You might want to take a look at the waiver wire right now for a streamable option if Young is your only quarterback. Kyler Murray against the Buffalo Bills next week could do the trick. 
 Chuba Hubbard was good, however. He scored a touchdown, rushed for 81 yards and caught seven balls for 38 more yards. Again, playing the Bills next week makes him a prime RB1. 
 

 

 Oct. 29: Week 8 streaming guide 
 

 By Michael F. Florio 

 Kyler Murray has used his legs more lately, with 51 and 34 rushing yards in his past two games. This week, he gets the Detroit Lions , who have allowed the most pass yards per game, most fantasy PPG to QBs and second-most passing touchdowns. Every QB but one who faced them has finished in the top eight and scored at least 21 fantasy points. Plus, if you stream him this week you can use him again next week against the Buffalo Bills .

 Jacoby Brissett is in play due to the matchup. He faces the Dallas Cowboys , who have allowed the sixth-most fantasy PPG and eighth-most passing touchdowns to QBs. Plus, the Arizona Cardinals likely will be trailing, which means added volume.

 Deeper QB plays: 

 
 Malik Willis is coming off his two best fantasy games of the season and has been running effectively. 
 Geno Smith gets a revenge game against the Las Vegas Raiders , who have allowed the sixth-most fantasy PPG and second-most passing touchdowns to QBs. 
 Michael Penix Jr . has thrown three touchdown passes in two straight games and faces the Tampa Bay Buccaneers , who are much easier to throw on than run against. 
 Tanner McKee faces the Washington Commanders , who are top five in passing yards per game and touchdowns allowed to quarterbacks. Overall, they have allowed the second-most fantasy PPG to the position. 
 
 Blake Corum played 43% of the snaps with 18 touches last week. He went for 101 yards and a touchdown, while having two called back due to penalty. He has picked up explosive runs at the seventh-highest rate in the NFL and faces the Los Angeles Chargers , who give them up at the eighth-highest rate. The Chargers are also top seven in rushing yards allowed per game and touchdowns allowed to RBs.

 Rhamondre Stevenson has 24 targets on the season, which by far leads the New England Patriots ' backfield. That is big this week as the Miami Dolphins are top 10 in catches and receiving yards allowed to backs. In total, they have allowed the third-most fantasy PPG to RBs.

 Jonah Coleman returned last week and led the Denver Broncos backs in snaps (50%), carries (nine) and rushing yards (54). He is by far their most explosive runner and I believe is their best dual-threat back as well. Even in a tough matchup, he is in play as a flex option.

 Rachaad White played just under 70% of the snaps in his first game without Jacory Croskey-Merritt . Volume wins out here, and the Eagles have allowed 275 rushing yards and two touchdowns to opponents' RB1 in the past two weeks.

 Carnell Tate is in play as long as he suits up. He has had at least a 25% target rate in five of his past six games. He has the fourth-highest target share against man coverage, which the Bengals play at an above-average rate. Tate, who has shown to have a safe floor, could show his upside this week as well.

 Keenan Allen has nine or more targets in three of four games. That has led to him scoring 16-plus fantasy points in two of those games. Now he faces the Jacksonville Jaguars , who allow in the top five in most yards and fantasy points per game to opposing WRs. The Indianapolis Colts will likely be in catch-up mode, so expect volume to go Allen's way.

 Ja'Kobi Lane and Rashod Bateman are in play due to the matchup against the Bills. Buffalo has allowed the most fantasy PPG and touchdowns to wide receivers this season. The two have split targets against zone coverage, which the Bills play 81% of the time. Lane is the preferred option, but Bateman brings upside this week.

 Chig Okonkwo saw a team-high seven targets in the Commanders' last game, and he turned them into seven catches for 69 yards. I expect him to be a top-two target moving forward for the Commanders. The volume has him in play as a streaming option.

 T.J. Hockenson is in play due to the matchup against the Lions. Detroit has allowed the most yards, touchdowns and fantasy PPG to tight ends. Plus, the Minnesota Vikings may have to put up more points than normal in this one.

 Injury watch for 'Thursday Night Football' 
 Packers WR   Matthew Golden   (shoulder/foot) is questionable for Thursday. If he suits up, as long as there are no reports that he will be on a snap count, fantasy managers should play him. If he were to sit, expect more volume to go to Christian Watson and Tucker Kraft .

title: Has Tyler Guyton become the Cowboys' franchise left tackle?
summary: The 2024 first-round draft pick has gone to liability to strength in protecting quarterback Dak Prescott.
full_text:
FRISCO, Texas --  Tyler Guyton 's first two years with the Dallas Cowboys was about injuries and inconsistencies for the left tackle.

 As he entered his third season, the 2024 first-round pick knew he needed to improve everywhere, from his nutrition to his body composition to how he played his position.

 He found himself asking questions. A lot of them.

 At different times in the offseason, he worked with the man he replaced, Tyron Smith , a future Hall of Famer. He spent time with NFL veteran Terron Armstead . And for a few days in Oklahoma, he worked with Philadelphia Eagles right tackle Lane Johnson , who retired earlier this season, as well as Tampa Bay's Tristan Wirfs and Buffalo's Dion Dawkins .

 "There's a level of finding yourself first as a young player," Guyton said. "You don't just want to interject on somebody else's process and becoming a pro. So I kind of tried to stay to my own and ask questions when I could. But as I grew older, I realized that the more that I'm in their ear, the more that I'm going to learn.

 "So it was just about going through the process and being able to shake hands and rub shoulders with people and build relationships before I just go and ask for the ways that they became great."

 

 The lessons learned about footwork and different pass sets, strong hands and balance have shone brightly through seven games. The Cowboys first caught a whiff of a change in Guyton in the offseason and in training camp.

 What was supposed to be a training camp competition with Nate Thomas never materialized. As Guyton kept playing, coaches, personnel people and the front office did not want to say much to avoid jinxing what they were seeing.

 "I think you see a guy, I'll use the word 'focused' and 'playing one play at a time,'" coach Brian Schottenheimer said. "This is a guy that's playing with tremendous confidence. But literally you see a guy that's bought into the mantra of one play at a time, do the play to the best of your ability, then move on.

 "And we actually don't talk about him a lot because he's playing really, really well and playing at one of the elite levels in the league in my opinion."

 Duke Manyweather trains a number of offensive linemen throughout the NFL in the offseason, including most Cowboys and Guyton. He saw an intentionality in Guyton's work that was different than his first two years. Guyton was detailed with how he trained in the weight room and the line-specific drills. His nutrition improved.

 "He's a more confident player in Year 3 because his preparation hasn't just been work, but deliberate work," Manyweather said. "Confidence is the positive story we tell ourselves, but confidence is 'What has our preparation prepared us for?' It's preparing for the moment. And it takes a village."

 

 In 431 snaps, Guyton has not given up a sack this season, and he has gone against top pass rushers, including  Brian Burns of the New York Giants , the Baltimore Ravens ' Trey Hendrickson and Houston Texans ' Danielle Hunter .

 Oddly, Guyton's pass block win rate is the lowest of his career (81.8%), but his run block win rate is the highest of his career (79.9%). His nastiness was on display in the Week 4 win against the Texans when he blocked linebacker Jake Hansen into the bench area on a Javonte Williams ' run.

 "That last 10% of the block opens up holes and opportunities for our backs and our playmakers to make plays, so I think that's what's extremely important," Guyton said. "Something that's harped on in our room is just that last 10% of that block. But being offensive line, you got to kind of be an ass---- so I'll take it."

 In his first two seasons, Guyton allowed 11 sacks. He also missed nine games due to injury, including seven last season with a concussion and high ankle sprain that ultimately ended his season.

 

 Before this season, the question around Guyton, the No. 29 pick in 2024, was why he hadn't performed like the other Cowboys' first-round offensive linemen over the years, such as Tyron Smith (2011), Travis Frederick (2013), Zack Martin (2014), Tyler Smith (2022) and even last year's first-rounder, Tyler Booker .

 "It probably is a little bit unfair to a guy that's maybe seen as a developmental player that needs time to develop, to think that you're just going to throw him in there," offensive coordinator Klayton Adams said. "I can tell you from experience, just having Paris Johnson Jr. in Arizona, that he walked in as a top-10 pick and played pretty good as a rookie and played every game, but he was far from a finished product at the end of Year 1."

 Quarterback  Dak Prescott saw back in February that Guyton was preparing differently and did not think there would be a competition with Thomas, who was traded to the Texans before the season started.

 "I think you look out there and you look at his style of play, the way that he believes in himself and prepares jumps out," Prescott said. "Credit for him to being a real pro, and he's a vocal guy throughout the game and a guy that I appreciate protecting [me]."

 The timing could not be better for the Cowboys or Guyton. A decision on picking up his fifth-year option for 2028 has become easier with how he has played thus far. He could find himself in discussions on a long-term deal next offseason if the organization wants to go down that path.

 Asked earlier in the season about Guyton, owner and general manager Jerry Jones said, "I'm not so sure it's not the highlight so far this year, because of his skill level."

 Jones, a former collegiate offensive lineman, has always preached patience with fellow lineman, oftentimes citing former Cowboys coach Tom Landry's rule of not making a judgement on them until the third year.

 "Now the dominance that we all knew was there, people are just seeing in public," Tyler Smith said. "So I think he deserves all the props in the world and that he's going to continue to get better week in and week out."

title: Answering 10 questions about Chiefs-Broncos showdown for first place in AFC West
summary: Can the Broncos slow Kenneth Walker III? Can the Chiefs' pass rush fluster Bo Nix? Answering the biggest questions in Sunday's AFC West showdown.
full_text:
Sixteen seasons and counting. That's the amount of time the Denver Broncos and Kansas City Chiefs have jointly controlled the AFC West.

 The Chiefs started the run in 2010, with the Broncos winning the division from 2011 to 2015 and again last season. In between, the Chiefs won nine straight AFC West titles from 2016 to 2024, with quarterback Patrick Mahomes leading the way for most of them. This season looks to continue the trend, as the 5-1 Chiefs and 5-2 Broncos have once again separated themselves from the Las Vegas Raiders and the winless Los Angeles Chargers .

 So as the Chiefs and Broncos get set for their second regular-season meeting Sunday at Empower Field at Mile High ( 4:25 p.m. ET, CBS ), AFC West supremacy seems to be on the line yet again. The Chiefs won the first meeting 31-10 in a Week 1 rout. So, Sunday's rematch will either place the Chiefs on the inside lane with a 1½-game lead and the head-to-head tiebreaker, or give Denver a half-game lead going into the back half of the season.

 "They're a great team, are at the top of the league again," Broncos tackle Mike McGlinchey said. "And they've been the litmus test since I've been in the NFL. A great challenge for us. And I'm super excited for it."

 ESPN Chiefs reporter Nate Taylor and ESPN Broncos reporter Jeff Legwold break down the matchup below.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Ramifications: Chiefs | Broncos 
 Walker vs. Broncos' run defense 
 Nix vs. Chiefs' pass rush 
 Chiefs WRs vs. Broncos DBs 
 X factors | How each team will win 

 

 

 How important is winning this game in each team's quest for the AFC West title? 

 

 A win Sunday will give the Chiefs a commanding lead in the race for the division before the halfway point of the season. Getting a leg up opening night was critical for the Chiefs, and this rematch is even more important if Kansas City wants to win the division and host a playoff game.

 

 The Chiefs want to demonstrate that last season was a blip in their dynastic run, and a victory over the Broncos could further prove their point. Kansas City could use the cushion over Denver in the standings, too. The Chiefs' schedule ramps up in the second half of the season, with opponents such as the Bills, Rams, Bengals, 49ers and Patriots looming. --  Taylor 

 

 Tiebreakers will matter if the Broncos want to make the playoffs, much less win the division, so a split with the Chiefs would go a long way to help. That split could be a boost to Denver, especially if it can get improved play from the offense and quarterback Bo Nix . After an extremely tough opening stretch of the season, the Broncos' schedule eases up after Sunday, with games against the Raiders (twice), Jets, Dolphins and Chargers. -- Legwold 

 

 

 

 Can the Chiefs depend on Kenneth Walker III as they did in the first meeting? 
 

 The Chiefs should believe they can have similar success with Walker. Although he was held to 36 rushing yards in the Week 7 loss to the Seahawks, the Chiefs should still lean on him to power their offense. A positive for their rushing attack is the expected return of right tackle Jaylon Moore , who missed last week's game while in the NFL's concussion protocol, and receiver Rashee Rice , who missed the past two games because of a strained right hamstring .

 One of Walker's strengths this season has been making defenders miss. Tackling has been a struggle for the Broncos at times this season, including in the opener, so the Chiefs should feed Walker to test them.

 "Kenneth is a special player, and he makes a lot of big plays happen," Mahomes said Wednesday. "We're not going to stop trying to run the ball. But if they're going to put so many resources into stopping him, and playing a shell over the top, we have to be able to hit them in that intermediate area and then guys have to be able to run after the catch and break tackles." --  Taylor 

 

 

 Has the Broncos' tackling gotten better since their struggles in Arrowhead? 
 It couldn't have been much worse after they missed an astounding 19 tackles in the season-opening loss to the Chiefs. And though the Broncos' defenders kept saying it was "easy to fix," citing it as a question of technique and/or "want to", it took them some time. They had eight missed tackles against the Jacksonville Jaguars in a Week 2 win , but have since reduced the missed tackles for the most part.

 The Broncos had quality tackling outings against the 49ers, Seahawks and last weekend against the Cardinals, with a choppy nine-missed-tackle effort against the Chargers mixed in. As for Sunday, more than five missed tackles could spell trouble against Walker & Co.

 "It's easy to sit here looking back on it and say, 'We sucked, we gave up 31 points' and all that,'" Broncos linebacker Alex Singleton said this week. "You have to go back and build off the good, too. ... It wasn't who we are. There was plays in that game that showed who we are. ... Just [need to find] those plays." --  Legwold 

 

 

 Is Bo Nix fixed after faring well against the Cardinals? 
 

 Nix and coach Sean Payton likely felt some relief and an injection of confidence after Nix showed more assertiveness with some throws, along with a 62-yard touchdown run that was the longest in his career and the longest scoring run for a QB in Broncos history, against Arizona. But an overly positive assessment would be a little naive.

 Nix is still 26th in QBR (45.2), 30th in completion percentage over expectation (minus-4.1%) and 31st in air yards per attempt (5.9). And if wideout  Jaylen Waddle misses Sunday's game because of  a chest injury he suffered in Arizona, an offense that already struggles to create explosive plays (28th in plays of 20 or more yards) will have to dig even deeper.

 "We're close, but I don't feel like we're really dominating or scratching the surface of what we can be," Nix said. "But we are doing what we're supposed to do to win the games. ... I do think we're leaving some things out there, as far as penalties and third downs, and it starts with me." --  Legwold 

 

 

 

 The Chiefs' pass rush has struggled since the opener. What's been the biggest issue? 

 One of the biggest problems is the lack of productivity from All-Pro defensive tackle Chris Jones , who has struggled to beat double-teams at the rate he has in the past. Jones has recorded only a half-sack this season. Edge rusher George Karlaftis has generated consistent pressure, but he has recorded only one sack.

 Too often opposing quarterbacks have escaped the Chiefs' pressure. The lone defender who has quickly gotten to the quarterback is rookie edge R Mason Thomas . Even so, he also has just one sack this season. --  Taylor 

 

 

 

 With all their injuries at receiver, where will big plays come from in the Chiefs' passing game? 
 The safe answer based on the past two games is tight end Travis Kelce , who, at age 37, is still Mahomes' most reliable pass catcher. The Chiefs are optimistic that Rice, who was hurt in Week 4, can be effective against the Broncos' zone coverage. But without receiver Tyquan Thornton , who is recovering from a dislocated left ankle , the Chiefs haven't produced deep completions.

 Xavier Worthy is still an option on deep throws, but he has only one reception in which the ball traveled more than 20 yards downfield. Rookie receiver Cyrus Allen should get more opportunities as the Chiefs continue to try to incrementally increase his development. "He'll get a little bit more [snaps] this week," coach Andy Reid said of Allen on Wednesday.--  Taylor 

 

 

 How is Denver's secondary looking? Will Pat Surtain II or Talanoa Hufanga be back? 
 There was plenty of hand-wringing when the Broncos used a first-round pick on cornerback  Jahdae Barron in the 2025 draft to improve what was already a good, deep secondary. But it has helped the Broncos have more versatility to deal with defensive back injuries better than most teams. His development, along with emerging third-year cornerback …

title: NFL Week 8 betting guide: The value bets to make on lines, props and anytime TDs
summary: Our experts dive into the odds and player props for Week 8 and offer their betting tips and favorite plays.
full_text:
Value is value, no matter where -- or how -- you find it. And that's what we'll aim to do each week in this space: find betting value.

 Ben Solak, Seth Walder and Matt Bowen bring different perspectives into how they approach sports betting. Solak leans on his expertise in player evaluation and the X's and O's to find edges, while Walder relies on statistical models to pick out plus-expected value bets, focusing mainly on defense. Bowen, a former NFL safety, predicts positive matchups and game winners from tape study and his understanding of the league. Also included are fantasy projection creator Mike Clay's top predicted anytime TD scorers for Week 8.

 From spreads and money lines to totals and defensive player props, a good price might be found anywhere. Results will be tracked throughout the season, with flat one-unit wagers for each listed bet. Let's get into it.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 
 Jump to: 
 Bowen's favorite bets 
 Solak's plays  | Walder's props 
 Clay's TD projections 

 

 

 Bowen's favorite bets 
 Looking at the Week 8 slate, we'll start with my top game in Detroit, as  Jared Goff  and an explosive  Lions  offense face the blitz-heavy  Minnesota Vikings . I also have a total I like in the Cleveland Browns - Pittsburgh Steelers matchup, and let's hit on another two-team teaser. As always, I'll give also give you some props I like.

 

 
 Minnesota Vikings at Detroit Lions 
1 p.m. ET on Fox, Ford Field, Detroit

 
 The Vikings' low-volume pass game has lacked rhythm with Kyler Murray under center, which has resulted in declining numbers for Justin Jefferson . It's a better matchup Sunday versus a Lions defense allowing a league-high 291.8 passing yards per game. This is the game to isolate and scheme for Jefferson.

 However, the key in-game matchup to watch is Goff versus Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores. Goff is going to see consistent pressure from the Vikings, who own a league-high blitz rate of 69.9%. Overload fronts, plus A/B gap blitzes to dent the pocket, which limits Goff's ability to climb/step up in the pocket. But Goff has been really good this season versus the blitz, completing 72.7% of his throws (third highest) while registering a 79.4 QBR (fifth highest).

 My take? The Lions have enough answers to create manageable pockets, while giving Goff quicker reads (and timing throws). Detroit covers the three points at home (-120) .

 Jahmyr Gibbs receptions OVER 4.5 (-03) 

 What are your immediate counters to pressure from the Vikings? Throw screens. Yes, Gibbs will be asked to play a critical role as a blocker in pass protection versus Flores' defense, but the Lions can deploy him on screens and quick releases from the backfield to beat the blitz, too. Gibbs has five or more receptions in five or six games played.

 Browns at Steelers OVER 39.5 (-105) 

 I get why the total is lower in this one. Both teams rank in the top 12 of defensive scoring and yards allowed per game. Plus, the Pittsburgh offense has lacked consistent big-play ability in recent weeks. However, when these teams me in Week 4 in Cleveland, the total hit 51. Aaron Rodgers threw for 299 yards and three touchdowns, and the Browns rushed for 112 yards. The weather looks good for Sunday in Pittsburgh. Give me the over.

 Two team, 6.5-point teaser (-143): Indianapolis Colts at Jacksonville Jaguars (-3.5) and Los Angeles Chargers at Los Angeles Rams (Even) 

 

 We hit on a two-team teaser last week, so let's bring it back, starting in Jacksonville. The Colts are unloading talent as part of a rebuild, with both Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner leaving via trade this week. So, we'll take the Jaguars off the bye. And teasing the spread down to 3.5 points is more comfortable than a touchdown and a field goal.

 What changes could have the 0-6 Chargers made during the bye week to jumpstart their offense? I expect to see some improvement, with more rhythm in the pass game for Justin Herbert . That's a start. But getting the Rams to even money (down from a 6.5-point favorite) is the play here.

 Omar Cooper Jr . receiving yards OVER 41.5 (-114) 

 Since returning from an ankle injury in Week 6, the rookie out of Indiana has been schemed up in the New York Jets ' game plan, and he's making plays. Cooper has posted back-to-back games of 100 or more yards receiving with at least five receptions in each. Cooper is an explosive, power strider who can produce numbers after the catch, plus he can get loose down the field on shot-play throws (three catches of 48 or more yards in his last two games). With his big-play potential and steady volume, I like the over to hit Sunday versus the Las Vegas Raiders .

 Derrick Henry total yards OVER 90.5 (-114) 

 This feels like a big number given that Henry has posted 60 or fewer total yards in back-to-back games. But the volume is there -- 18 or more touches in every game played this season -- and Henry gets a positive matchup versus a Buffalo Bills defense allowing 120 total yards per game to opposing running backs. This should be a get-right game for Henry.

 Rhamondre Stevenson total yards OVER 70.5 (-115) 

 The Miami Dolphins are allowing 148.2 total yards per game to opposing running backs. While I'd like to see Stevenson's rushing efficiency improve (3.7 YPC), he has posted at least 71 scrimmage yards in three of his last four games, catching 11 passes for 141 yards during that stretch.-->

 

 George Pickens anytime TD (+100) 

 Pickens has scored a touchdown in two of his last three games, and he has matchup advantages versus the Arizona Cardinals defense. This unit has allowed a league-high 17 touchdown passes this season and gave up 23 receptions of 20 or more yards (tied for sixth most). The Cardinals also play a bunch of Cover 2 (36.2% of opponent dropbacks), so there will be opportunities to isolate Pickens on a safety this Sunday.

 Kyle Pitts Sr . anytime TD (+285) 

 Pitts, who is playing his best football of the season, has seen his usage elevate over his last three games. During this stretch, Pitts has posted five-plus receptions in three straight -- with at least one touchdown grab in each -- and he has seen a total of six red zone targets. The Tampa Bay Buccaneers ' ability to dial up zone pressure is a factor here, but that defense has also allowed an average of 5.7 receptions per game to tight ends this season.

 

 

 
 Solak's plays 
 

 Zay Flowers OVER 6.5 receptions (+112) 

 The Bills are one of the worst coverage teams in football, and the performance of WR1s against them is evidence to that point. In Week 2,  Amon-Ra St. Brown  had nine catches for 142 yards. In Week 5, Puka Nacua had a whopping 17 receptions for 138 yards. Even Tre Tucker of the Raiders (5 catches, 97 yards) and Romeo Doubs of the Patriots (6 catches, 58 yards) had big performances going up against Buffalo.

 I continue to be enamored with Flowers' usage in Declan Doyle's offense. He has lined up more in the slot this season than ever before, and the Ravens easily manufacture him quick touches on crossing patterns and in the screen game. Flowers has had at least eight catches in three of his last four games and, in the two games to start the season (five catches apiece), he was hampered by a hamstring injury. The Ravens are going to use him at a high volume in every game, but this Bills matchup is particularly ripe for plenty of targets.

 Flowers is also +145 to score a touchdown in this game. The Bills have given up 11 receiving touchdowns to wide receivers this season, more than any other defense in football. In fact, the Bills are coming off of their bye week ... and still lead the league in receiving touchdowns surrendered to wide receivers. I will be tracking both of these bets.

 Kyler Murray OVER 24.5 rushing yards (-104) 

 We might finally see the Vikings in a trailing game script, as they are 3-point dogs at Detroit this Sunday. This Detroit defense is also a pass-funnel unit…

title: Have teams figured out DeMeco Ryans and the Texans' defense?
summary: Houston has gone from one of the best defenses in the NFL to one of the most scored upon.
full_text:
HOUSTON -- Coming into this season, there were high expectations for the  Houston Texans ' defense -- a unit coming off a dominant year.

 Houston added former  Philadelphia Eagles  starting safety Reed Blankenship in free agency and returned all of its key members after allowing the fewest yards per game (277.2) and the second-fewest points per game (17.4) last season.

 But the unit has woefully underperformed. It ranks 19th in points allowed (24.3) and has allowed 30 or more points in three of the Texans' seven games, which is already the second most in a season since coach DeMeco Ryans arrived in 2023.

 

 There was an offseason narrative surrounding quarterback C.J. Stroud that if he could give Houston just an average level of quarterback play, the Texans had a chance to win a Super Bowl behind that defense.

 Fast-forward to Week 8, and Stroud's play has soared well past average. He's fourth in passing yards (1,867), 10th in passer rating (100.7) and 13th in touchdowns (11).

 That's what makes the surprising regression from the defense more of a talking point. But Ryans doesn't believe Houston (2-5) needs an overhaul from a roster or schematic standpoint, feeling the biggest problem is execution; the Texans have the fifth-most missed tackles (70).

 "We have plenty of players, we have plenty of scheme," Ryans said. "We just have to execute. We have to execute a little bit better. If we execute a little bit better, the result can be different."

 The most jarring defensive issue is their pass defense -- featuring three Pro Bowlers in the secondary -- has regressed the most. Led by the cornerback duo of  Derek Stingley Jr . and Kamari Lassiter , Houston ranked fifth in passing yards allowed per game (179) and had 19 interceptions last season.

 This year, Houston ranks 27th in passing yards allowed (244 per game), with only three interceptions, while also giving up the highest explosive rate (19%) in the league.

 

 Opposing offenses have been able to gut the unit on first and second downs. Teams have a better grasp on Houston's coverages and rules within those calls on early downs -- which could explain defensive end  Will Anderson Jr .'s comments about having to "play perfect."

 "Teams know us," said Anderson, who leads the NFL with 7.5 sacks. "You know what I'm saying? They know how we play. They know our style of play."

 On first and second downs, Houston goes zone 72% of the time, the 10th-highest rate in the league. But it is usually lining up in either Cover 3 (44.2%) or Cover 4 (21.6%), according to ESPN Research. And teams have attacked in various ways.

 The area where offenses have targeted them the most is the seams, leading to 706 yards (fifth most) on early downs with a passer rating of 110 and 995 passing yards (third most) overall when quarterbacks throw in that area.

 But general manager Nick Caserio also agrees that it still comes back to execution.

 "We have enough scheme," Caserio said. "In the end, like, we don't have defensive calls where the calls are to let the receiver run open. If the defense calls for it to be pressed, to reroute the receiver at the line of scrimmage, and you don't reroute the receiver at the line of scrimmage, letting them go to the route, is that a scheme issue? Is that a player issue?"

 Ryans took over playcalling from defensive coordinator Matt Burke after the Texans' 0-4 start during which they allowed 27.3 points and 343.8 yards per game. But in the three matchups since, the results haven't changed drastically under Ryans.

 

 The scoring allowed dropped to 21 points per game, but one of those matchups included the struggling Tennessee Titans , who average the second-lowest points (15.4), in Week 5. Houston held the Titans to three points to claim its first win of the season, but as safety Calen Bullock acknowledged, "It was Tennessee. No offense [to them, but] we're supposed to do that."

 Bullock added the following matchup against the Jacksonville Jaguars was the "real test." But quarterback Trevor Lawrence threw for 306 yards and four touchdowns despite Houston getting the 34-31 win.

 And after its two-game win streak, Houston lost 27-21 in overtime to the New York Giants , allowing J.J. McCarthy to throw for a career-high 252 yards in his first start of the season. So instead of heading into their Week 8 bye on a high note, the Texans are back to the drawing board. 

 The loss summarized the season: It marked the fourth time that the defense allowed a game-winning drive in the closing minutes.

 "It's not a good feeling, it's not a good position to be in," Anderson said. "We keep talking about the same things over and over."

title: 2026 NFL trade deadline updates: Jeffery Simmons, Quenton Nelson on the move
summary: The NFL trade deadline is Nov. 10, but deals have already started. We're tracking all moves, including a blockbuster sending Jeffery Simmons to Chicago.
full_text:
The  2026 NFL trade deadline  is Nov. 10, at 4 p.m. ET. But the deals have already kicked off.

 The Giants traded for Vikings quarterback J.J. McCarthy , the Steelers traded  Joey Porter Jr . to the Cowboys, the Eagles sent center  Cam Jurgens  to the Ravens and the Texans acquired wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr . The Colts traded away guard  Quenton Nelson  and defensive tackle  DeForest Buckner , too. And the biggest deal yet happened on Oct. 29, with the Titans sending defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons to the Bears and landing two first-round picks in return.

 We're tracking all in-season moves and trade-related buzz right through the deadline. The most recent deals will be added at the top.

 
 More coverage: 
 Transactions  |  Depth charts 

 

 
 Oct. 29 
 

 Titans trade DT Simmons to Bears 
 Bears get:  DT Jeffery Simmons , 2028 fifth-round pick 
 Titans get: 2027 first-round pick, 2027 fourth-round pick, 2028 first-round pick

 The Bears are acquiring All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons from the Titans, sources told ESPN's Adam Schefter. The Titans are receiving 2027 and 2028 first-round picks, plus a 2027 fourth-round pick from the Bears in exchange for Simmons and a 2028 fifth-round pick, the sources told Schefter.

 Simmons, 29, signed a three-year, $105.8 million extension with $100 million guaranteed with the Titans in June. He is under contract through the 2030 season.

 Oct. 27 
 

 Colts trade DT Buckner to 49ers

 Colts get:  2027 fourth-round pick

 The Colts are trading three-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle DeForest Buckner back to the 49ers, the team that made him a 2016 first-round pick before dealing him to Indianapolis in 2020, sources told ESPN's Adam Schefter and NFL Network's Ian Rapoport.

 The Colts will receive a 2027 fourth-round pick from the 49ers, sources said.

 Colts trade G Nelson to Seahawks 
 Seahawks get: G  Quenton Nelson 
 Colts get: 2027 third-round pick, 2028 fifth-round pick

 The Colts have agreed to trade eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to the Seahawks, sources told ESPN's Adam Schefter and NFL Network's Ian Rapoport. Nelson is on an expiring contract, and the Colts are opting to get back draft capital now before they could lose him in free agency.

 Oct. 11 
 

 Cardinals trade WR Harrison to Texans 
 Texans get: WR Marvin Harrison Jr ., 2027 seventh-round pick  
 Cardinals get: 2027 second-round pick, 2027 sixth-round pick

 The Texans have completed a trade for Cardinals wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr ., coach DeMeco Ryans told reporters. The Texans sent 2027 second- and sixth-round draft picks to the Cardinals for Harrison and a 2027 seventh-round selection, sources told ESPN's Adam Schefter and NFL Network's Ian Rapoport. Harrison reunites with his former Ohio State QB C.J. Stroud in Houston.

 Oct. 7 
 

 Eagles trade C Jurgens to Ravens 
 Eagles get:  2027 fifth-round pick, 2028 second-round pick 
 Ravens get: C  Cam Jurgens , 2027 seventh-round pick

 The Eagles are trading two-time Pro Bowl center Jurgens and a 2027 seventh-round pick to the Ravens in exchange for a 2027 fifth-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick, sources told ESPN's Adam Schefter on Wednesday.

 The Eagles had moved Jurgens to left guard after Landon Dickerson was placed on injured reserve because of a knee injury. Jurgens self-reported concussion symptoms Monday morning, was evaluated and is now in the concussion protocol, a source told NFL Network's Mike Garafolo on Monday.

 
 Walder: Grading the deal from both sides 
 
 

 Sept. 30 
 

 Steelers trade CB Porter to Cowboys 
 Steelers get : 2027 sixth-round pick, 2028 second-round pick

 The Steelers are trading Porter to the Cowboys for a 2027 sixth-round pick and a 2028 second-round selection, sources confirmed to NFL Network's Cameron Wolfe and ESPN's Todd Archer. 

 The trade marks the end of a monthslong saga that stretched throughout the Steelers' offseason as Porter, one of the team's 2023 second-round picks, awaited an extension and was sidelined with a back injury.

 Vikings trade QB McCarthy to Giants

 The Giants traded for Vikings quarterback McCarthy on Monday, sending a 2027 fifth-round draft pick to Minnesota for the 2024 first-round pick. McCarthy, taken by the Vikings with the No. 10 pick, was the third-string quarterback in Minnesota behind starter Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz .

 Giants coach John Harbaugh said after their Week 3 victory over the Titans that Jameis Winston would remain the Giants' starter even if the team added another quarterback. He reiterated that Monday after the trade for McCarthy.

title: Why Jeremiah Smith is a generational NFL draft receiver prospect for 2027
summary: Smith could be the first wideout to be selected No. 1 in the draft in 31 years. What makes him so special? Who are his comps? Which NFL teams could pick him?
full_text:
For the past 30 years, the No. 1 pick of the NFL draft has been exclusively populated by three positions -- quarterback, edge rusher and offensive tackle. But Ohio State wide receiver  Jeremiah Smith  could be primed to break into that prime spot.

 The 6-foot-4, 222-pound junior has dominated since joining the Buckeyes as a freshman in 2024 and is having his best season yet in 2026. Smith has used his combination of size, top-level speed and sure hands to haul in 52 passes (tied for 10th best in the FBS) for 984 receiving yards (second in the FBS) and 12 touchdowns (also second) through seven games this season. As the No. 2-ranked Buckeyes get set to play at USC on Saturday ( 7:30 p.m. ET, NBC ), we had NFL draft analyst Jordan Reid and senior college football writer Jake Trotter canvas their sources to talk all things Smith and his next-level projection.

 Is Smith the best prospect of Ohio State's current pipeline of first-round receivers? How does he compare to the best receiver prospects overall of the past quarter century? What does he do best, and where could he still get even better? Will he be the first receiver since 1996 to go No. 1, and which teams could fit best? Reid and Trotter size up the talented receiver roughly six months out from the draft.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Why Smith is special | Best OSU WR ever? 
 Best WR prospect since ...? | Top play to watch 
 Things to work on | How to defend him 
 Three NFL team fits 

 
 

 What makes Smith so special to watch on tape? 
 Smith's unique combination of size, speed and power is what sets him apart. Most bigger receivers sacrifice downfield speed or have less change-of-direction ability, but Smith is the complete package. He moves like a smaller receiver but still shows the power that would be expected of a player his size. And he can make plays downfield, averaging 18.9 yards per catch, 15th in the nation this season.

 

 He is a quarterback's best friend, capable of making tough catches even when it looks like he's covered. Simply put, if the ball is in Smith's vicinity, he's going to figure out how to come down with it. His 15 contested catches are tied for second in the country. And he has only one drop this season -- and only six over his three-year career.

 Smith has dominated since arriving in Columbus as a true freshman in 2024, immediately taking a starring role despite having to share a receiver room with future first-round receivers such as Emeka Egbuka (No. 19 pick, 2025) and Carnell Tate (No. 4, 2026). But Smith led the Buckeyes with 76 receptions for 1,315 receiving yards and 15 touchdowns in 2024. And he has somehow gotten even better since.

 

 Smith entered the 2026 season as my No. 1-ranked overall player , and I don't see why that would change between now and the first night of the draft, barring injury. Double-teams, triple-teams ... it doesn't matter what coverage a defense throws at him. Smith continues to have a consistent impact every week. -- Reid 

 
 Where does Smith rank in Ohio State's recent run of elite-level wide receivers? 
 The Buckeyes have produced six first-round wide receivers over the past six NFL drafts: Chris Olave (2021), Garrett Wilson (2021), Jaxon Smith-Njigba (2023), Marvin Harrison Jr . (2024), Egbuka and Tate. But Smith-Njigba and Wilson both told ESPN they believe Smith is No. 1.

 "I think he's the best receiver we've seen at that level, with all his ability and his talent," Wilson said. "He's been league-ready since Year 1. ... He's unbelievable."

 Smith has broken Ohio State's career records for receptions, receiving yards and receiving touchdowns. He could bolster his case even further by winning the Biletnikoff Award and becoming the first wide receiver since Alabama's DeVonta Smith in 2020 to capture the Heisman Trophy. Smith is currently the Heisman front-runner at plus-122, according to DraftKings .

 "Having those accolades would definitely be the cherry on top," said Smith-Njigba, the reigning NFL Offensive Player of the Year. "For him to already break these records speaks volumes. Numbers never lie, so I would have to put him at the top of the mountain."

 Ohio State coach Ryan Day said Smith's mindset and discipline separate him from other gifted players.

 "He's won the genetic lottery -- we know that," Day said. "But the easy thing to do when you're talented is be undisciplined and unskilled and just lean on your talent. Jeremiah's not done that. And I'd love to say that he came in and we sort of developed that part of him. But he had that mindset when he walked in." -- Trotter 

 

 

 
 Smith is the best overall wide receiver prospect since ...? 
 Smith isn't quite in Calvin Johnson territory, but I believe he should at least be mentioned in the same breath as Megatron (No. 2 pick in 2007) and some of the other top receiver prospects this century -- like Larry Fitzgerald (No. 3 in 2004), Julio Jones (No. 6 in 2011) and Andre Johnson (No. 3 in 2003). Due to Smith's talent and the current lack of a consensus QB1 in this draft, he has a strong argument to top all of them and be the first receiver selected with the No. 1 pick since the New York Jets took Keyshawn Johnson to begin the draft in 1996.

 "He was dominant from the moment he touched the field like Larry [Fitzgerald]," an NFC assistant general manager said of Smith. "He's like a perfect football blend of Julio Jones, Andre Johnson and Terrell Owens."

 Jones and Johnson have been the two most popular comparisons to Smith from scouts I've talked to over the past few months. Smith has the powerful strides and ability to glide past defenders like Johnson, but he also shows the run-after-catch ability that Jones consistently showed throughout his career. I give very few All-Pro grades when scouting prospects. But I've already given Smith one. In fact, he's my highest-graded player at any position since Myles Garrett in 2017.

 

 It's rare to see a player be dominant right away in college and continue to improve, but Smith has accomplished that. So I expect him to do the same thing when he arrives in the NFL -- make an early impact as a premier talent and continue to build on that ability. -- Reid 

 
 What is one play that every scout will be watching to show Smith's incredible ceiling? 
 Smith has delivered plenty of spectacular highlights during his Ohio State career, but one NFL front office executive told ESPN that Smith's overall performance against Penn State last season offered perhaps the best glimpse of his extraordinary potential.

 "To me, that was the game where you saw everything," the executive said. "Short passes. Running around from the slot. Playing outside. With these big guys sometimes, you wonder, how much can they do? He literally did everything."

 Smith finished with six receptions for 123 yards and two touchdowns in that game. Four of those catches came from the slot, where he has lined up far more frequently in 2026 (50 routes in seven games) than his previous two seasons.

 "He's a true three-level threat," another NFL front office executive said. "And he makes crazy plays down the field."

 Ohio State quarterback  Julian Sayin  also singled out the Penn State game -- specifically a 57-yard reception in the third quarter. "They were double-teaming him and he ran a fade, and I threw back-shoulder," Sayin recalled, "and he made the catch -- it was pretty sick."

 

 

 Smith capped the performance with a one-handed, 11-yard touchdown catch off a tipped pass, helping the Buckeyes roll to a 38-14 victory. -- Trotter 

 
 What does Smith need to work on to truly become a generational player? 
 There aren't a lot of actual weaknesses in Smith's game, but for the sake of this exercise, I'd like to see improvement in Smith's change-of-direction skills on short and intermediate routes. He can drift on some routes in which he has to work back to the QB. Being more crisp when changing directions and avoiding taking extra steps up the field is one of the…

title: When will the Raiders make Fernando Mendoza the starting QB?
summary: Making the case for and against the Raiders switching to Fernando Mendoza as QB1.
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev. --  Fernando Mendoza 's time is coming. Just not yet.

 Las Vegas Raiders coach Klint Kubiak said Monday there's no quarterback controversy in Las Vegas, as Kirk Cousins remains QB1 amid a four-game losing streak.

 Kubiak's support for Cousins comes as no surprise. Cousins has been far from the Raiders' issues during this dreadful stretch. He can't help that the run game is nonexistent, the defense has allowed 35.8 points per game since Week 4, and the offensive line's production has taken a step back. On top of that, Cousins has played at a high level, ranking first in touchdown passes (16), despite the limitations he's dealt with on offense.

 It's the right decision to stick with Cousins. But the clock on Cousins' time as a starter is ticking. Kubiak said part of the reason the Raiders signed Cousins was that the veteran signal-caller went 4-0 in his final four starts with the Atlanta Falcons last season. Simply put, winning matters.

 Right now, he is doing the opposite in spite of playing surprisingly well. If the Raiders don't start racking up wins, starting on Sunday against the New York Jets ( 1 p.m. EST, Fox ), they might have no choice but to evaluate the future by starting Mendoza.

 "There's so much [that goes into] playing quarterback at a high level in this league, and [Cousins] displays so many of those attributes," Kubiak said. "And right now the highest level is winning football games and that ultimately falls on myself and the quarterback. So those are the things that we got to improve on."

 

 Cousins has been everything the Raiders have asked for since he signed with the organization in the offseason. Among qualified passers, Cousins is third in passing yards (1,877), fourth in passing yards per game (269), 12th in passer rating (97.4), 17th in completion rate (62.6%) and tied for eighth in EPA per dropback (0.11).

 Through Cousins' play, the Raiders have been a modest offense. They rank sixth in points per game (26.1) and 14th in total yards per game (343.7). Even in losses to the Kansas City Chiefs and Buffalo Bills , when the Raiders went toe-to-toe with a pair of Super Bowl contenders, Cousins was a big reason why they had a fighting chance down the stretch. He threw for 300-plus yards in both games.

 More importantly, Cousins has a firm understanding of Kubiak's offense, and that knowledge has been valuable for the rest of the team. Cousins has been able to put players in the right positions and make necessary adjustments at the line of scrimmage.

 "When you have that experience in the NFL, that's big time," tight end Michael Mayer said. "Personally for me, being able to talk with him out there [about] how he sees this, how he sees that, where he wants me, that's huge.

 "You want to be able to have that with your quarterback. If you don't, you're not always going to be on the same page."

 

 Mayer added that Cousins' veteran leadership and ability to stay even-keeled in any situation have been beneficial. He said Cousins "calms everybody down."

 However, Cousins' performance hasn't translated into wins, and the blueprint to stop him is out. The Los Angeles Rams used it to perfection in the first half of last week's 35-21 loss . Los Angeles pressured early and often. In the first half, the Rams blitzed Cousins on 40.9% of his dropbacks and recorded 10 pressures.

 Cousins was sacked twice and pressured 19 times during that game, the most this season. He faced Cover 0 on four dropbacks, completing just one pass -- a 15-yard touchdown to running back Ashton Jeanty in the fourth quarter.

 The New England Patriots followed a similar script in Week 5. Cousins was pressured on 48.4% of his dropbacks -- the highest rate of the season -- and was sacked three times.

 

 This is where the Mendoza aspect factors in. With teams expected to continue pressuring Cousins at a high rate, taking advantage of his lack of mobility, Mendoza can at least extend plays with his legs if needed. Also, Mendoza has a stronger arm and has the potential to make downfield throws on a consistent basis.

 The Raiders have been pleased with Mendoza's development behind the scenes. Quarterback coach Mike Sullivan said Mendoza has improved his command of the offense and communication at the line of scrimmage.

 When Mendoza made his debut during the Raiders' final possession against New England, Sullivan noticed the rookie looked more relaxed in the pocket compared to the preseason. Mendoza completed 6 of 8 passes for 48 yards and faced heavy pressure during his short time on the field. He was blitzed on 22.2% of his dropbacks.

 "He just seemed a lot smoother, relaxed, and he trusted his training," Sullivan said. "He handled it well, and it was an important part of his development."

 Mendoza has made strides, but that doesn't necessarily mean the Raiders should act hastily and start him, hoping he could help them climb out of the hole they put themselves in. Replacing Cousins with Mendoza wouldn't fix the other issues on the team that have been problematic during their losing streak.

 

 Mendoza will have to play with an insufficient run game. Las Vegas is 31st in rushing yards per game (74.7) and rushing first downs (28). The Raiders' offensive line has struggled to create open lanes for Jeanty and rookie running back Mike Washington Jr . Las Vegas has averaged 1.17 rushing yards before first contact.

 While the Raiders have struggled to run the ball, the defense has gotten run over in recent weeks. Since Week 4, Las Vegas has allowed 164 rushing yards per game. The Rams rushed for 199 yards last week.

 When factoring in the Raiders' inability to run the ball consistently and stop opponents' rushing attack, they are unable to be balanced on offense since they have been frequently playing from behind.

 That's something a quarterback change won't fix.

 "We're not going to run the ball until we stop the run. Until you make the game competitive. You can't be in the fourth quarter chasing points and expect to be a good run team," Kubiak said. "...We got to be more of a well-rounded offensive football club."

 Mendoza will eventually play, said Kubiak. The Raiders have a plan for Mendoza, but they do not have a timeline for when to turn to the reigning Heisman Trophy winner.

 At 3-4, Las Vegas is still in the hunt with Cousins under center, and a victory against the Jets would put the team back at .500. That's why the Raiders are not rushing to play Mendoza. An honest conversation must be had if Las Vegas loses to New York, but the best-case scenario is Mendoza starting after the bye week.

 By that time, the Raiders would have gone through a tough stretch and have a clearer picture of where they stand from a competitive standpoint. If they ultimately find themselves out of playoff contention, it would make more sense to play Mendoza, especially with a favorable schedule at the back end of the season. Three of the final five games are at home. Plus, they face the Los Angeles Chargers , Tennessee Titans and Arizona Cardinals , who currently have a combined 3-17 record.

 

 It's smart to stick with Cousins. He hasn't done anything that should warrant an immediate change at starting quarterback.

 Still, the Raiders are a rebuilding team and need to have the future in mind. If they cannot overcome their losing streak, they will need to consider making a change. Not because of Cousins' abilities, but because they need to look at Mendoza -- the future face of the franchise.

 But Las Vegas is not at that point.

 "We're prioritizing winning the next game," Kubiak said. "That's the most important thing to us, and we're developing [Mendoza] along the way, and that has not changed. That's been the plan all along."

title: Michael Vick's iconic MNF game is now in the ESPN Fantasy Football Hall of Fame
summary: Michael Vick scored 49.32 fantasy points in a Hall of Fame-worthy Monday Night Football performance in 2010
full_text:
Fantasy football is all about fun, competition and camaraderie, but it's also another way to appreciate the best of the best in the NFL. For more than three decades, ESPN Fantasy has been here with you, celebrating peak performers and magical moments.

 Presenting the ESPN Fantasy Football Hall of Fame   , which honors the best players and acknowledges the most memorable moments since the advent of our game in 1995, the first year that fantasy football was available on ESPN.com. 

 Take me to the ESPN Fantasy Football Hall of Fame 

 Class of 2026 Week 8 Inductee: Michael Vick's Monday Night Football Game 
 Nov. 15, 2010 (Week 10) 
 49.32 fantasy points 
 333 passing yards, 4 passing TDs; 80 rushing yards, 2 rushing TDs 

 After leaving the Eagles' Week 4 game against the Redskins early due to injury, Vick delivered a historic performance in the rematch on "Monday Night Football". He completed an 88-yard touchdown to DeSean Jackson on the first play from scrimmage, leading the Eagles to a 31-point advantage at halftime, and finished the 59-28 victory as the only player in NFL history with at least 300 passing yards, 50 rushing yards, four touchdown passes and two rushing touchdowns in a game. Vick's 49.32 fantasy points set a then-record for quarterbacks, and he'd finish the 2010 season with a position-best 310.32 points.

 Vick will be inducted Sunday during " Fantasy Focus Countdown " (10 a.m. ET on ESPNEWS, 11:30 on ESPN2). Tune in each week through Week 16 as we reveal all 18 members of the inaugural class of the ESPN Fantasy Football Hall of Fame.
